Every composition is YbBa2-xSrxCu3O7 and the paper is on structure and superconductivity in LnBa2-xSrxCu3O7. This is the 123 cuprate with ytterbium in place of yttrium -- the YBa2Cu3O7 structure, orthorhombic Pmmm, with CuO2 planes, a CuO chain layer and the rare earth between the planes -- and the whole LnBa2Cu3O7 series is isostructural, which is why substituting the rare earth is a standard experiment. The taxonomy entry is named for YBCO and covers it. [ref 2] does not return the 123 phase with ICSD support: its best-attested entries are BaYb2CuO5 Pnma mp-6323 and Ba4Yb(CuO3)3 Pm-3n mp-653337, which are the green-phase and related impurity compounds of this chemistry rather than the superconductor, and the one 123 entry it does give, Ba2YbCu3O7 Pmmm mp-1214570 at hull 0.040, carries no ICSD reference. The composition and the paper title decide this, not the reference ranking; that is the precedence the project sets and this host is a clean example of why.

dopant_roles.site: the barium site between the CuO2 plane and the CuO chain layer
dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions running from Sr0.1 to Sr0.3 of two barium atoms, which is five to fifteen per cent of that site -- alloying rather than dilute doping, and the variable named in the paper title. Strontium is isovalent with barium and smaller, so this is chemical pressure: it contracts the lattice without changing the carrier count, which is a way of separating the structural and doping contributions to the transition temperature. The oxygen content stays at seven throughout, confirming that the carrier count is not what is being varied.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [47], ICSD-backed references for this host report [62, 65, 223]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All five samples are Ba8Cu12.8Zn11.2P28.8 from a paper whose title is itself the warning -- breaking the tetra-coordinated framework rule: new clathrate Ba8M24P28. The compound is unambiguously a clathrate: eight barium guests in cages built from a covalent framework of copper, zinc and phosphorus, which is the structural definition and the reason it was made. What does not fit is the arithmetic of type I. An ideal type-I framework has 46 atoms enclosing 8 guests, and this one has 52.8 -- the extra framework atoms are exactly the rule the title says is broken, since a tetrahedral framework cannot accommodate them and some of the phosphorus must be three-coordinate instead. So clathrate_i is assigned as the nearest and most likely relative, at medium confidence, with the discrepancy recorded rather than smoothed over: stage 2 should not force these compositions into a 46-atom type-I cell, and the paper is needed to establish the actual framework. Neither reference block returns anything for this chemistry.

dopant_roles.site: the transition-metal sites of the covalent framework
dopant_roles.basis: Zn11.2 against Cu12.8 -- these are not dopant and host but two constituents sharing the framework metal sites in nearly equal amounts. In a clathrate the framework composition is what sets the electron count and therefore whether the compound is a semiconductor at all, so the Cu/Zn ratio is the design variable, in the same way the Ga/Ge ratio is in Ba8Ga16Ge30. Recorded as framework_substitution for that reason and not as alloying or doping; the level is meaningless as a doping figure.

basis: The curator composition details settle this host outright. The parsed strings look like one seven-element phase, but the paper writes each sample as (La0.5Ba0.5Co1/3Mn1/3Fe1/3O3)0.6(BaZr1-zYzO3)0.4 -- a two-phase composite cathode for a protonic ceramic fuel cell, sixty per cent of a mixed-conducting cobaltite perovskite and forty per cent of an yttrium-doped barium zirconate proton conductor. Both constituents are ABO3 perovskites, which is why a single prototype is correct here and the host is not flagged mixed: the composite is two perovskites, not two structures. That also explains the 297-1073 K window and the rod-shaped samples, which are fuel-cell electrode geometry rather than thermoelectric specimens. composite_multiphase is recorded as an alternative because the two-phase nature is real and stage 2 will need to resolve two separate structures for one composition. Neither reference block returns anything, which is expected for a composite that exists only as a mixture.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site of the barium zirconate constituent
dopant_roles.basis: The curator detail gives BaZr1-zYzO3 with z from 0 to 0.20 across the five samples, so yttrium sits on the zirconium site of the second phase only, not on any site of the cobaltite. Trivalent yttrium replacing tetravalent zirconium creates oxygen vacancies, and those vacancies are what hydrate to carry protons -- this substitution is the entire function of that constituent, and z is the variable the paper sweeps. The parsed fraction of 0.02 to 0.08 for the whole formula understates it badly; on its own site it reaches a fifth.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site of the cobaltite constituent, shared equally with Fe and Co
dopant_roles.basis: Fixed at one third of the B site of the first phase in every sample, alongside iron and cobalt at one third each. Not a dopant in any sense -- it is a third of a deliberately equimolar three-metal B site, and it appears under the 5 at.% cut only because the cut is taken over a composite formula with two perovskites in it. Stage 3 should compute no level.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site of the cobaltite constituent, shared equally with Mn and Co
dopant_roles.basis: One third of the B site of the first phase, on the same footing as the manganese and cobalt. Same treatment.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site of the cobaltite constituent, shared equally with Mn and Fe
dopant_roles.basis: One third of the B site of the first phase. It is the cobalt that makes this constituent a mixed ionic and electronic conductor and hence a cathode, so it is a defining component rather than an additive.

basis: Two compositions with the same cation ratio and different structures, which is the case the project keeps warning about. NdBaMn2O6 with four samples is the A-site ordered double perovskite -- neodymium and barium in alternating layers along one axis rather than at random, tetragonal P4/mmm -- and the first paper is on the physical properties and crystal structure of a double perovskite. Nd0.5Ba0.5MnO3 with one sample is the same stoichiometry with the A site disordered, and the third paper says so in its title: A-site randomness effect on structural and physical properties. The two are separate prototypes and the host must be split, but the composition strings alone almost hide it, since the only signal is which of two equivalent formulas the curator transcribed. [ref 2] supports the ordered phase -- BaNdMn2O6 P4/mmm (123) mp-25004 with 2 ICSD references -- and its top-ranked entry, BaNd2Mn2O7 I4/mmm mp-18861 with 4 references, is not this compound at all but the n=2 Ruddlesden-Popper phase of the same chemistry; that ranking should not be followed here. Confidence is medium because the split rests on reading the formula convention rather than on any measurement.

Two unrelated titanate families in one host. Nd1-xBaxTiO3 at x of 0.3, 0.6 and 0.7 is a simple ABO3 perovskite with neodymium and barium sharing the A site, and the first paper is on the band-filling dependence of the electrical transport of Nd1-xAxTiO3 -- the point being that mixing a trivalent and a divalent A cation sets the titanium valence between 3+ and 4+, which is a band-filling knob rather than a structural one. Ba6Nd8Ti18O54 with two samples is something else entirely, and the second paper names it: a tungsten bronze. That structure is a tetragonal framework of corner-sharing TiO6 octahedra enclosing pentagonal and tetragonal tunnels, with the large cations distributed among the tunnels, and it is a different prototype rather than a distorted perovskite. The host is split three samples to two and the perovskite is the primary on that count. [ref 2] returns neither family: BaNd2Ti3O10 Cmcm mp-6622 with 5 ICSD references is the n=3 Ruddlesden-Popper phase of this chemistry, a third structure that nothing here was made at, and following the reference ranking would have mislabelled both compositions.

All five samples are Ba2TiSi2O8 single crystals cut along different directions, from a paper on the thermal and piezoelectric properties of fresnoite -- the compound and the structure type have the same name and the taxonomy carries the entry. [ref 1], which takes precedence, gives Ba2Ti(SiO4)2 P4bm (100) mp-6081 at hull 0.000 with 8 ICSD references: the right composition, the right space group for fresnoite and ICSD-backed, which is as clean as an assignment in this project gets. The structure is a layered tetragonal one built from Si2O7 groups and unusually five-coordinate TiO5 square pyramids, and the polar P4bm setting is why it is piezoelectric and why the samples are oriented crystals rather than pellets. The other reference entries, BaTi(SiO3)3 in P-6c2 and P31c, are a different compound of the same three elements and were not made here.

Four of the five samples are BaZrO3 and [ref 1] gives BaZrO3 Pm-3m (221) mp-3834 at hull 0.000 with 8 ICSD references. BaZrO3 is the textbook cubic perovskite -- its tolerance factor is close to one, so unlike most perovskites it stays undistorted to the lowest temperatures and has no octahedral tilting sequence to cross. The third paper, on zirconates as thermal barrier coatings, explains the 276-1295 K window: this is measured for low thermal conductivity and refractoriness rather than as a thermoelectric. The first two paper titles are about barium molybdate and strontium ruthenium oxide, so they cover this composition only as part of a perovskite survey. [ref 2] also lists BaZrO3 in I4/mcm mp-1019544 with 1 ICSD reference, a tilted tetragonal setting; that is not what forms at ambient conditions in this composition and it is not recorded as a phase.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site
dopant_roles.basis: BaZr0.8Co0.2O3 in one sample -- a fifth of the B site, so alloying rather than dilute doping. Cobalt is smaller than zirconium and takes a lower oxidation state, so it brings oxygen vacancies with it and turns an insulating, closed-shell perovskite into a mixed conductor. It is the only sample in the host that is doped at all.

basis: Both compositions are BaxPd4SnySb12-y and the paper title is a direct statement of the structure -- BaxPd4SnySb12-y: a new palladium-containing skutterudite. The framework matches the archetype exactly: four metal atoms to twelve pnictogen atoms per formula unit, which is the M4X12 corner-sharing octahedral framework with X4 rings, and barium at close to full occupancy in the icosahedral void makes it filled rather than binary. What is unusual is the framework chemistry -- palladium in place of cobalt, with tin and antimony sharing the pnictogen sites -- and that is precisely because palladium contributes a different electron count, so the Sn/Sb ratio has to compensate to keep the framework balanced. Neither reference block returns anything, which is expected for a compound this paper introduces, and no mp_id is recorded.

All three compositions are members of the Bi-Sr-Ca-Co-O misfit series -- Bi2SrCaCo2O8, Bi2Sr1.6Ca1.4Co2O9 and Bi1.8Pb0.2Sr2Ca2Co3O12 -- and the third paper is on textured Bi-based cobaltite thermoelectrics. These are incommensurate composites: CdI2-type CoO2 sheets carrying the transport, interleaved with rocksalt-like Bi-Sr-Ca-O blocks, with the two subsystems having different in-plane periodicities that do not share a common cell. That is why the formulas look irregular and why the oxygen count drifts between 8, 9 and 12 for what is structurally one family. Neither reference block returns anything, which is the expected outcome rather than a gap in coverage -- a misfit composite has no single Materials Project entry, and the taxonomy already flags this prototype as needing two subsystems resolved separately in stage 2. The samples include a single crystal and textured bulk, both consistent with a strongly anisotropic layered structure.

dopant_roles.site: the bismuth site of the rocksalt block
dopant_roles.basis: Bi1.8Pb0.2Sr2Ca2Co3O12 in one composition -- a tenth of the bismuth site. Lead is divalent against trivalent bismuth, so it dopes holes into the CoO2 sheets from the block layer, and in the Bi-based layered oxides it is also the standard additive for stabilising the higher-order members during synthesis. Both effects are structural rather than incidental, so it is a genuine substituent and not a contaminant.

basis: Every composition is Bi1.7Pb3-xNdxSr2Ca3Cu4O12 from a paper on thermoelectric power and thermal conduction in Nd-substituted Bi-Pb-Sr-Ca-Cu-O. Four copper atoms with three calcium layers between them is the four-CuO2-layer member of the BSCCO series, the 2234 phase, which is the natural extension of the 2212 and 2223 compounds the taxonomy entry is built around: a rocksalt-like Bi2O2 double layer alternating with a block of CuO2 planes separated by calcium. The lead content is high here even for this family, which is normal -- lead substitution for bismuth is what makes the higher-layer members form at all, and without it the 2223 and 2234 phases are very difficult to stabilise. The BiO layers in this family are themselves incommensurately modulated, so like the cobaltite above this is a structure that no single Materials Project entry captures; neither reference block returns anything and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.site: written inside the lead stoichiometry, so nominally the Bi-Pb site of the rocksalt block
dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions from Nd0.025 to Nd0.1, against Pb3, and the paper title calls it Nd substitution. The composition string puts neodymium in the lead position and the site is taken from there, at medium confidence: in the cuprates a trivalent rare earth is also a very common substituent on the calcium site between the CuO2 planes, and the two readings differ in whether the carriers are removed from the charge reservoir or from the planes themselves. Either way it is an electron donor into an overdoped p-type cuprate, which is the point of the series, but only the paper can say which site.

basis: All four compositions are ZrCoBi1-x-ySbxSny and the paper title is explicit -- discovery of ZrCoBi based half Heuslers with high thermoelectric conversion efficiency. XYZ at 1:1:1 with an 18-electron count is the half Heusler structure, F-43m, three interpenetrating face-centred lattices with one of the four sublattices empty, and ZrCoBi is the heavy bismuth member of the family that paper introduced as a high-temperature p-type material. Neither reference block returns anything for this four-element host, but the composition and the title settle it without help. The 298-976 K window is the intended operating range and nothing structural happens inside it -- half Heuslers are refractory and stable, which is much of their appeal.

dopant_roles.site: the Z site of the half Heusler cell
dopant_roles.basis: Sb0.05, Sb0.10 and Sb0.15 against Bi in three of the four compositions, written inside the same stoichiometry. Antimony and bismuth are both group 15 and both sit on the Z site, so this adds no carriers; what it does is introduce mass and strain disorder on that sublattice, which scatters phonons and lowers the lattice thermal conductivity. That is the standard alloying strategy in half Heuslers and it is a band and phonon engineering variable, not a doping level.

basis: The papers name both structures in one breath -- physical properties of rare-earth-based Heusler phases REPdZ and REPd2Z -- and the compositions follow the same split. DyPdBi with four samples is the 1:1:1 half Heusler, F-43m, and [ref 2] gives DyBiPd F-43m (216) mp-1009543 at hull 0.000, the right structure in the right space group. DyPd2Bi with one sample is the 1:2:1 full Heusler, the same lattice with the fourth sublattice filled, Fm-3m. They are related but distinct prototypes -- the half Heusler is a semiconductor or semimetal at the right electron count while the full Heusler is metallic -- so the host is flagged mixed and split four samples to one. The rare-earth bismuth half Heuslers are studied as candidate topological semimetals, which is why a 10-300 K transport measurement exists.

Both compositions are Bi13S18I2, from a paper on manipulating band structure through reconstruction of binary metal sulfides. That is not BiSI and the distinction has to be made explicitly, because [ref 2] ranks BiSI Pnma (62) mp-23514 first with 2 ICSD references and following it would name the wrong compound. Bi13S18I2 is a large-cell hexagonal phase built from bismuth sulfide columns with iodide filling the channels between them -- a quasi-one-dimensional structure quite unlike the Pnma chain compound BiSI -- and the reference block does carry something closer to it, Bi19(S9I)3 R3 (146) mp-1227984 at hull 0.011, which is the same chemistry at a nearly identical Bi:S:I ratio with no ICSD backing. bi_chalcogenide_complex is the taxonomy entry for exactly this situation: large-cell bismuth chalcogenides where each composition is effectively its own structure and stage 2 has to resolve them individually. Confidence is medium because the entry is a family rather than a type, and because the reference block and the composition point at different compounds.

dopant_roles.site: the halide channel site
dopant_roles.basis: Two samples written (Bi13S18I2)0.98(BiCl3)0.02, so chlorine enters as bismuth trichloride at two per cent. Chlorine and iodine are both halogens and the channel site is where a halide belongs, so the substitution adds no carriers by itself -- what it does is shrink that site substantially, since chloride is much the smaller ion, which is the band-structure reconstruction the title refers to. Recorded at medium confidence because a halide landing on a sulfur site instead would be a donor rather than an isoelectronic substituent, and at two per cent both are possible.

basis: All three compositions are Y2-xBixIr2O7 and the paper is on the spin-glass-like transition and Hall resistivity of that series. A2B2O7 with a rare earth on A and a tetravalent transition metal on B is the pyrochlore structure, Fd-3m: two interpenetrating networks, corner-sharing IrO6 octahedra and a separate Y2O tetrahedral array, both on corner-sharing tetrahedral lattices, which is the geometric frustration the magnetism in this family comes from. The iridate pyrochlores are studied for exactly that, and for the metal-insulator transition that moves with the A-site radius -- which is what substituting the larger bismuth for yttrium is doing across these three compositions. Neither reference block returns anything for the host and no mp_id is recorded. Bismuth is written on the A site in every composition at a third to three fifths of it, so it is an alloying variable rather than a dopant and is not listed separately.

All four compositions are ABO3 manganites with lanthanum and bismuth sharing the A site -- LaBiMn2O6.20 is La0.5Bi0.5MnO3 written over two formula units, and the others substitute on one site or the other. The papers are on ferromagnetic-insulating perovskite manganites and their substitution chemistry, and mixed-valence manganites are the classic perovskite family. Two of the compositions, LaBiMn1.5Co0.5O6.04 and La0.6Bi0.4Mn0.6Ni0.4O2.9, are close to the LaBiMnNiO6 and LaBiMnCoO6 double perovskites where the two B-site metals order alternately, which would be a different prototype, so double_perovskite is recorded as an alternative and confidence is medium. Bismuth on the A site is the point of this chemistry: its lone pair drives the ferroelectric distortion of BiMnO3 and makes these candidate multiferroics, so the A-site mixture is a structural variable and not a dilution. [ref 2] returns only computed La-Mn-Bi-O entries in Pm and Pmc2_1 at unrelated stoichiometries with no ICSD support, and no mp_id is recorded. The fourth composition is written La0.6Bi04Mn0.6Ni0.4O2.9, where Bi04 should be read as Bi0.4 for the A site to sum to one.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site
dopant_roles.basis: LaBiMn1.5Co0.5O6.04 -- a quarter of the B site, which is alloying rather than doping, and at that level the Mn and Co may order into a double perovskite rather than mix at random. The first paper is on enhancement of ferromagnetism by Co and Ni substitution, so this is a magnetic-exchange variable: Mn and Co on alternating sites give a ferromagnetic superexchange that Mn alone does not.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site
dopant_roles.basis: La0.6Bi0.4Mn0.6Ni0.4O2.9 -- two fifths of the B site, the nickel counterpart of the cobalt composition and from the same line of work. The Mn-Ni pair is the best-known ferromagnetic-insulating double perovskite combination, which is what makes the ordering question real here.

dopant_roles.site: the A site, shared with bismuth
dopant_roles.basis: La0.55Bi0.3K0.15MnO3 -- fifteen per cent of the A site. Potassium is monovalent against trivalent lanthanum, so each substitution oxidises two manganese ions, and in a manganite the Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio is what controls the double-exchange ferromagnetism and the conductivity together. A strong aliovalent acceptor rather than a size substituent, which is why it is recorded as substitutional while the B-site metals are alloying.

basis: Four compositions at or near MnBi4S7 and the lead paper is titled XBi4S7 with X = Mn and Fe, which names the family directly. [ref 2] gives MnBi4S7 C2/m (12) mp-1095372 at hull 0.010 with 1 ICSD reference -- the right composition and a monoclinic layered setting, consistent with slabs of NaCl-like bismuth sulfide stitched together by octahedral manganese. The taxonomy had no entry for it: mnsb2se4_type is the nearest, but its own discriminant fixes the M:pnictogen ratio at 1:2 while this is 1:4, a different member of the homologous construction with thicker slabs, so extending that entry would have contradicted its definition. mbi4s7_type is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl. The 300-772 K window and twenty curves make this one of the better-measured small hosts in the chunk.

dopant_roles.site: the chalcogen sites of the slab
dopant_roles.basis: MnBi4S6.51Se0.35, and the second paper is on the MnBi4S7-7xSe7x solid solution, so this composition is one point on a series that runs to the full selenide rather than a doped sulfide. Selenium and sulfur are both group 16 on the same sites, so no carriers are added; the substitution tunes the band gap and scatters phonons by mass contrast. Only five per cent of the chalcogen site here, at the dilute end of that axis, which is why it reads as a dopant candidate at all.

basis: Five compositions written MoBi2(Se1-xTex)5 from one paper on fibrous reticulate nanocrystalline material of that formula. The arithmetic is what decides this record and it is worth showing: MoBi2X5 is exactly Bi2X3 plus MoX2, so the most likely reading is not a ternary molybdenum bismuth chalcogenide -- no such line compound is established at this stoichiometry, and neither reference block returns anything -- but a two-phase product of tetradymite Bi2(Se,Te)3 with layered MoSe2 or MoTe2 alongside it. Tetradymite is the primary because Bi2X3 is three fifths of the formula and carries the transport, mos2_2h is the alternative for the molybdenum dichalcogenide, and composite_multiphase records that the sample may be neither phase cleanly. Confidence is low and the host is flagged mixed: this is an inference from stoichiometry about a nanostructured product, and the paper is the only thing that can say whether a genuine ternary formed. The 303-498 K window crosses nothing structural in either constituent.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the chalcogen sites, in both the bismuth chalcogenide and the molybdenum dichalcogenide constituents
solid_solution_axis.note: Selenium and tellurium are group 16 and share the chalcogen sublattice, so the axis is real, and the paper sweeps it deliberately from x of 0.2 to 0.8. No end member applies to the host: at the selenium-rich end the bismuth constituent is Bi2Se3 and at the tellurium-rich end it is Bi2Te3, which are the same prototype but different compounds with different gaps and carrier signs. If the two-phase reading is right, the axis applies to both constituents at once and they need not share the same x.

basis: All five samples are SrBi2Nb2O9 and [ref 2] gives SrNb2Bi2O9 Cmc2_1 (36) mp-23614 at hull 0.000 with 2 ICSD references. That is the m=2 Aurivillius phase: fluorite-like Bi2O2 sheets alternating with two-octahedra-thick perovskite SrNb2O7 blocks, and the polar Cmc2_1 setting -- usually written A2_1am in the ferroelectric literature -- is the room-temperature structure, which is why the paper is on the thermal conductivity of SrBi2Nb2O9 ferroelectric thin films. The taxonomy entry covers the family directly. Most of the samples are films, and while the chunk file flags films as a route to metastable polymorphs, the Aurivillius structure is the equilibrium one here and nothing suggests otherwise; the film geometry is because this material is used as a ferroelectric memory capacitor. The ferroelectric-to-paraelectric transition of SrBi2Nb2O9 is well above the 12-292 K window, so nothing is crossed.

Both compositions are Nd2-xBixRu2O7 and the paper title states the structure -- thermoelectric properties of Ln2-xBixRu2O7 pyrochlores. A2Ru2O7 is the pyrochlore Fd-3m, corner-sharing RuO6 octahedra with a separate A2O network threaded through them, and the ruthenate pyrochlores are measured for thermoelectric transport because the bismuth substitution drives them from insulating to metallic. [ref 2] disagrees and the disagreement should be read carefully rather than followed: it gives NdBiRu2O7 Imma (74) mp-1220214 and two rhombohedral R-3m entries, all at hull distances under 0.005 and none with any ICSD reference. Those are computed models in which neodymium and bismuth are ordered onto distinct A sites, which lowers the symmetry from Fd-3m by construction; the real material has them mixed at random on one site and is cubic. A computed ordering of a disordered sublattice is not evidence against the parent structure, and no mp_id from that block is recorded.

Both compositions are Yb2-xBixRu2O7 and they come from the same paper as the neodymium host above -- thermoelectric properties of Ln2-xBixRu2O7 pyrochlores, with Ln being Nd and Yb. The two hosts are one experiment: the same A2Ru2O7 pyrochlore in Fd-3m measured with a large and a small rare earth, since the A-site radius is what tunes the Ru-O-Ru angle and hence the bandwidth and the conductivity. Neither reference block returns anything for this host, so unlike the neodymium case there is no computed ordered model to argue with; the assignment rests on the composition and the paper title, which are unambiguous. The 300-999 K window is a high-temperature thermoelectric measurement and the pyrochlore structure is stable across it.

All five compositions are written (TlBiS2)y(PbS)z and the paper is on the thermoelectric properties of the TlBiS2-PbS alloys, so this host is a pseudobinary tie-line rather than a compound. Both ends are rocksalt-derived and that is what makes the line continuous: PbS is the plain rocksalt, and TlBiS2 is the same cation and anion array with thallium and bismuth ordered alternately into layers, which drops the symmetry to the rhombohedral alpha-NaFeO2 setting. Mixing them disorders that ordering, so the PbS-rich alloys are simple cubic rocksalt while the TlBiS2-rich ones retain the layered order. rocksalt is the primary because the compositions run from 0.2 to 0.9 of TlBiS2 with three of the five below the midpoint, and alpha_nafeo2_layered is the alternative for the thallium-rich end; the host is flagged mixed because where the ordering disappears along the line cannot be decided from the composition. [ref 2] returns only TlBiPbS3 Imm2 mp-1216860 at hull 0.042 with no ICSD reference, a computed ordered model of the one-to-one mixture, which does not settle the question either way.

Cr3C2 is the matrix of four of the five samples -- two of it alone and two as Cr3C2-SiC composites -- and [ref 2] gives Cr3C2 Pnma (62) mp-20937 at hull 0.000 with 9 ICSD references. That is the orthorhombic chromium carbide with carbon in trigonal prisms, and the taxonomy had no entry for it, so cr3c2_orthorhombic is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl; rocksalt_nitride_carbide would have been wrong, since chromium does not form a stable rocksalt carbide (MP lists CrC Fm-3m mp-579 at hull 0.256). The papers are on plasma-sprayed coatings and on carbide composites, so what was measured is mostly not single-phase: two compositions carry SiC at ten and nineteen per cent, and one is (Cr2AlC)32(Cr7C3)68, which is a MAX phase with a second chromium carbide rather than anything Cr3C2 at all. The host is flagged mixed for that reason and the two alternatives cover the composite character and the MAX phase respectively. [ref 2] ranks Cr23C6 Fm-3m with 11 ICSD references above Cr3C2; that is the carbide of the chromium-rich end of this binary and is not what any composition here was made at, so the ranking is not followed.

dopant_roles.basis: Present only as SiC in the two composite compositions, at ten and nineteen per cent by the composite formula, and the third paper is titled thermal conduction in Cr3C2/SiC composite. Silicon carbide is a discrete second phase added to raise the hardness and change the thermal conduction path; no silicon enters the carbide lattice. Stage 3 should compute no doping level.

Present only in (Cr2AlC)32(Cr7C3)68, where it belongs to the Cr2AlC MAX phase rather than to any Cr3C2. It is a constituent of a distinct compound in a two-phase mixture, not a substituent in this prototype, which is why the MAX phase entry is listed as an alternative for that composition.

basis: The compositions are Mn3GaC with small substitutions on either metal site and the papers are on the transport properties of Mn3-xMxGaC and Mn3Ga1-xZnxC. Mn3GaC is the antiperovskite: the perovskite arrangement with the cation and anion roles reversed, gallium at the corners, manganese on the faces and carbon in the octahedral centre surrounded by six manganese atoms. [ref 2] gives Mn3GaC Pm-3m (221) mp-21313 at hull 0.000 with 5 ICSD references, which matches the prototype directly. Mn3GaC has a well-known first-order transition near 160 to 250 K, inside the 80-543 K window, from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic with a discontinuous volume change; it is not recorded in phases because the structure stays cubic Pm-3m on both sides -- the cell jumps in size without changing symmetry or prototype -- but it is worth knowing about, since it is what all three substitution series here are tuning and it will show as a step in any transport curve across it.

dopant_roles.site: the corner site of the antiperovskite cell
dopant_roles.basis: Mn3Ga0.95Zn0.05C and Mn3Ga0.85Zn0.15C, with the second paper titled transport properties of Mn3Ga1-xZnxC. Zinc is written inside the gallium stoichiometry and sits on the corner site; it has one electron fewer than gallium, and since the magnetic transition temperature of this compound tracks the electron count and the cell volume, that substitution moves the transition, which is the experiment. At fifteen per cent of its site the upper composition is alloying rather than doping.

dopant_roles.site: the face-centre site, the one coordinating the carbon octahedron
dopant_roles.basis: Mn2.95Fe0.05GaC, matching the Mn3-xMxGaC series of the first paper. Iron replaces manganese in the magnetic sublattice itself, so unlike the zinc it changes the moment and the exchange directly rather than through the electron count.

dopant_roles.site: the face-centre site, the one coordinating the carbon octahedron
dopant_roles.basis: Mn2.95Cr0.05GaC, the chromium member of the same Mn3-xMxGaC series and made as the counterpart to the iron composition -- the paper title names M as Cr and Fe.

basis: Four of the five samples are conjugated polymers and the curator details name them: P3HT, poly(3-hexylthiophene), in three, and PBTTT in one, both doped and measured as films. These have no crystal structure in the sense the rest of this taxonomy uses -- they are semicrystalline, with ordered lamellae of pi-stacked backbones in an amorphous matrix, and the anisotropy the third paper reports comes from aligning those lamellae rather than from a lattice. The fifth sample is something quite different: CsC24(C2H4)1.4 is a caesium graphite intercalation compound, from the paper on thermoelectric properties of caesium-graphite intercalation compounds, in which caesium and ethylene sit between intact graphene sheets. That is a real layered crystal and belongs in graphite_layered, so the host is flagged mixed and split four to one. [ref 2] returns a list of unrelated metal-organic entries matched on C and H alone and supports nothing here; no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Sulfur is the heteroatom of the thiophene ring and therefore part of the repeat unit of both polymers -- one sulfur per monomer in P3HT, four per monomer in PBTTT. It is a constituent of the host molecule, not an additive, and it reads as a dopant candidate only because the 5 at.% cut is applied to a formula dominated by carbon and hydrogen. The role vocabulary has no term for a constituent of a molecular repeat unit, so this is recorded as unknown with the reason stated rather than forced into substitutional or alloying_component; the one thing that must not happen is stage 3 computing a doping level from it.

dopant_roles.site: between the polymer chains, as the metal of the counter-anion
dopant_roles.basis: (C42H62S4)(FeCl3)0.012 in the PBTTT sample, and the curator detail on the P3HT samples records doping by an iron salt as well. Iron trichloride is a charge-transfer p-dopant for conjugated polymers: it oxidises the backbone and the reduced chloride complex remains between the chains as a counter-ion. So iron is not on any lattice site and not bonded to the polymer -- it is an ionic guest in the amorphous space between chains, which is the closest the vocabulary comes at interstitial.

dopant_roles.site: between the polymer chains, as the counter-anion
dopant_roles.basis: The chlorine of the same FeCl3 dopant, present at the same level and in the same place. Recorded separately because the parser sees it as a separate element, but it is one dopant with the iron, not two.

dopant_roles.site: the galleries between graphene sheets
dopant_roles.basis: CsC24(C2H4)1.4 -- one caesium per 24 carbons, which is the stage-2 stoichiometry of a graphite intercalation compound. The graphene sheets stay intact and caesium enters the gallery between them, donating an electron to the pi system; the ethylene is co-intercalated alongside it. This is intercalation rather than substitution, and it applies only to the one sample that is not a polymer.

basis: All five samples are CH3NH3SnI3 and the paper is on charge transport in the tin-iodide perovskite CH3NH3SnI3. This is the hybrid organic-inorganic halide perovskite: a corner-sharing SnI6 octahedral framework with the methylammonium cation in the twelve-coordinate A site, the tin analogue of the more familiar lead compound. The prototype was proposed earlier in this project and is used here rather than proposed again. [ref 2] returns a list of tin-iodine-carbon-nitrogen entries at quite different stoichiometries with one ICSD reference each -- none is CH3NH3SnI3 -- so no mp_id is recorded. Worth noting for the measurement: this compound goes through octahedral tilting transitions inside the 11-298 K window, cubic to tetragonal near room temperature and a further one below about 110 K. They are not recorded in phases because tilting changes the space group without changing the prototype, in the same way it does for an inorganic perovskite, but a structure refined at 15 K and one refined at 290 K will not have the same symmetry.

The curator details name both materials outright. Four samples are PEDOT:PSS, the poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) and poly(styrenesulfonate) blend, and the fifth is polyaniline doped with p-toluenesulfonic acid, written C6H7N(C7H8SO3)0.5. Both are conducting polymers with no crystal structure in the lattice sense: PEDOT:PSS in particular is a colloidal blend of a conducting oligomer and an insulating polyelectrolyte, with conduction through percolating PEDOT-rich grains, so what a structural prototype can say about it is limited to that. organic_polymer is the entry for exactly this and the assignment is not in doubt even though the material is disordered. [ref 2] matches on C, H and O alone and returns metal-organic salts that have nothing to do with either polymer; no mp_id is recorded. The 101-320 K window fits thin-film and pellet transport on materials that would decompose well before the temperatures most of this dataset reaches.

dopant_roles.basis: Sulfur appears in both materials and in two distinct chemical roles, neither of them doping in the crystallographic sense. In PEDOT:PSS it is both the thiophene heteroatom of the conducting chain and the sulfonate group of the PSS counter-polymer, which is what holds the oxidised backbone in its doped state. In the polyaniline sample it is the sulfonate of the p-toluenesulfonic acid dopant, which plays the same counter-ion role. Recorded as unknown because the vocabulary has no term for a constituent of a molecular repeat unit, with the caution that a computed doping level would be meaningless.

Nitrogen appears only in the polyaniline sample, where it is the amine nitrogen of the backbone itself -- one per repeat unit, alternating between amine and imine as the polymer is doped. A constituent of the host molecule rather than an additive, and the same caution applies.

basis: Every composition is written (Mo)x(TiC)y and the paper is on the microstructure and thermal conductivity of Mo-TiC cermets, so this is a two-phase metal-ceramic composite by construction and not a compound. The two phases are body-centred cubic molybdenum and rocksalt titanium carbide, which have no mutual solubility worth speaking of, and the five samples simply walk the volume fraction from ten to seventy per cent TiC -- that sweep is the experiment, since the thermal conductivity of the cermet is what the paper is measuring against composition. composite_multiphase is the honest primary and rocksalt_nitride_carbide is the alternative covering the ceramic constituent, which is the one of the two that this taxonomy has an entry for. [ref 2] returns only TiMoC2 R-3m mp-1216711 at hull 0.045 with no ICSD reference, a computed ternary carbide that is not what a cermet is, and no mp_id is recorded.

All five samples are SmNiC2 and [ref 2] gives SmNiC2 Amm2 (38) mp-999144 at hull 0.000 with 2 ICSD references. That is the CeNiC2 structure: a noncentrosymmetric orthorhombic stacking of rare-earth layers with NiC2 units in which the carbon is present as a covalently bonded C2 dimer rather than as an interstitial atom. The taxonomy had no entry for the RNiC2 family, so cenic2_type is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl -- rocksalt_nitride_carbide would have been badly wrong, since the defining feature here is the carbon dimer and its ability to distort. That distortion is the subject of the paper, which is on magnon gap formation and the charge density wave effect on thermoelectric power: SmNiC2 has a CDW transition near 148 K, inside the 10-299 K window, and it is unusual in being destroyed rather than reinforced by the ferromagnetic ordering below it. Nothing is recorded in phases because a CDW superstructure is a modulation of this structure rather than a different prototype, but a low-temperature refinement would not find the ideal Amm2 cell.

The composition is CO2 and the first paper is on the low-temperature thermal conductivity of cryocrystals formed by linear molecules, so this is solid carbon dioxide measured as a molecular crystal -- dry ice, cubic Pa-3, with the linear molecules on a face-centred lattice and their axes along the body diagonals. The taxonomy carries the entry and [ref 2] confirms it: CO2 Pa-3 (205) mp-20066 at hull 0.000 with 6 ICSD references. The robust measured range of 10-119 K is exactly a cryocrystal measurement and sits well below the 195 K sublimation point. Two notes on the reference block and the second paper. The MP entry ranked second, CO in P2_13 at hull 0.665, is flagged AMBIGUOUS and is carbon monoxide, a different compound. And the second paper, on the magnetic and transport properties of chromium films, has no carbon dioxide in it; it has evidently been keyed to this host through a parsing route rather than its content, and the full span reaching 347 K comes from there rather than from any solid CO2.

All five samples are SiOC and the paper is on polymer-derived silicon oxycarbide ceramics. Polymer-derived SiOC has no crystal structure to assign: pyrolysing a siloxane precursor leaves an amorphous network of mixed SiOxC4-x tetrahedra with free carbon dispersed through it, and it stays amorphous up to temperatures well above the 303-872 K measured here. That is the point of the material -- the disorder is what gives it its very low thermal conductivity and its resistance to crystallisation -- so amorphous is the correct assignment rather than a fallback. [ref 2] returns computed Si-C-O entries at hull distances from 0.17 to 1.49, which is what a reference database does when asked for a structure that does not exist; none is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: The curator details say the two composite samples are SiOC containing 1 and 5 weight per cent hexagonal boron nitride, so boron is present only as h-BN platelets dispersed in the matrix. A discrete crystalline second phase in an amorphous host, not a dopant in a network that has no lattice sites to dope, and stage 3 should compute no level.
The nitrogen of the same h-BN additions, at the same levels and in the same platelets. One additive with the boron rather than two.

basis: All five samples are Ca2FeReO6 and the paper is on the narrow conduction bands of Ca2FeReO6 detected by thermopower. A2BB-prime-O6 with iron and rhenium alternating on the octahedral sites is the B-site ordered double perovskite, the family the taxonomy entry is built for, and [ref 2] gives Ca2FeReO6 P2_1/c (14) mp-31763 at hull 0.000 with 2 ICSD references. The monoclinic setting rather than a cubic one is expected: calcium is small enough to force octahedral tilting on top of the B-site ordering, and this compound is the tilted, insulating member of the series where Sr2FeReO6 is a half-metal. That difference is why it is measured at all. Worth recording for the measurement: Ca2FeReO6 has a first-order metal-insulator transition near 140 K, inside the 10-402 K window, which is accompanied by a jump in the monoclinic angle rather than a change of space group. It is not entered in phases because both sides are the same tilted double perovskite, but the transport curves will show it.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [87, 225], ICSD-backed references for this host report [14]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All four compositions are Sm1-xCaxFeO3 with x from 0.25 to 0.50, which is the GdFeO3-type orthorhombic perovskite -- SmFeO3 with calcium substituting samarium on the A site. Samarium is small enough to force a strongly tilted Pnma setting rather than a cubic one. The papers are on oxygen permeation through mixed-conducting Sm1-xCaxFeO3 membranes, so a perovskite is what was deliberately made, and the 295-1273 K window is a membrane measurement rather than a thermoelectric one. No reference entry is offered for this chemistry and no mp_id is recorded. One caution rather than a disagreement: at x = 0.5 and above about 1000 K these ferrites lose a large amount of oxygen, and heavily reduced A-site-substituted ferrites can order their vacancies into a brownmillerite-like arrangement. Every composition here is written ABO3 and nothing in the titles reports a vacancy-ordered phase, so the assignment stays perovskite, but the top of the measured window is where that would appear.

Both compositions are Sm0.5Ca0.25Sr0.25MnO3, which is the half-doped manganite Sm0.5Sr0.5MnO3 with a quarter of the strontium replaced by calcium. That is an orthorhombic Pnma perovskite; the papers say what the substitution is for, being on phase separation in Sm0.5Sr0.5MnO3 under changes of cation size and on a metamagnetic transition in a polycrystalline member, so calcium is there to lower the average A-site radius and widen the tolerance-factor mismatch. The 15-296 K window crosses the charge- and orbital-ordering and the metamagnetic transitions these materials are measured for, but those are electronic and magnetic orderings that produce a superstructure of the same tilted perovskite rather than a different prototype, so nothing is entered in phases. No reference entry is offered and no mp_id is recorded.

Every composition is written CaV1-xMoxO3 with x from 0.3 to 0.6, and the papers are on the structure, thermal stability and electrical properties of Ca(V0.5Mo0.5)O3 and on the effect of molybdenum concentration in CaV1-xMoxO3. That is the metallic orthorhombic perovskite CaVO3 with molybdenum entering the B site, and the compositions form a continuous series rather than clustering at one ratio, which is the signature of a disordered B site. Here I disagree with the reference: [ref 2] returns Ca2VMoO6 P2_1/c (14) mp-1227834 at hull 0.054 with no ICSD backing, a B-site-ordered double perovskite. Rock-salt ordering of V and Mo would need a large charge and size difference between them, and V4+ and Mo4+ in this series have neither, so I read the samples as the disordered solid solution and record perovskite with double_perovskite as the alternative. Confidence is medium because ordering at exactly x = 0.5 cannot be ruled out from composition alone, and no mp_id is taken.

The five compositions walk Ca1-xYxVO3 from x = 0.3 to x = 0.7 and the paper is on local-moment formation and the metal-nonmetal transition in Ca1-xYxVO3. Both end members are GdFeO3-type orthorhombic perovskites and the series is continuous, with yttrium substituting calcium on the A site and driving V4+ towards V3+. The metal-nonmetal transition the paper measures is a Mott transition, electronic rather than structural, so it is not entered in phases. Worth noting for the 18-298 K window: the yttrium-rich end approaches YVO3, which has a monoclinic distortion below roughly 200 K tied to orbital ordering. That is a change of space group within the perovskite prototype, in the manner of a distortion series, so it does not split the assignment, but a low-temperature refinement of the x = 0.7 sample would not find the ideal Pnma cell. No reference entry is offered and no mp_id is recorded.

The parent is CaZn2P2 and both papers name the family outright -- light-element-containing Zintl compounds, and the high Seebeck coefficient AMXP2 Zintl phases with A = Ca or Yb. CaZn2P2 is the CaAl2Si2 structure type: trigonal P-3m1 with a Zn2P2 anionic slab of corner-sharing tetrahedra and calcium in octahedral coordination between the slabs. [ref 1] agrees and is ICSD-backed, giving Ca(ZnP)2 P-3m1 (164) mp-9569 at hull 0.000, though on only 2 ICSD references, so it counts as weak by the chunk rules. The composition and the reference point the same way and the assignment is not in doubt.

dopant_roles.basis: CaZn1.9Cu0.1P2 and CaZn1.8Cu0.2P2 put copper on the tetrahedral zinc site of the anionic slab. Cu1+ for Zn2+ removes an electron from the polyanion, so this is the p-type carrier knob for the AMXP2 series and is the M-site substitution the second paper is built around.
Ca0.99Na0.01Zn2P2 substitutes on the cation site between the slabs. Na1+ for Ca2+ is the other way of taking an electron out, an acceptor on the A site rather than on the framework.

basis: Three of the five compositions are Ca2Si carrying parts-per-million sodium, and the second paper is on the effect of sodium addition on Ca2Si sintered compacts, so Ca2Si is the material of interest. Ca2Si is not the cubic antifluorite that Mg2Si is: it takes the orthorhombic Co2Si or anti-cotunnite structure, Pnma, and [ref 1] confirms it ICSD-backed at Ca2Si Pnma (62) mp-2517, hull 0.000, 5 references. Assigning it to tinisi_co2si stretches that entry, whose formula archetype reads as the ordered equiatomic ternary RTX, but the entry names Co2Si as its parent and this is that binary aristotype, so reusing it is more honest than creating a near-duplicate; flag it at v4 review. The host is genuinely mixed: CaSi is the CrB-type chain structure, Cmcm, which [ref 2] gives as mp-1563 with 14 ICSD references, and that is the alternative recorded. Ca5Si3 is a third structure, the Cr5B3 type in I4/mcm, mp-793 in the same reference block; the taxonomy has no entry for it and it is left unassigned rather than forced into either of the other two. Splitting this host by composition is straightforward from the Si:Ca ratio.

dopant_roles.basis: The three Ca2NaySi compositions sit at y of 0.00006 to 0.0002, which is 20 to 70 parts per million -- far below any level at which a substitutional acceptor on the calcium site would be detectable by diffraction. The paper calls it sodium addition rather than doping, and at that level the sodium may equally be acting as a sintering aid or a grain-boundary phase in a compact of a very air-sensitive silicide. Recorded as substitutional on the calcium site with low confidence, and stage 3 should treat the computed level with suspicion.

basis: The curator transcribes the series as Cd1-xNixFe2O4 and the lead paper is on the DC resistivity and thermoelectric power of Ni-Cd ferrites. AB2O4 with two trivalent iron atoms per divalent cation is the cubic spinel, Fd-3m, and the Ni-Cd ferrites are the textbook mixed spinel: Cd2+ has a strong tetrahedral A-site preference while Ni2+ takes the octahedral B site, so varying x moves iron between the two sublattices, which is what the resistivity and Seebeck data are reading. I disagree with [ref 2] here, which returns CdFe4NiO8 R3m (160) mp-1226789 at hull 0.066 with no ICSD reference. That is a computed cation-ordered rhombohedral variant of exactly this stoichiometry; a real ferrite prepared by ceramic sintering is a cation-disordered cubic spinel, so no mp_id is recorded and the space group is taken as 227 rather than 160.

All five compositions are YbCd2-xMnxSb2 and the paper title names it as the Zintl phase YbCd2-xMnxSb2. That is the CaAl2Si2 type, trigonal P-3m1, with an anionic (Cd,Mn)2Sb2 slab of corner-sharing tetrahedra and divalent ytterbium between the slabs -- the same structure as the CaZn2P2 host two ranks earlier and one of the best-studied Zintl thermoelectric families. Manganese substitutes cadmium on the tetrahedral site across the whole range measured, from x = 0.4 to x = 1.5, which is isovalent and keeps the structure while shortening the phonon mean free path, and that is the enhancement the paper reports. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

Every composition is CeCo1-xFexGe3 with x from 0.3 to 0.7, a continuous solid solution between CeCoGe3 and CeFeGe3. Both end members take the BaNiSn3 type, the non-centrosymmetric tetragonal I4mm variant of the ThCr2Si2 arrangement in which the loss of the inversion centre gives the antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling these compounds are studied for. The reference block for the neighbouring Ce-Fe-Ge host confirms the end member directly, CeFeGe3 I4mm (107) mp-20722 at hull 0.000. The paper is on the transformation between antiferromagnetic and Kondo behaviour across this series, measured from 10 to 300 K, which is a magnetic and electronic crossover within one structure rather than a structural change, so nothing is entered in phases. Cobalt and iron are both far above the 5 per cent split and neither is a dopant candidate; they are the two ends of the transition-metal site.

The single composition is LaCeFe3CoSb12, and both papers are on rare-earth-filled CoSb3-based skutterudites, the second naming LaCeFe3CoSb12 in its title. This is the filled skutterudite: a (Fe,Co)4Sb12 framework of corner-sharing octahedra with Sb4 rings, and the two large icosahedral voids per cell occupied by lanthanum and cerium. The iron-for-cobalt substitution on the framework is what makes room for the fillers, since each trivalent filler has to be charge-compensated by replacing Co3+ with Fe2+, and at Fe3Co that compensation is close to complete. La and Ce each sit at 5.9 atomic per cent, just above the 5 per cent split, so neither is listed as a dopant candidate and dopant_roles is empty -- but their role is cage filling, not substitution, and stage 3 should not treat them as dilute dopants. No reference entry is offered for this five-element host and no mp_id is recorded.

This host holds two stoichiometries and they are two different structures. Three compositions are (Ce,La)Cu5In and two are (Ce,La)Cu4In. The Cu4In members are the clear part: RCu4In is the cubic MgCu4Sn type, the ordered ternary variant of AuBe5 in F-43m, which is exactly what the aube5 entry is for -- its exemplar YbAgCu4 is the same type -- and CeCu4In is a well-studied member of that Kondo series. The Cu5In members I read as the hexagonal CaCu5 type, P6/mmm, with indium on one of the copper sites, but I cannot corroborate that: no reference entry is offered for this host at all, the chunk gives neither a TEDesignLab nor a Materials Project line, and the papers on specific heat, magnetotransport and thermoelectric power do not settle the structure from their titles. Confidence is therefore low on the primary and the host must be split by the Cu:In ratio in stage 2. Both papers work the Ce/La axis rather than the Cu:In one, which is recorded in solid_solution_axis.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth cation site
solid_solution_axis.note: Ce/(Ce+La) over 5 compositions, all of them near the middle of the range. This is the deliberate experiment rather than a doping series: lanthanum is the non-magnetic analogue diluting the cerium 4f lattice, so the axis measures the crossover from a Kondo lattice to single-impurity Kondo behaviour. Neither element is a dopant at these fractions.

basis: Four of the five samples are CeFeGe3 or CeCo1-xFexGe3 close to the iron end, and the reference block confirms the structure ICSD-backed: CeFeGe3 I4mm (107) mp-20722 at hull 0.000, the non-centrosymmetric BaNiSn3 type, matching the Ce-Co-Fe-Ge host at the previous rank. The lead paper is on CeFeGe3 as a concentrated Kondo compound with a stable valency. The fifth sample is CeFe2Ge2, which is a different structure entirely -- the centrosymmetric ThCr2Si2 type, I4/mmm, given by the same reference block as Ce(FeGe)2 mp-21882 at hull 0.000 with 4 ICSD references -- so the host is mixed and splits cleanly on the Ge:Fe ratio, 3:1 against 1:1. The two types are closely related, the RTX3 BaNiSn3 arrangement being the ordered non-centrosymmetric derivative of the 122, which is why a single label would look plausible and still be wrong for one composition in five.

dopant_roles.basis: CeCo0.2Fe0.8Ge3 and CeCo0.1Fe0.9Ge3 are the iron-rich end of the CeCo1-xFexGe3 series that the Ce-Co-Fe-Ge host covers at higher x. Cobalt takes the transition-metal site of the BaNiSn3 cell and adds one electron per substitution, which is how the series is tuned across its magnetic crossover -- a genuine substitutional dopant here rather than an alloy end member only because these two compositions happen to fall below the 5 per cent split.

basis: Four of the five samples are CeGa2, which is the AlB2 type: hexagonal P6/mmm with cerium between planar honeycomb nets of gallium. [ref 2] backs it strongly, CeGa2 P6/mmm (191) mp-912227 at hull 0.000 with 12 ICSD references, the best-attested entry in the block, and the third paper is on the transport properties of the RGa2 series. The fifth sample, CePd0.2Ga3.8, does not belong to that structure: it sits on the CePdxGa4-x solid solution of the first paper, and the x = 1 member CePdGa3 is the BaNiSn3 type in I4mm. Whether that tetragonal structure persists down to x = 0.2, or whether the gallium-rich end reverts to something like the CeGa6 arrangement that the same reference block lists at P4/nbm (125) mp-711 with 4 ICSD references, is not established here. It is recorded as the alternative with the host marked mixed, and confidence on the host label is medium for that one sample rather than for CeGa2.

dopant_roles.basis: CePd0.2Ga3.8 is written as palladium substituting gallium, and the paper title says solid solution CePdxGa4-x, so palladium enters the gallium sublattice of a Ga-rich ternary rather than sitting interstitially. The effect reported is the suppression of ferromagnetism, i.e. it is tuning the cerium environment through the electron count. Confidence is low because this composition is not the CeGa2 host structure and its own structure is unsettled here.

basis: All five compositions are CePt4Ge12-xSbx with x from 1 to 3. CePt4Ge12 is a filled skutterudite of the germanide branch of that family: a Pt4Ge12 framework of corner-sharing PtGe6 octahedra enclosing Ge4 rings, cubic Im-3, with cerium filling the oversized icosahedral void -- the same topology as CoSb3 with platinum on the metal site and germanium taking the pnictogen role. Antimony substitutes germanium on the framework, adding one electron per atom, and that is what the paper is doing: it probes strong Kondo disorder through thermoelectric power, and the disorder comes precisely from random Sb-for-Ge on the cage that surrounds the cerium. Antimony runs from 6 to 19 atomic per cent so it is well above the split and is not a dopant candidate; its role is framework substitution rather than doping. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded. The 10-144 K window is a low-temperature Kondo measurement.

Three of the four compositions are CeTi1-xNixGe3, and the second paper is on ferromagnetic quantum critical behaviour in CeTi1-xNixGe3. CeTiGe3 takes the BaNiO3 type: hexagonal P6_3/mmc with chains of face-sharing TiGe6 octahedra and cerium between them, which is the 2H hexagonal perovskite polytype and is confirmed by [ref 2] at CeTiGe3 P6_3/mmc (194) mp-1205531, hull 0.000. Using the hexagonal_perovskite_polytype entry for an intermetallic germanide stretches an entry written around ABO3 oxides, but it names BaNiO3 2H as one of its prototypes and the structure really is that one, so it is reused rather than duplicated; flag it at v4 review. CeTiGe itself is a different structure and the first paper is about exactly that -- a new high-temperature modification of CeTiGe -- so the host is mixed. Its ambient form is the CeScSi type, I4/mmm, which the reference block lists as mp-1077736 (139) and for which the taxonomy has no entry; the high-temperature modification is the CeFeSi type, P4/nmm, mp-19860, an ordered PbFCl derivative, and that is what the alternative records. The curator details show the two CeTiGe samples were annealed differently, 1180 K for 210 h against 1373 K for 1 h, so which modification each one is cannot be decided from composition -- that split is sample-level, not compositional.

dopant_roles.basis: CeTi0.9Ni0.1Ge3 and CeTi0.8Ni0.2Ge3 put nickel on the octahedral titanium site of the hexagonal perovskite chain. That is the tuning parameter of the second paper: it drives the ferromagnetic ordering temperature towards zero, so the substitution is there to reach a quantum critical point rather than to set a carrier concentration.

basis: Every composition is (Ce,La)In3, and RIn3 is the AuCu3 or L12 structure -- cubic Pm-3m with the rare earth at the corners and indium at the face centres. CeIn3 in particular is the canonical cubic heavy-fermion antiferromagnet and both papers are thermoelectric-power studies of dilute-Kondo cerium compounds, measured from 11 to 291 K. [ref 2] offers only LaCeIn6 P4/mmm (123) mp-1223179 at hull 0.000 with no ICSD reference; that is a computed cell with lanthanum and cerium ordered on alternating layers of exactly this 1:1 composition, which is what a database does with a 50:50 substitutional alloy, not a distinct structure. The real samples are disordered on the rare-earth site, so I record L12 and take no mp_id. One composition, (Ce0.2La0.8)In2.88, is indium-deficient by 4 per cent; that is non-stoichiometry on the indium sublattice rather than a dopant, and indium is far above the split so it is not listed as a candidate.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth corner site of the L12 cell
solid_solution_axis.note: Ce/(Ce+La) over 5 compositions spanning most of the range. Lanthanum is the non-magnetic dilutant of the cerium 4f lattice, which is the point of both papers, so neither end is a dopant and the parent compound depends on the composition.

basis: This host holds three structures at three stoichiometries and cannot carry one label. CeRhIn5, two of the five samples and the subject of the paper on tuning the pairing interaction in a d-wave superconductor, is the HoCoGa5 or 115 type: tetragonal P4/mmm, layers of CeIn3 alternating with RhIn2, and [ref 2] gives it ICSD-backed at CeIn5Rh P4/mmm (123) mp-20294, hull 0.000, 5 references, the strongest entry in the block. CeRhIn and CeRh0.9Ge0.1In, from the paper on CeRh1-xGexIn, are the equiatomic ZrNiAl type in P-62m -- the reference block gives CeInRh P-62m (189) mp-1079553 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references -- and Ce2Rh2In is the Mo2FeB2 ordered U3Si2 type in P4/mbm, listed as Ce2InRh2 mp-1205710. All three prototypes exist in the taxonomy, the split is unambiguous from the Ce:Rh:In ratios, and 115 is recorded as primary because it has the most samples and the best-attested reference; confidence is medium because the host label itself is not a structure.

dopant_roles.basis: CeRh0.9Ge0.1In is written with germanium replacing rhodium, and the paper title reads CeRh1-xGexIn, so germanium takes the transition-metal site of the ZrNiAl cell. Its effect is to change the cerium hybridisation and move the compound out of its intermediate-valence state, which is what the paper measures. Note this dopant belongs to the equiatomic member of the host, not to CeRhIn5.

basis: Both compositions are CePd3-xPtx, and the first paper is titled for the enhanced thermoelectric properties of CePd3-xPtx. CePd3 is the AuCu3 or L12 structure, cubic Pm-3m, and it is one of the classic intermediate-valence thermoelectrics; platinum substitutes palladium on the face-centred site, which is isovalent and is used to expand the lattice and tune the hybridisation gap rather than to add carriers. [ref 2] returns CePd2Pt P4/mmm (123) mp-1226474 at hull 0.000 with no ICSD reference, which is a computed tetragonal ordering of Pd and Pt at exactly the 2:1 composition; as with the (Ce,La)In3 host, that is a database artefact of a substitutional alloy rather than an observed structure, so the assignment is the disordered cubic L12 and no mp_id is taken. Palladium and platinum are both far above the 5 per cent split, so no dopant candidate is listed and dopant_roles is empty even though the pair shares one site.

The single composition is CePtSn, four of the five samples are single crystals, and both papers are transport and specific-heat studies of CeTX equiatomic compounds including CePtSn. CePtSn is the TiNiSi type, the ordered Co2Si arrangement in Pnma, and [ref 2] gives it as the best-attested entry for this chemistry: CeSnPt Pnma (62) mp-20834 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references. The same block lists a hexagonal CeSnPt in P-62m, mp-22763, at hull 0.005 with 1 ICSD reference -- the ZrNiAl type that equiatomic RTX compounds commonly form as the competing alternative -- and that is recorded in other_polymorphs rather than as a thermal phase, since nothing suggests the orthorhombic form converts to it on heating within the 10-297 K window. Ce(SnPt)2 P4/nmm and Ce4Sn25Pt12 in the same block are different stoichiometries, not polymorphs of CePtSn.

other_polymorphs.note: The hexagonal ZrNiAl-type polymorph of CePtSn, 1 ICSD reference against 3 for Pnma and 5 meV above the hull. Equiatomic RTX compounds often form either type depending on synthesis route, so which one a given sample is depends on preparation rather than on temperature; recorded as a separate structure with occurrence unknown rather than as a phase in a heating sequence.

basis: The single composition is CeRu4Sb12, the curator transcribes it as skutterudite-type heavy fermion, and the second paper is on transport in the filled skutterudites RERu4Sb12. That is unambiguous: a Ru4Sb12 framework of corner-sharing octahedra with Sb4 rings and cerium in the icosahedral void, cubic Im-3, which [ref 2] confirms as Ce(Sb3Ru)4 Im-3 (204) mp-1189811 at hull 0.000, though on a single ICSD reference so it counts as weak by the chunk rules. CeRu4Sb12 is measured as a non-Fermi-liquid and intermediate-valence system rather than as a device material, which is why the window runs from 11 K, but it also reaches 844 K and no transition is expected across it -- the filled skutterudite cage is robust to well above that.

Every composition is PbS with chlorine added, four of them written as a PbS block plus a Pb0.067Cl0.134 term, which is PbCl2 used as the chlorine source, and the second paper is titled for n-type Cl-doped PbS. PbS is rocksalt, Fm-3m, and nothing in this host perturbs that -- chlorine on the sulfur site and bismuth on the lead site are both dilute donors in a cubic lattice measured from 297 to 824 K, well below any transition. Chlorine itself reaches about 6 atomic per cent in the PbCl2-balanced formulas, just above the 5 per cent split, so it is not listed as a dopant candidate and does not appear in dopant_roles; its role is nevertheless substitutional on the anion site, and the excess lead that comes with it is there to keep the PbCl2 charge-balanced rather than to form a second phase. No reference entry is offered for this ternary and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Three compositions carry Bi at 0.005 to 0.015 per formula unit on the lead site. Bi3+ for Pb2+ is the standard n-type donor in the lead chalcogenides, and here it is being used together with chlorine on the anion site -- two donors at once, which is what the first paper means by enhancing n-type PbS from earth-abundant materials.

basis: All five compositions are Sr2-xCaxCu2CoO2S2 and the paper is on the electronic nature of the layered oxysulfide Sr2-xCaxCu2CoO2S2 with CoO2 planes, which names both the structure and the feature that matters. This is an intergrowth: a K2NiF4-like Sr2CoO2 slab, in which cobalt sits in a square-planar CoO2 sheet, alternating with an antifluorite Cu2S2 layer, tetragonal I4/mmm. Nothing in v3 covers it -- zrcusias_1111 is the nearest, and it puts a single fluorite-like REO sheet against the Cu2X2 layer at the formula REMXO rather than a two-cation oxide block -- so a2mo2cu2s2_oxysulfide is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here. The chunk file offers no reference entry at all for this five-element chemistry, so the space group is from materials knowledge and is uncorroborated, and no mp_id is recorded. The strontium deficiency in the Sr1.5 to Sr1.9 compositions is worth flagging for stage 3: it is the hole-doping variable of the paper, non-stoichiometry on a host site rather than a foreign atom, and strontium is far above the split so no record of it appears in dopant_roles.

dopant_roles.basis: Sr1.6Ca0.4Cu2CoO2S2 is the one calcium-bearing composition and the paper writes the series as Sr2-xCaxCu2CoO2S2, so calcium takes the strontium site between the blocks. Isovalent, so it works by contracting the lattice and changing the interlayer spacing rather than by adding carriers -- chemical pressure alongside the strontium-deficiency hole doping.

basis: All five compositions are Nd1-xSrxFe1-yCoyO3 with x from 0.3 to 0.7 and y from 0.3 to 0.6, and both papers are on the crystal structure, oxygen nonstoichiometry, thermal expansion and conductivity of exactly that series. These are the standard mixed-conducting ferrocobaltite perovskites: strontium on the A site, cobalt and iron sharing the octahedral B site, measured as rods from 297 to 1358 K for membrane and electrode use rather than as thermoelectrics. Within the perovskite prototype the setting shifts with strontium content, from orthorhombic Pnma at the neodymium-rich end towards rhombohedral R-3c and effectively cubic at high Sr and high temperature, and the papers name oxygen nonstoichiometry explicitly -- both are distortions and vacancy chemistry of one prototype rather than separate structures, so nothing is entered in phases. No reference entry is offered for this five-element host and no mp_id is recorded.

Four of the five compositions are Ho(Co1-xAlx)2 and the fifth is HoCo2, and the paper is on the effect of static and dynamic disorder on electronic transport in RCo2 compounds. HoCo2 is a cubic Laves phase, MgCu2 or C15 in Fd-3m, and [ref 2] gives it as the best-attested entry in the block: HoCo2 Fd-3m (227) mp-1072130 at hull 0.000 with 20 ICSD references. The other Ho-Co stoichiometries in that block, HoCo3, Ho2Co17, HoCo5 and Ho3Co, are different compounds and none of them appears among the compositions. HoCo2 orders ferrimagnetically near 80 K, inside the 10-299 K window, and the ordering carries a magnetostrictive distortion away from perfect cubic symmetry, but that is a symmetry lowering of the same Laves framework rather than a new prototype, so nothing is entered in phases.

dopant_roles.basis: The series is written Ho(Co1-xAlx)2 with x from 0.005 to 0.075, so aluminium takes the cobalt site of the C15 network. The paper is about disorder, and that is what the substitution supplies: aluminium dilutes the cobalt 3d sublattice, weakening the itinerant magnetism and adding static scattering, which is the effect being separated from the dynamic spin-disorder contribution.

basis: The compositions are HoCoO3 and Ho0.9Ca0.1CoO3, and the first paper is titled Ca-doped HoCoO3 as a p-type oxide thermoelectric material while the second compares the rare-earth site across the RCoO3 series. HoCoO3 is an orthorhombic GdFeO3-type perovskite -- holmium is small, so the octahedral tilting is large -- and [ref 2] agrees at HoCoO3 Pnma (62) mp-24875, hull 0.012, on 2 ICSD references, which is weak by the chunk rules but consistent with the composition. The 361-1165 K window crosses the gradual spin-state crossover of the Co3+ ion and the insulator-to-metal crossover that follows it, both of which change the lattice parameters without changing the structure, so nothing is entered in phases.

dopant_roles.basis: Four of the five samples are Ho0.9Ca0.1CoO3, with calcium on the A site. Ca2+ for Ho3+ is an acceptor: it forces Co3+ towards Co4+ and is what makes the material p-type, which the first paper says in its title. The straightforward substitutional case.

basis: All three compositions are LaCo1-xTixO3 with x from 0.3 to 0.5, and the papers are on the crystal structure and physical properties of LaCo1-xTixO3 plus minus delta and on a neutron structural characterisation of the same oxide, so the series is written and measured as a continuous B-site solid solution of a lanthanum perovskite. That is what I record. The reference block pushes back harder here than in the Ca-Mo-O-V case and deserves saying so: [ref 2] returns La2TiCoO6 Fm-3m (225) mp-1078893 at hull 0.117 with 1 ICSD reference and a monoclinic La2TiCoO6 P2_1/c (14) mp-1211314 at hull 0.012, both of them rock-salt-ordered double perovskites. Unlike V4+ and Mo4+, Co2+ and Ti4+ differ by two in charge and appreciably in size, which genuinely favours partial B-site ordering at x = 0.5, so the double perovskite is a real possibility rather than a database artefact. Confidence is medium with double_perovskite as the alternative, and the degree of ordering is a question for the neutron paper rather than for composition; no mp_id is taken.

All five compositions are NbCo(Sn,Sb) and all three papers say half-Heusler in their titles, one of them for the NbCoSn-NbCoSb system directly. This is the MgAgAs structure, cubic F-43m, with niobium and cobalt on the ordered metal sites and tin or antimony on the main-group site; substituting Sb for Sn adds an electron and is the n-type doping route, which is what the second paper measures. Two details worth recording for stage 2 rather than as separate prototypes. NbCoSb is not a clean 18-electron half-Heusler -- it has 19 and is stabilised by niobium vacancies, which the third paper is entirely about, so the Sb-rich compositions carry intrinsic non-stoichiometry on the Nb site. And NbCo1.05Sn0.75Sb0.25 has excess cobalt, which in this structure goes onto the vacant tetrahedral site and takes the composition a step towards the full Heusler; at 5 per cent it is a small interstitial excess rather than a second phase. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

Every composition is Co1-xRhxSb3, one of them written in the equivalent 4-12 form as (Co0.8Rh0.2)4Sb12, and the second paper is on transport in Co1-xRhxSb3. That is the binary unfilled skutterudite: a cubic Im-3 framework of corner-sharing MSb6 octahedra with planar Sb4 rings and two empty icosahedral voids per cell. Rhodium and cobalt are both group 9, so rhodium substitutes isovalently on the octahedral metal site across the whole measured range without filling anything or changing the electron count, and the first paper separates that from the effect of thallium filling -- no thallium appears in these compositions. I disagree with [ref 2], which offers only CoSbRh2 I4/mmm (139) mp-1206379 at hull 0.083 with no ICSD reference: that is a computed tetragonal ordered phase at a 1:2:1 stoichiometry, not a skutterudite and not any of these compositions, so no mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: octahedral transition-metal site of the skutterudite framework
solid_solution_axis.note: Co/(Co+Rh) over 5 compositions, spanning the middle of the range, so the parent compound is CoSb3 at one end and RhSb3 at the other and neither element is a dopant. Both are group 9 and the substitution is isovalent, which is why the structure is unchanged across the series while the lattice thermal conductivity falls.

basis: All four compositions are CoSb3-xSex with x from 0.2 to 0.32, and both papers say so: CoSb3 doped with selenium, and the structure and thermoelectric properties of Se- and Se/Te-doped CoSb3. The host is the unfilled binary skutterudite, cubic Im-3, with selenium substituting antimony in the planar Sb4 rings -- one extra electron per substitution, so this is n-type framework doping of an empty-cage skutterudite rather than filling. Selenium reaches 7 per cent of the formula, just above the 5 per cent split, so it is not a listed dopant candidate and dopant_roles is empty; its role is framework substitution. I disagree with [ref 2], which returns CoSbSe P2/m (10) mp-1226035 at hull 0.022 with no ICSD reference. Equiatomic CoSbSe is a real compound of a different family, closer to the paracostibite entry than to a skutterudite, and it is not what a CoSb2.7Se0.3 sample is, so no mp_id is recorded. The 78-699 K window stays below the temperature at which CoSb3 decomposes.

The host splits on the oxygen-to-metal ratio and both halves are named by a paper. Three compositions are CuFe1-xCrxO2, ABO2 with linearly coordinated Cu1+ between sheets of edge-sharing (Fe,Cr)O6 octahedra, which is the delafossite structure in R-3m; the first paper is on spin entropy and lattice strain from mixed-trivalent Fe3+/Cr3+, and mixing two trivalent ions on the octahedral site is what a delafossite lets you do. The other two compositions are CuCr0.4Fe1.6O4 and CuCr0.5Fe1.5O4, AB2O4 copper ferrites with chromium on the octahedral B site, which is the spinel of the second paper on Cu-Cr ferrites. Delafossite is recorded as primary on three compositions of five with spinel as the alternative, and the split is unambiguous from the ratio. For stage 2, note that copper ferrite spinels are usually tetragonally distorted to I4_1/amd by the Jahn-Teller Cu2+ ion rather than staying in Fd-3m -- a distortion within the spinel prototype, not a different one. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

Like the Cr-Cu-Fe-O host, this one splits on the anion-to-cation ratio. Three compositions are CuCr1-xInxSe2, which is the CuCrS2 type: rhombohedral R3m, sheets of edge-sharing CrSe6 octahedra with copper in tetrahedral sites between them, and the first paper is on the CuCrSe2 ternary chromium chalcogenide and its doping. The other two, (Cu0.46In0.54)Cr2.08Se4 and CuCr1.38In0.62Se4, are ABX4 and belong to the CuCr2Se4 selenospinel instead, which is what the reference block is pointing at with Cr4InCuSe8 F-43m (216) mp-20809 at hull 0.000, an indium-ordered spinel derivative on 1 ICSD reference. So the host is mixed, layered CuCrSe2 is primary on three compositions of five, and spinel is the alternative. Confidence is medium for two reasons: the reference names only the spinel side, and CuCrSe2 has a first-order copper order-disorder transition near 360 K, inside the 292-673 K window, above which the copper becomes mobile between the CrSe2 sheets. That is a disordering of the copper sublattice within the same layered framework rather than a change of prototype, so it is not entered in phases, but a diffraction pattern taken above it will not look like the ordered R3m cell.

All four compositions are La1-xSrxCr1-yFeyO3 and all three papers are on strontium-rich lanthanum chromium ferrites as symmetrical solid oxide fuel cell electrodes and as CO2 electrolysis cathodes. That is a single-phase perovskite by design: strontium on the A site, chromium and iron sharing the octahedral B site, and the whole point of the composition is that it stays perovskite under both oxidising and reducing conditions, which is what makes it usable as the same material on both electrodes. The samples are disks measured from 423 to 1173 K. Oxygen vacancies are deliberately introduced -- the second paper is on modulating them -- but they are vacancy chemistry within the prototype rather than a second structure. [ref 2] returns only Sr4LaCrFe4O15 Cm (8) mp-1218634 at hull 0.039 with no ICSD reference, a computed vacancy-ordered monoclinic cell at a stoichiometry none of these compositions has; no mp_id is recorded.

The five compositions are written as (SrRuO3)1-y(GdCrO3)y with y from 0.3 to 0.7, and the paper is on the effect of gadolinium and chromium substitution on the structural, electronic and magnetic properties. The bracket notation looks like a two-phase mixture but it is not: both end members are perovskites, and the paper treats the series as mutual substitution -- gadolinium for strontium on the A site and chromium for ruthenium on the B site -- giving one perovskite phase with two mixed sublattices.
