Orthorhombic tilting is expected across the whole range, since GdCrO3 is strongly tilted and even SrRuO3 is orthorhombic at room temperature. No reference entry is offered for this five-element host and no mp_id is recorded. If stage 2 finds evidence that these were sintered as two-phase composites rather than solid solutions the assignment would have to move to composite_multiphase, but nothing in the composition or the title suggests that.

The compositions are PrCrO3 and Pr1-xAxCrO3 with A = Ca or Sr, and the paper is on the transport and magnetic properties of Pr1-xCaxCrO3. PrCrO3 is a GdFeO3-type orthorhombic perovskite and [ref 2] confirms it at PrCrO3 Pnma (62) mp-1105822, hull 0.000, 2 ICSD references. Two other entries in that block are worth separating out rather than following: PrCrO4 I4_1/amd is a zircon-type chromate at a different stoichiometry and oxidation state, not a polymorph of the perovskite, and the PrCrO3 Pm-3m (221) entry at hull 0.040 with 1 ICSD reference is the untilted cubic aristotype, which is not what a small A-site cation like Pr3+ gives at the 51-657 K measured here. Space group 62 rather than 221 is the assignment.

dopant_roles.basis: Three compositions are Pr1-xCaxCrO3 with x from 0.05 to 0.2, calcium on the A site. Ca2+ for Pr3+ is an acceptor, pushing Cr3+ towards Cr4+, and the paper measures what that does to the transport -- the standard hole-doping route in a rare-earth chromite.

Pr0.95Sr0.05CrO3 does the same on the same site with a larger divalent cation, so it separates the electronic effect of the acceptor from the size effect of the substituent. Same role, different ionic radius.

basis: The five compositions are Ti1-xCrxOz with the oxygen content falling from z = 1.6 to z = 1.0 as chromium rises, and the paper is on the fabrication and microstructure of Ti1-xCrxOz. Read as metal-to-oxygen ratios these are the reduced titanium oxides, and two prototypes cover them. At z = 1.5, Ti0.75Cr0.25O1.5 is exactly M2O3, and Ti2O3 and Cr2O3 are both corundum and fully miscible in each other, so the middle of this series is a corundum solid solution -- that is the primary. At z = 1.0, Ti0.5Cr0.5O is MO, and titanium monoxide is rocksalt with a high vacancy concentration on both sublattices, so rocksalt_oxide is the alternative; the host is mixed and splits on the O:metal ratio. Confidence is medium because the intermediate z values of 1.3 and 1.4 lie between the two and are most likely two-phase mixtures rather than either single structure, which is consistent with a paper about microstructure. Note the Magneli series is not the answer here: TinO2n-1 sits at z between 1.67 and 1.8, above everything measured. I disagree with [ref 2], whose five entries -- Ti2CrO5, Ti2Cr3O12, TiCr2O5 and two P1 cells -- are computed oxygen-rich mixed oxides at stoichiometries none of these samples has; no mp_id is recorded.

All five compositions are Cr1-xTixSi2 with x from 0.2 to 0.8 and the paper is on the physical properties of Cr1-xTixSiy solid solutions. The two disilicides are not the same structure: CrSi2 is the hexagonal C40 type, P6222, while TiSi2 is the orthorhombic C54 type, Fddd, and the two are only partially miscible, so a series that runs from 20 to 80 per cent titanium on the metal site passes from one to the other. C40 is recorded as primary because CrSi2 is the thermoelectric member of the pair and the series is written as substitution into it, with tisi2_c54 as the alternative and the host marked mixed; the split is by the Cr:Ti ratio, with the crossover somewhere near the middle and a two-phase field around it, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. Titanium and chromium are adjacent but not isovalent, so this is not an isoelectronic axis and the chunk file flags none. I disagree with [ref 2]: its five entries are computed Ti-Cr-Si ternaries at stoichiometries such as Ti2Cr4Si5 and Ti3Cr17Si12, none with an ICSD reference and none matching a disilicide solid solution, so no mp_id is recorded.

The curator details settle this: a W-10Cr-1Hf alloy in weight per cent, ball-milled for 28 h and spark plasma sintered, plus a low-alloyed W-3Cr-2HfC, and the paper is on the microstructure and phase stability of a W-Cr alloy prepared by spark plasma sintering. Tungsten and chromium are both body-centred cubic and form a continuous solid solution at high temperature, so mechanical alloying followed by fast sintering gives a supersaturated bcc W(Cr) single phase -- which is exactly why phase stability is in the title, since the system has a miscibility gap at lower temperature and wants to decompose. solid_solution_alloy is the right entry rather than an ordered compound, and I disagree with [ref 2] on that point: CrW Cmmm (65) mp-1226162 at hull 0.124 with no ICSD reference is a computed ordered structure at a 1:1 ratio, neither the composition nor the state of these samples, so no mp_id is recorded. This is a fusion plasma-facing material measured for thermal transport rather than a thermoelectric candidate.

dopant_roles.basis: Hafnium is at 0.76 and 1.83 atomic per cent, and the curator names the second material W-3Cr-2HfC, so the hafnium is added as hafnium carbide. In this class of alloy HfC is a deliberate dispersoid: fine particles that pin grain boundaries and getter oxygen during milling, sitting as a discrete second phase rather than dissolving in the bcc lattice. Not a dopant, and stage 3 should compute no substitutional level for it.

basis: All five compositions are alpha-CsCu5Se3 or its antimony-substituted variants, and the paper is the discovery paper: alpha-CsCu5Se3 as a low-cost bulk selenide with high thermoelectric performance. No entry in v3 covers a ternary alkali copper chalcogenide at this stoichiometry, so acu5q3_layered is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here. The compound identity is not in doubt; the structure is the uncertain part, and the reference block shows why. [ref 2] returns three neighbouring compositions -- Cs3(Cu4Se3)2 C2/m (12) mp-1188128, Cs2Cu5Se4 Cmcm (63) mp-28467 and CsCuSe4 P2_12_12_1 (19) mp-17095 -- and not one of them is CsCu5Se3, so the Cmcm setting recorded in the proposal comes from materials knowledge of the alpha form rather than from either reference, and no mp_id is taken. Confidence is medium on that basis. The alpha prefix in the paper implies a second modification of the same compound, so the 326-989 K window may cross a transition; nothing in the chunk file flags one and none is entered in phases, but it is the first thing to check against the paper.

dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions are Cs(Cu1-xSbx)5Se3 with x from 0.01 to 0.04, written with antimony inside the copper bracket, so it substitutes on the copper site of the anionic framework. Sb3+ for Cu1+ adds electrons and is the carrier-concentration knob of the paper, which needs one because the undoped compound is a very low-carrier p-type semiconductor.

basis: All four compositions are Ni1-xCuxFe2O4 with x from 0.4 to 0.6, and both papers are thermoelectric power studies of copper-substituted nickel ferrites. AB2O4 with two trivalent irons per divalent cation is the cubic spinel, Fd-3m, and the Ni-Cu ferrites are an inverse spinel series in which the divalent cations take octahedral sites and iron is split between both sublattices; the hopping conduction that the Seebeck data reflects is Fe2+ to Fe3+ on the octahedral sublattice. As with the Cd-Fe-Ni-O host, I disagree with [ref 2], which offers Fe4CuNiO8 C2/m (12) mp-1225235 at hull 0.083 with no ICSD reference -- a computed cation-ordered monoclinic cell where the real material is a cation-disordered cubic spinel, so no mp_id is recorded and the space group is taken as 227. One caution for stage 2: copper-rich ferrites tetragonally distort to I4_1/amd through the Jahn-Teller Cu2+ ion, and at x = 0.6 that is near the onset, though it is a distortion of the spinel prototype rather than a different one.

The single composition is CuFeSe2 and the first paper calls it chalcopyrite outright, in a study of cobalt-doped Cu1-xCoxFeSe2, while the second makes CuFeSe2 nanocrystals. CuFeSe2 is the mineral eskebornite and it belongs to the chalcopyrite family -- a diamond-like framework of corner-sharing tetrahedra with copper and iron ordered on the cation sublattice. The two references agree with each other and both disagree slightly with the ideal type, which is worth recording: [ref 1], ICSD-backed, gives FeCuSe2 in space group 112, and [ref 2] gives P-42m (111) mp-1079566 with 2 ICSD references, where ideal chalcopyrite is I-42d (122). That is not an error in the references -- eskebornite really is reported in a lower-symmetry chalcopyrite-derived tetragonal ordering rather than in the CuFeS2 setting -- so the assignment is the chalcopyrite family with the caveat that the space group is a derivative, and confidence is medium for that reason. The hull distance of 0.128 in the 2019 dump also looks unphysical for a mineral that exists, which is the usual dump artefact for these chalcogenides.

Four of the five samples are Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32 and two of the papers name the structure for us -- one on the structural and thermoelectric properties of Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32 single crystals, the other explicitly on selenospinel Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32. A selenospinel is the spinel prototype with selenium on the anion sublattice, so that is the assignment; note the cation count, 22 metals to 32 selenium against 24 to 32 for an ideal AB2X4, which makes it a cation-deficient spinel and explains the variable-range-hopping conduction and very low thermal conductivity the third paper reports. The fifth sample is Cu2FeSnSe4, a different structure: the tetragonal stannite type, which [ref 1] gives ICSD-backed as FeCu2SnSe4 I-42m (121) mp-22612 at hull 0.040 with 3 references. So the host is mixed and splits on the Se:metal ratio. Confidence is medium on the primary because the reference block backs only the stannite member, while for the selenospinel [ref 2] offers computed cells at hull 0.036 to 0.041, one of them flagged AMBIGUOUS and containing cadmium that is not in any composition here; no mp_id is recorded for the spinel.

Every composition is (La,Pr)2-xSrxCuO4 and the papers are on the solid-state chemistry of high-temperature oxide superconductors and on the structural and superconducting properties of La1-xPrSrxCuO4. That is the T-phase cuprate, K2NiF4 or Ruddlesden-Popper n = 1 in I4/mmm: single CuO2 planes separated by rock-salt (La,Pr,Sr)O layers, the parent of La2-xSrxCuO4 itself. The 12-79 K window is a thermopower measurement through the superconducting transition. Two structural notes that stay inside the prototype rather than splitting it: this family has an orthorhombic Bmab distortion below a few hundred kelvin from octahedral tilting, and praseodymium substitution of the kind used here is what pushes such cuprates towards the low-temperature tetragonal tilt pattern instead -- both are tilt variants of one n = 1 RP structure. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Strontium appears in all five compositions at 0.1 to 0.3 per formula unit on the rare-earth site of the rock-salt block. In a cuprate this is not an ordinary dopant but the doping variable itself: Sr2+ for La3+ puts holes into the CuO2 plane and sets where the sample sits on the superconducting dome, which is what both papers are measuring. Stage 3 should treat the computed level as the hole count per copper.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth site of the rock-salt block
solid_solution_axis.note: La/(La+Pr) over 5 compositions. Isovalent substitution on the A site, used to shrink the block and change the octahedral tilt rather than to dope, so the parent compound depends on the composition. Note this axis is independent of the strontium hole doping recorded in dopant_roles -- both act on the same site.

basis: Every composition is PbTe with a copper chalcogenide added, written as (PbTe)x(Cu2Te)y or PbTe(Cu2Se)0.09, and the curator transcribes three of them as percentages of PbTe plus Cu2Te. The first paper is on PbTe-based composites, so the samples are a rocksalt PbTe matrix -- which carries the transport and is what a Seebeck coefficient here measures -- with a few per cent of a second phase in it. rocksalt is therefore the primary with composite_multiphase as the alternative and the host marked mixed, rather than calling the whole thing a composite and losing the matrix. Confidence is medium because how much of the copper is dissolved in the PbTe and how much is a discrete Cu2Te or Cu2Se phase is a real question rather than a formality: copper is highly mobile in PbTe and partly enters interstitially, which is the synergistic role the third paper is about, while the second paper reports deliberate Sb and CuTe core-shell nanostructures. No reference entry is offered for this ternary and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Selenium appears only in PbTe(Cu2Se)0.09, where it arrives as part of the Cu2Se addition rather than being added on its own. Recorded as a second-phase constituent for that reason, with the caveat that some of it will dissolve into the matrix and sit isoelectronically on the tellurium site as PbTe1-xSex; which fraction does so cannot be decided from the formula, so confidence is low and stage 3 should not read a clean anion-substitution level from it.

Antimony appears only in (PbTe)81Sb2Te3Sb0.6(Cu2Te)5, which carries both an Sb2Te3 addition and excess elemental antimony, and the paper for it reports coherent Sb/CuTe core-shell nanostructures. So the antimony is there as a deliberate nanoprecipitate for strain and phonon scattering, not as a substitutional donor on the lead site.

basis: All three compositions are Cu12Sb4-xTexS13 with x near 1.8, and the first paper is on the crystal structure, electronic band structure and high-temperature thermoelectric properties of exactly that substitution. Cu12Sb4S13 is tetrahedrite, cubic I-43m, a large cell built from copper in both tetrahedral and trigonal-planar coordination with antimony in trigonal pyramids and a sulfur at the centre of the copper cluster. Tellurium substitutes antimony on that pyramidal site; Te4+ for Sb3+ donates an electron, which fills the hole in the copper-sulfur band and turns a metallic tetrahedrite semiconducting -- that is the whole point of going to x near 2, and it is why the substitution sits so close to a fixed value rather than sweeping. Tellurium is at 6 atomic per cent, just above the 5 per cent split, so it is not a listed dopant candidate and dopant_roles is empty; its role is substitutional on the antimony site. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

Four of the five compositions are Cu2SnSe3-xSx, and the third paper is on boosting the thermoelectric performance of Cu2SnSe3. Cu2SnSe3 is the Cu2GeSe3 structure type: a monoclinic diamond-like framework of corner-sharing tetrahedra, ordered on the cation sublattice, and that entry is the assignment for those four. The fifth, Cu4Sn7.5S14Se2, is a different compound -- the paper for it is on solid solution Cu4Sn7.5S16 -- in which tin is octahedrally coordinated rather than tetrahedral. Nothing in v3 covers that, so cu4sn7s16_type is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and recorded as the alternative rather than parking a real named compound in unresolved_crystalline; its rhombohedral setting is provisional, since the chunk file gives no reference entry for the formula. The host is mixed and splits on the Sn:Cu ratio, 1:2 against nearly 2:1. Confidence is medium for the host label because of that split, not because of doubt about Cu2SnSe3.

dopant_roles.basis: Two compositions carry indium at 3 to 7.5 per cent of the tin site, written inside the formula as Cu2Sn1-xInxSe3-yS y. In3+ for Sn4+ removes an electron, so it is the p-type acceptor for Cu2SnSe3 and is the band-engineering route the third paper takes. A straightforward substitutional dopant on the tetrahedral cation site.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: anion site of the tetrahedral framework
solid_solution_axis.note: S/(S+Se) over 5 compositions. Sulfur and selenium are both group 16 and share the anion sublattice, so this is a genuine isoelectronic axis -- but the top of the range, x = 0.87, is the Cu4Sn7.5S14Se2 composition, which is a different structure rather than the sulfur-rich end of one series. The axis is therefore only meaningful across the four Cu2SnSe3-xSx members, where it runs to about x = 0.3.

basis: The compositions are DyVO3 and Dy1-xCaxVO3 with x up to 0.2, and the paper is on transport and magnetic properties in Dy1-xCaxVO3 ceramics. DyVO3 is a GdFeO3-type orthorhombic perovskite and [ref 2] carries it at DyVO3 Pnma (62) mp-25144, hull 0.000, though on 1 ICSD reference. This host is a clean example of the reference describing the chemistry rather than the sample: the best-attested entry in the block by a wide margin is DyVO4 I4_1/amd (141) mp-18784 with 9 ICSD references, which is a zircon-type orthovanadate with V5+ in isolated tetrahedra -- a different stoichiometry, a different oxidation state and not a perovskite at all. Every composition here is written ABO3 with V3+ or mixed V3+/V4+, so the perovskite is the assignment and the space group taken is 62, not 141. The 10-338 K window crosses the magnetic and orbital ordering of the vanadate, which in the DyVO3 end member carries a monoclinic distortion; that is a symmetry lowering within the prototype rather than a new one.

dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions are Dy1-xCaxVO3 with x from 0.05 to 0.2, calcium on the A site. Ca2+ for Dy3+ is an acceptor that converts V3+ to V4+ and drives the series towards the metallic side of a Mott transition, which is what the transport measurement is following.

basis: All five compositions are Er1-xHoxNiSb and the paper title says half-Heusler phases Er1-xHoxNiSb outright. RNiSb with a heavy rare earth is the MgAgAs structure, cubic F-43m: the 18-electron half-Heusler with one of the four interpenetrating sublattices left empty, which is what makes it a semiconductor rather than a metal. Erbium and holmium are neighbouring trivalent lanthanides of nearly the same radius, so substituting one for the other keeps the structure and the electron count untouched and acts only on the phonons -- mass and strain fluctuation scattering on the rare-earth site -- which is why the whole series was measured to 994 K. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth site of the half-Heusler cell
solid_solution_axis.note: Er/(Er+Ho) over 5 compositions spanning most of the range. Both are trivalent lanthanides on the same site, so the substitution is isovalent and the parent compound depends on the composition; the purpose is mass-fluctuation phonon scattering rather than doping.

basis: All four compositions are Sr2ErRuO6 with or without lanthanum on the strontium site, and the second paper names it: the high-temperature thermoelectric properties of the double-perovskite ruthenates. A2BB-prime-O6 with erbium and ruthenium alternating on the octahedral sites is the B-site ordered double perovskite, and the ordering here is strongly driven -- Er3+ and Ru5+ differ in both charge and size, which is exactly the condition that gives rock-salt ordering rather than a disordered B site. [ref 2] agrees and is ICSD-backed: Sr2ErRuO6 P2_1/c (14) mp-6294 at hull 0.000 with 3 references. The monoclinic rather than cubic setting is expected, since strontium with these B cations leaves a tolerance factor below one and the octahedra tilt on top of the ordering.

dopant_roles.basis: Three compositions are (Sr1-xLax)2ErRuO6 with x from 0.05 to 0.2, lanthanum on the A site. La3+ for Sr2+ is a donor, reducing Ru5+ towards Ru4+, and in a wide-gap double perovskite measured to 1250 K that is the way to raise a very low carrier concentration -- the first paper describes the same thing for the yttrium analogue.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [87, 225], ICSD-backed references for this host report [14]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: The single composition is Er2SbO2, better written Er2O2Sb, and the second paper is a review of the crystal chemistry of the rare-earth pnictide oxides (RE,Ca)mPnnOm with Pn = Sb or Bi. These are layered: fluorite-like Er2O2 slabs alternating with square nets of antimony, which is the Bi2O2Se arrangement -- the same anti-ThCr2Si2 stacking with the rare-earth oxide layer in place of Bi2O2 and a pnictogen net in place of the selenium one. The hypervalent square net is what makes the compound interesting, and the first paper is on decoupling electrical conductivity from the Seebeck coefficient in this family. Two reasons for medium confidence. [ref 2] gives Er2SbO2 Imm2 (44) mp-1225518 at hull 0.000 but with no ICSD reference, an orthorhombic distortion rather than the tetragonal I4/mmm parent -- plausible rather than wrong, since for a small rare earth the antimony net can dimerise, which is a distortion within this prototype. And the rest of the block is different chemistry entirely: Er2Sb2O7, Er3Sb5O12, Er3SbO7 and ErSbO4 are oxide-rich phases with Sb5+, not pnictide oxides with a reduced antimony net. No mp_id is recorded.

The compositions are EuMnO3, Eu0.8Sr0.2MnO3 and Dy0.2Eu0.8MnO3, with a fourth written Dy0.0Eu1.0MnO3 which is EuMnO3 again with a zero coefficient left in. The third paper is on the structural, transport and magnetic properties of RMnO3 perovskites and [ref 2] confirms the structure ICSD-backed at EuMnO3 Pnma (62) mp-25667, hull 0.000, 3 references. Worth the discrimination: the RMnO3 series splits by rare-earth size, and for holmium and smaller the hexagonal YMnO3 structure takes over, which the taxonomy carries separately. Europium is on the large side of that boundary, so the orthorhombic tilted perovskite is right here and ymno3_hexagonal would be wrong. Two other entries in the block to set aside: EuMn2O5 Pbam and Eu2Mn2O7 Fd-3m are different stoichiometries, and the EuMnO3 Pm-3m entry at hull 0.046 is the untilted aristotype, not what a Eu3+ A site gives. The robust window is 12-298 K; the 1364 K upper span is an outlier from the thermal study rather than a transport curve.

dopant_roles.basis: Eu0.8Sr0.2MnO3 puts strontium on the A site, and the first paper is on the Eu1-xSrxMnO3 series. Sr2+ for Eu3+ is an acceptor: it creates Mn4+ alongside Mn3+ and sets up the double-exchange and charge-ordering physics the magnetic and electrical measurements are after.

Dy0.2Eu0.8MnO3 comes from the paper on Dy1-xEuxMnO3, so dysprosium and europium are the two ends of one isovalent rare-earth series rather than a host and a dopant. Both are trivalent, so no carriers are added; what changes is the A-site radius and hence the octahedral tilt, which is what modifies the low-temperature magnetic interactions the paper reports. Recorded as isoelectronic substitution rather than as substitutional doping for that reason, and the level stage 3 computes is an alloy fraction.

basis: The single composition string STF2I3 is not a fluorine sulfide. STF is the standard abbreviation for BEDT-STF, the selenium-substituted analogue of the organic donor BEDT-TTF, and the paper is on the band structure and physical properties of alpha-STF2I3 and its Dirac electrons. The material is therefore the radical-cation salt (BEDT-STF)2I3 -- two donor molecules per triiodide anion in the alpha packing motif -- which is the same layered arrangement as alpha-(BEDT-TTF)2I3, the salt whose pressure-induced Dirac cone this work is following up. The host_system key is a parse artefact and should be read as one: the parser took the letters S, T and F of the abbreviation as element symbols, could not place T, and picked up H from the ethylenedithio groups, so neither F nor H is a real independent species here. Only iodine is genuine, and it is the closed-shell counter-anion rather than part of the conducting layer. The 12-300 K window is the low-temperature transport this family is measured for; the charge-ordering metal-insulator transition that alpha-(BEDT-TTF)2I3 shows near 135 K would sit inside it, but the selenium-substituted salt is reported to stay metallic, so no phase sequence is recorded.

All five compositions are FeGa3-xGex with x between 0.20 and 0.35, and the papers name the parent directly: improved thermoelectric properties in heavily doped FeGa3, and the substitution solid solutions FeGa3-xEx. FeGa3 is a narrow-gap semiconducting intermetallic in its own tetragonal structure type, with iron in trigonal-prismatic coordination and Ga-Ga dimers, and that is what the taxonomy entry fega3 is for. Germanium at these levels is a dilute electron donor on the gallium framework, not an alloying partner towards a different compound, so the host keeps a single prototype. I disagree with the reference here and want that on the record: [ref 2] returns only GaFeGe Fddd (70) mp-1225119 at hull 0.048 with no ICSD backing, which is an equiatomic 1:1:1 ternary and not what any composition in this host is -- FeGa2.75Ge0.25 is FeGa3 with about 8% of the gallium replaced. The MP snapshot appears simply not to contain the dilute solid solution, and a 1:1:1 entry is the closest formula it could offer. No mp_id is recorded. A second, smaller disagreement is with the taxonomy itself rather than the data: the fega3 entry gives its typical space group as P-42m (111) / P4n2, where the FeGa3 structure type is tetragonal P4_2/mnm (136). Worth correcting at v4 review; it does not change the assignment.

dopant_roles.basis: Fe0.85Co0.15Ga2.65Ge0.35 and Fe0.90Co0.10Ga2.65Ge0.35 put cobalt on the iron site. Co has one more d electron than Fe, so this is the electron-doping knob on the transition-metal site, working alongside the Ge-for-Ga substitution on the framework. Both papers are about driving FeGa3 into degenerate conduction, and these are the two independent ways to do it.

basis: Every composition is FeV1-x-y-zNbxHfyTizSb with the four transition metals summing to one against one iron and one antimony, which is the 1:1:1 half-Heusler stoichiometry with a single mixed site. The second paper names the family outright -- mechanical and thermoelectric properties of FeVSb-based half-Heusler alloys -- and the first is on Nb doping of FeV0.64Hf0.16Ti0.2Sb. FeVSb is an 18-electron half-Heusler in F-43m, and the point of loading the vanadium site with niobium, hafnium and titanium is mass and strain fluctuation to suppress the lattice thermal conductivity while holding the valence electron count at 18. Because the substituents all sit on one crystallographic site and none of them exceeds it, the host stays a single prototype rather than splitting. No reference block is returned for this host at all, which is expected for a five-element mixed-site solid solution -- neither TEDesignLab nor the MP snapshot carries entries at this level of substitution -- so the assignment rests on the stoichiometry and the paper titles, and no mp_id is recorded. Note that the host has no dopant candidate line: every element is above the 5 at.% cut, so all of the substitution here is alloying on the M site rather than doping, and stage 3 should treat the V:Nb:Hf:Ti ratios as site fractions.

Four of the five compositions are written in the homologous form outright -- InFeO3(ZnO)2, (ZnO)3, (ZnO)4 and (ZnO)5 -- and the fifth, InFeZnO4, is the n=1 member of the same series written as a single formula. This is exactly the InMO3(ZnO)n family the taxonomy carries, with iron as the trivalent M cation in place of the more familiar gallium of InGaZnO4. The structure is a natural superlattice: InO2 octahedral sheets alternating with (M,Zn)O blocks of trigonal-bipyramidal and tetrahedral cations, whose thickness is set by n, and the paper is on thermal transport and structural properties across the series precisely because increasing n lengthens the period and changes the phonon scattering. The homologous index is the variable being swept, so there is one prototype here, not several -- the members differ in block thickness rather than in structure type. No reference entry is returned for any member, which is unsurprising for a homologous series in a 2019 snapshot, so no mp_id is recorded. The measured 291-1273 K window is wide but these oxides are stable across it and no transition is expected.

All five compositions are Pb0.85Fe0.15Te with iodine between 0.002 and 0.01 on the tellurium site, and the paper is on the preparation and thermoelectric properties of Pb1-xFexTe alloys doped with iodine. This is PbTe, the archetypal rocksalt thermoelectric, with iron dissolved on the cation site. Iron at 15% is above the host cut and is treated as an alloying constituent rather than a dopant, which is the right reading: Fe in PbTe is a substitutional solid solution up to a few per cent that is often driven beyond its equilibrium limit by quenching, and its interest is band-structure modification and nanoscale precipitation, not carrier donation. The rocksalt lattice is preserved throughout -- PbTe has no structural transition below its melting point, and the measured 295-852 K window crosses none. No reference block is returned for this host, so no mp_id is recorded; PbTe itself is well covered elsewhere in the project, but nothing here pins the Fe-substituted composition.

dopant_roles.basis: Every composition carries iodine on the anion site at 0.002 to 0.01 per formula unit, and the paper title says doped. Iodine has one more valence electron than tellurium, so it is the standard n-type donor for PbTe and the series is a carrier-concentration sweep at fixed iron content. The level is left to stage 3; what matters here is that the iodine is on the tellurium sublattice and not interstitial.

basis: This host holds three different structures across five compositions and cannot be given one label. The paper is a survey -- thermoelectric properties of ternary transition metal antimonides -- so a spread of line compounds is expected rather than anomalous. Zr5Fe0.44Sb2.56 and Zr5Fe0.63Sb3.21 are both Zr5Sb3 with iron in the axial interstitial site, which is the filled Mn5Si3 (D8_8) arrangement in P6_3/mcm, and [ref 2] backs it with Zr5FeSb3 P6_3/mcm (193) mp-1189764 at hull 0.000. That is the entry taken as the primary label because it covers two compositions and because the interstitial-filled Mn5Si3 is the structural idea the other two share least. ZrFe0.7Sb and ZrFe0.5Sb are half-Heusler MgAgAs-type at F-43m with a heavily vacant iron site -- ZrFeSb is the 17-electron member where the vacancies are what make it a semiconductor -- and [ref 2] gives ZrFeSb F-43m (216) mp-961652. Zr6FeSb2 is the third: an ordered Fe2P derivative in P-62m, which the taxonomy carries as zr6coas2_type, confirmed by Zr6FeSb2 P-62m (189) mp-12962 at hull 0.000. All three reference entries are ICSD-backed at one reference each, so the evidence is thin per phase but consistent across them. Marked mixed and left for a composition-level split, which separates cleanly on the Zr:Sb ratio: 5:3 for the Mn5Si3 phase, 1:1 for the half-Heusler, 6:2 for the Fe2P derivative. Iron is not a dopant in any of them -- it is an interstitial filler in the first, a vacant framework site in the second and a stoichiometric site in the third -- which is exactly the kind of case where the role only becomes readable after the prototype is fixed.

All five compositions are Fe1-xZrxSi2 with x from 0.18 to 0.30 and the paper is on the effects of Zr substitution on phase transformation and thermoelectric properties. The parent is FeSi2, and the semiconducting modification of it is beta-FeSi2, orthorhombic Cmce, which is the phase any thermoelectric study of this system is after -- the metallic tetragonal alpha form and the eutectoid decomposition into epsilon-FeSi plus alpha are what the phase-transformation half of the title is about. Zirconium on the iron site is the intended handle. Medium rather than high for two reasons, both about how much zirconium these samples carry. At x up to 0.30 the nominal substitution is far beyond any plausible solubility limit of Zr in beta-FeSi2, so the real samples are very likely beta-FeSi2 plus a zirconium silicide second phase rather than a single-phase solid solution, and the paper reporting a phase transformation is consistent with that. And I disagree with the reference: [ref 2] offers only Zr-Fe-Si ternary line compounds -- Zr4Fe4Si7 I4/mmm mp-17435 with 3 ICSD references, Zr3Fe2Si3 Cmcm, Zr(Fe2Si)2, Zr2Fe3Si, Zr6Fe16Si7 -- and not one of them is a Zr-substituted disilicide. Those are the equilibrium ternaries of this system, which supports the second-phase reading, but none of them is what a composition written as Fe0.76Zr0.24Si2 is aiming at. No mp_id is recorded. The measured 295-1173 K window stays below the beta to alpha transition near 1255 K.

The five compositions are GayIn8-ySn2O16 with y from 1.4 to 2.7, and the paper is on the synthesis and thermoelectric properties of an oxygen-deficient fluorite derivative. That phrase is the key: the C-type sesquioxide, bixbyite, is exactly the oxygen-deficient fluorite derivative -- a 2x2x2 fluorite supercell with a quarter of the anions removed and ordered -- and In2O3 is its best-known member. The stoichiometry agrees. Ten cations against sixteen oxygens is one oxygen more than the M10O15 a pure M2O3 bixbyite would give, and that surplus is exactly what charge balance requires for two Sn4+ among eight trivalent cations, so these are tin-doped indium oxide with gallium alloyed onto the cation site and the extra oxygen taken up in the structural vacancies. That is the standard ITO defect chemistry. Medium rather than high because of two things. The reference disagrees: [ref 2] gives only InGaSnO5 P2/m (10) mp-1212081 at hull 0.004 with no ICSD backing, a 1:1:1 ordered ternary at a quite different cation ratio, which I do not think describes these samples -- the MP snapshot appears not to hold the doped bixbyite solid solution and offered the nearest ordered line compound instead. And I considered and rejected the rhombohedral M7O12 defect-fluorite phase that In4Sn3O12 adopts, which would be the other candidate in this chemistry: it needs roughly 43% tin on the cation site where these samples have 20%, so it does not fit. No mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: cation
solid_solution_axis.note: Ga/(Ga+In) over five compositions, median 0.25. Both are trivalent and both take the six-coordinate bixbyite cation sites, so this is isovalent alloying that contracts the lattice and widens the gap rather than doping. Tin is the electrically active species and is held at two per sixteen oxygens throughout, so the gallium axis and the carrier concentration are independent knobs here. The shared_site call is confident: unlike the O and Se case the schema warns about, Ga and In are both group 13 and both cations in the same sublattice.

basis: All four compositions are InxGa1-xSb across essentially the whole range, from In0.12Ga0.88Sb to In0.90Ga0.10Sb, and the second paper is on optimising the thermoelectric properties of III-V ternaries. Both end members are zincblende: GaSb and InSb are F-43m, the solid solution is continuous, and there is no ordering or miscibility gap that would take it to another structure, so a single prototype covers the host even though the parent end member changes with composition. The curator composition detail records Be at 4e19 per cubic centimetre on three of the samples -- beryllium is the conventional p-type acceptor on the group-13 site in these antimonides -- but beryllium does not appear in any parsed composition string, so it is noted here rather than entered in dopant_roles, where stage 3 would try to compute a level for it from fractions that do not exist. I disagree with the reference block, which returns InGa4Sb5 R3m (160) mp-1223963, InGaSb2 P-4m2 mp-1223638 and InGaSb2 R3m mp-1223646, all at hull 0.026 to 0.040 and none ICSD-backed. Those are computed ordered superstructures of the alloy, which is what a DFT database produces when asked for a random solid solution; the measured material is the disordered zincblende alloy and none of these mp_ids should be attached to it. No mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: cation
solid_solution_axis.note: Ga/(Ga+In) spans 0.10-0.88 over four compositions, so this host covers both ends of the GaSb-InSb line and the middle. Isovalent group-13 substitution on the zincblende cation site: it tunes the gap continuously from 0.72 eV at GaSb to 0.17 eV at InSb and cuts the lattice thermal conductivity by alloy scattering, without adding carriers -- the carriers come from the beryllium. The parent compound is therefore a per-composition question, not a host-level one.

basis: All four compositions are Ni2MnGa or a near-stoichiometric variant of it -- Ni50Mn25Ga25 is the same thing in atomic per cent, and Ni49.4Mn30Ga20.6 and Ni47.3Mn30.6Ga22.1 are the manganese-rich off-stoichiometric versions -- and the first paper names the system: electrical transport and thermal properties of a ferromagnetic shape memory alloy. The parent is the L2_1 full Heusler, Fm-3m, and [ref 2] confirms it strongly and ICSD-backed: MnGaNi2 Fm-3m (225) mp-20228 with 17 references, by far the best-attested entry for this host. The reason for medium and for the phases array is the shape memory itself. Ni2MnGa undergoes a martensitic transformation on cooling, and the measured 24-326 K window contains it for every composition here: stoichiometric Ni2MnGa transforms near 200 K, and manganese enrichment pushes the martensite start upward, so Ni49.4Mn30Ga20.6 transforms at or above room temperature. The low-temperature phase is therefore martensite, not austenite, throughout. I have departed from the schema convention that prototype_id names the low-temperature phase, and want that recorded rather than left implicit: the martensite of Ni-Mn-Ga is usually a 10M or 14M modulated monoclinic structure and only sometimes the non-modulated tetragonal one, the taxonomy has no entry for a modulated martensite, and the transformation temperature moves by more than a hundred kelvin across these four compositions. Naming the cubic austenite keeps the host on the structure all four share and the one the reference attests, with the martensite recorded in phases at low confidence. l10_tetragonal is used there as the nearest available approximation to the non-modulated martensite and should not be read as a claim that the modulation is absent.

Two unrelated materials share this host and it has to be split. NdGaO3, three samples, is an orthorhombic tilted perovskite: [ref 2] gives NdGaO3 Pnma (62) mp-3196 with 21 ICSD references, the strongest evidence in this host by a wide margin, and the Pm-3m entry at hull 1.467 is the untilted aristotype which a Nd3+ A site does not give. Note that NdGaO3 is almost certainly here as a substrate rather than as the thermoelectric: two of the four papers are on NaxCoO2 thin films and on epitaxial NdNiO3, both of which are grown on NdGaO3, so the curator has recorded the substrate composition. That does not change the structure assignment but it does mean the samples are not measurements of NdGaO3 as a bulk material, and a review pass should check whether these rows belong in the thermoelectric set at all. Nd3Ga5SiO14, two samples and both single crystals cut along the a and c axes, is something else entirely: it is neodymium langasite, the trigonal P321 framework the taxonomy carries as langasite, and the paper is on its paramagnetic ground state and field-induced partial order -- a frustrated-magnetism study on the langasite triangular lattice. [ref 2] returns Nd3Ga5SiO14 P3 (143) mp-1220307 at hull 0.020, which is the same framework in a lower-symmetry computed setting. Marked mixed with perovskite as the label because it carries three of the five samples; the split is trivial on composition since the two formulas share no stoichiometry.

dopant_roles.basis: Silicon is not a dopant here and should not be treated as one in stage 3. It is a full stoichiometric site of the langasite formula Nd3Ga5SiO14, occupying the small tetrahedral 2d position of the framework, and it falls below the 5 at.% cut only because the formula has 23 atoms. framework_substitution is the closest role in the vocabulary and is apt in the sense that langasite and langatate are distinguished by exactly which cation sits on that site -- but the level stage 3 computes for it will be a fixed 1 per formula unit, not a doping level.

basis: Two intermetallics, and the reference block separates them cleanly. GaPd2, four of the five samples and the subject of the paper on the physical properties of the GaPd2 intermetallic catalyst in bulk and nanoparticle form, is orthorhombic Pnma: [ref 2] gives GaPd2 Pnma (62) mp-1869 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references. That is the Co2Si (PbCl2, C23) structure type, and the taxonomy carries it as tinisi_co2si. GaPd, the fifth sample, is the B20 FeSi structure -- chiral cubic P2_13, no inversion centre -- confirmed by GaPd P2_13 (198) mp-1078526 at hull 0.000 with 4 ICSD references, which is the taxonomy entry b20_fesi. Marked mixed and split on the Pd:Ga ratio. I want one scope objection on the record: the tinisi_co2si entry is written for equiatomic RTX ternaries with a rare earth, a late transition metal and a p-block element, and GaPd2 is the binary Co2Si parent of that ordered ternary, not an RTX compound. The structural call is right -- Pnma Co2Si-type is what the reference attests -- but the entry as worded does not cover a binary, and either its scope should be widened at v4 review or a separate co2si binary entry should exist. That mismatch, not the structure, is why this is medium. The three remaining reference entries, Ga3Pd5 Pbam, Ga7Pd3 Im-3m and Ga2Pd5 Pnma, are other line compounds of this binary and none of them matches a composition in the host.

Every composition is written as a mixture and should be read as one: (ZnSb)90(GaSb)10 through (ZnSb)50(GaSb)50, and the paper is on the thermoelectric properties of (ZnSb)1-x-(MSb)x binary systems. The sample form field says Other for all five, which fits a pressed or melt-processed two-phase body rather than a single crystal or a phase-pure polycrystal. These are not solid solutions. ZnSb is orthorhombic Pbca with Zn2Sb2 rhomboid rings, the taxonomy entry znsb_cdsb; GaSb is cubic zincblende, F-43m. They share neither a cation valence nor a coordination motif, mutual solubility in this system is negligible, and at 10 to 50 mole per cent the minority phase is a bulk constituent rather than a dilute inclusion. So composite_multiphase is the honest label at host level, with the two constituent prototypes recorded as alternates and marked mixed, because a stage 2 shard for this host has to carry both structures rather than pick one. No reference block is returned at all, which is consistent with there being no single compound to return. No mp_id is recorded. What this host really needs is a sample-level or at least composition-level treatment of a phase fraction, which the ledger has no field for; the composite label is a placeholder for that rather than a structural claim.

The single composition Gd2SbO2 is better written Gd2O2Sb, and the second paper is the review of rare-earth pnictide oxides (RE,Ca)mPnnOm with Pn = Sb or Bi. These are layered compounds: fluorite-like Gd2O2 slabs alternating with square nets of antimony, the Bi2O2Se arrangement with the rare-earth oxide layer in place of Bi2O2 and a hypervalent pnictogen net in place of the selenium one. The square net is the point -- it is what makes the electronic structure interesting and what the first paper, on decoupling electrical conductivity from the Seebeck coefficient in this family, is exploiting. This follows the same reading given to Er-O-Sb and applied again below to Nd-O-Sb, so the three records are consistent. Medium, and the reason is a straightforward absence rather than a conflict: [ref 2] returns no Gd2SbO2 entry at all. Everything it does return -- Gd3SbO3 C2/m, Gd3SbO7 Cmcm and C222_1, Gd8Sb3O8 C2, GdSbO4 P-1 -- is oxide-rich chemistry with antimony in a high oxidation state, which is a different family from a reduced antimony net, and none of it should be attached to this composition. No mp_id is recorded.

The composition strings are mangled -- (UO2.00)(Gd2.00), (UO2.06)(GdO2.06) and so on, with the gadolinium content lost or duplicated by the parser -- but the paper settles it: the effects of oxidation on the thermal conductivity of (U,M)O2 pellets. These are gadolinia-doped urania nuclear fuel pellets, (U,Gd)O2+x, and UO2 is the archetypal fluorite oxide at Fm-3m. Gd2O3 dissolves into that lattice on the cation site over a wide range while the fluorite anion array is retained, which is exactly why gadolinium is used as a burnable absorber in fuel. The oxygen figures above 2.00 are the oxidation the paper is measuring, taken up as interstitials in the fluorite cage on the way towards U4O9 and U3O8, and they are the reason the reported thermal conductivity falls. Note that gadolinium is not a dopant in the dilute sense at these levels and that the axis detected here is real but its numbers should not be trusted, since they come from the broken formula strings. No reference block is returned for this host, so no mp_id is recorded. The robust measured window is 288-1408 K; the 1505 K figure in the full span is an outlier from the same high-temperature thermal study.

dopant_roles.basis: Oxygen is a host element, not a minor one, but the excess above O2.00 is the variable the paper actually sweeps and is recorded here so stage 3 does not read it as a stoichiometric constant. In (U,Gd)O2+x the extra oxygen enters interstitial positions of the fluorite anion sublattice and oxidises U4+ to U5+; it is non-stoichiometry on a host site, not an impurity, and it is what degrades the thermal conductivity.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: cation
solid_solution_axis.note: Gd/(Gd+U) as reported, but treat these numbers with suspicion: they are derived from composition strings the parser has mangled, and a gadolinia-doped fuel pellet in a thermal conductivity study would normally carry a few per cent Gd2O3, not half the cation site. The axis itself is real -- Gd3+ substitutes for U4+ on the fluorite cation site and is charge-compensated by oxygen vacancies or by U5+ -- but it is not isoelectronic, which is why the substitution and the oxygen stoichiometry are coupled here rather than independent.

basis: Four of the five samples are Tl9GdTe6 or a near-stoichiometric variant of it, and two papers name the series directly: the thermoelectric properties of Tl10-xLnxTe6 and of hot-pressed Tl9LnTe6. These are the Tl5Te3 structure type, tetragonal I4/mcm, where a trivalent rare earth takes one of the thallium sites of Tl10Te6 -- and [ref 2] supports it with Gd(Tl3Te2)3 I4/m (87) mp-1188567 at hull 0.022, which is the same framework in the ordered subgroup setting that the Tl and Gd ordering produces. The fifth sample, TlGdTe2, is a different structure: the layered alpha-NaFeO2 or O3 arrangement in R-3m with alternating Tl and Gd layers between close-packed tellurium sheets, confirmed by GdTlTe2 R-3m (166) mp-1065609 at hull 0.000. The third paper covers it -- thermoelectric properties of TlGdQ2 with Q = Se, Te, and Tl9GdTe6 -- and treats the two as distinct compounds, which they are. Marked mixed; the split is clean on the Tl:Gd ratio, 9:1 against 1:1. Both reference entries rest on a single ICSD reference each, which is why this is medium rather than high, but they agree with the chemistry and with each other.

All five compositions are GeTe with indium in it, written two ways: In0.1Ge0.9Te and In0.15Ge0.85Te as direct substitution, and (In2Te3)0.15(GeTe)2.55, (In2Te3)0.2(GeTe)2.4 and Ge12In2Te15 as pseudo-binary In2Te3-GeTe mixtures, which is the same solid solution expressed through the charge-balanced end member. The papers agree: thermoelectric properties of InxGe1-xTe, the highly efficient (In2Te3)x(GeTe)3-3x series, and the solid solution series Ge12M2Te15 with M = Sb or In. GeTe at ambient is the rhombohedral R3m structure, a rocksalt lattice distorted by a polar displacement along the body diagonal, which is the taxonomy entry gete_rhombohedral, and it converts to undistorted cubic Fm-3m on heating near 700 K. The measured window is 32-823 K, so every sample crosses that transition and the phases array records both. The transition temperature is composition-dependent and indium suppresses it -- carrier and defect content shift the Curie point of the ferroelectric distortion downward, often well below 700 K at these indium levels -- so 700 K is the taxonomy default and not a measured value, and transition_basis says so. Indium at 10-15% is above the host cut and is an alloying constituent rather than a dopant; its interest is as a resonant level in the valence band, which is what both thermoelectric papers are after. [ref 2] returns only InGeTe2 R-3m (166) mp-1223647 at hull 0.040 with no ICSD backing, a 1:1:2 ordered computed phase at a far higher indium content than any sample here, so it is not attached and no mp_id is recorded for either phase.

Four distinct line compounds across five samples, and the three papers make clear why: they are studies of the cerium analogues -- CeNi2Ge2, Ce2Ni3Ge5, Ce3NiGe2 -- with the lanthanum members measured as the non-magnetic reference against which the heavy-fermion and Kondo behaviour of the cerium compounds is judged. So the host is a set of reference compounds, not a doping series. LaNi2Ge2, two of the five samples, is ThCr2Si2 in I4/mmm, the 122 body-centred layered intermetallic, and [ref 2] confirms it ICSD-backed at La(NiGe)2 I4/mmm (139) mp-19979, hull 0.000, 4 references -- the best-attested entry in this host. That is the label. The other three are single samples of structures the taxonomy does not carry: La2Ni3Ge5 is the U2Co3Si5 type in Ibam, and La3NiGe2 and La2NiGe3 are further ternaries of this system whose structures I cannot fix from the composition alone. I have not proposed prototypes for them -- one sample each, with the structure resting on my recall rather than on anything in the chunk -- and have marked the host mixed with unresolved_crystalline as the alternate instead, which is the documented way to park a composition rather than mislabel it. Medium for that reason: the label is right for the compositions it covers and covers only two of five samples. Note that the reference block returns LaNiGe2 Cmcm mp-21077 and La11(Ni2Ge3)2 C2/m mp-627405, both ICSD-backed, neither of which matches a composition in this host; it is describing the chemistry, not these samples.

Every composition is LaPt4Ge12 or a lightly Sb-substituted version of it, and the first paper says what it is in its title: from superconductivity towards thermoelectricity, Ge-based skutterudites. LaPt4Ge12 belongs to the MPt4Ge12 family, the germanium analogue of the filled skutterudite -- body-centred cubic Im-3, with a Ge12 icosahedral cage built from the [Pt4Ge12] framework and the rare earth rattling inside it. [ref 2] confirms it ICSD-backed: La(Ge3Pt)4 Im-3 (204) mp-1188305 at hull 0.007, which is LaPt4Ge12 written with the cage stoichiometry rearranged, and Im-3 is exactly the filled skutterudite space group. Lanthanum is the cage filler but it sits well above the 5 at.% cut, so it appears as a host element rather than in dopant_roles; that is the same situation as the R fillers in RxCo4Sb12 once x approaches one. The 10-293 K window is low-temperature transport, consistent with the second paper on the superconducting and normal state properties of La1-xMxPt4Ge12. The remaining reference entries -- La(GePt)2 at P2_1/m, P2_1/c and P4/nmm, and LaGePt I4_1md -- are other La-Ge-Pt line compounds at different stoichiometries and none matches a composition here.

dopant_roles.basis: LaPt4Ge11.5Sb0.5 and LaPt4Ge11.75Sb0.25 put antimony on the germanium site of the [Pt4Ge12] cage framework. This is framework substitution rather than ordinary doping: antimony has one more valence electron than germanium, so it changes the electron count of the polyanionic cage itself, which is the same mechanism as Ga or Al for Ge in a clathrate. In this family that count controls both the superconducting transition and the position of the Fermi level, which is the point of the second paper.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [204], ICSD-backed references for this host report [11, 14, 31, 109]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All five compositions are (Sn0.25Pb0.25Mn0.25Ge0.25)Te with gallium from 0.015 to 0.03 on the cation site, and the paper is on enhanced thermoelectric performance in the high-entropy alloy Sn0.25Pb0.25Mn0.25Ge0.25Te. The anion sublattice is pure tellurium and the cation sublattice carries four species in equal fractions, which is a rocksalt solid solution, Fm-3m. The high-entropy framing is not an alternative structural claim -- it is a statement about the configurational entropy on one sublattice, and the structural consequence is the interesting part: GeTe on its own is rhombohedral below about 700 K and MnTe on its own is the NiAs type, but mixing four cations raises the configurational entropy enough to stabilise the undistorted cubic rocksalt across the whole measured 299-824 K window. That is exactly what the second paper of the neighbouring Ge-Mn-Sb-Te host describes for MnTe alloying of GeTe. So no transition is recorded and spans_transition is false, which is a substantive call rather than a default. No reference block is returned for this host, which is expected for a four-cation solid solution, and no mp_id is recorded. high_entropy_alloy was considered and set aside: that entry is for multi-principal-element metals in fcc or bcc packing, and this is an ordered two-sublattice semiconductor where only one sublattice is mixed.

dopant_roles.basis: Four of the five compositions carry gallium at 0.015 to 0.03 per formula unit, written explicitly as Ga0.02(Sn0.25Pb0.25Mn0.25Ge0.25)0.98Te, so it displaces the four-cation mixture proportionally rather than any one species -- Sn is named as the substitution target only as the largest single share of that site. Gallium in a IV-VI telluride is the classic resonant-level dopant, and a sweep from 0.015 to 0.03 at fixed host composition is a carrier-concentration optimisation. The level is left to stage 3.

basis: Two compositions, two structures. Ge3MnSb2Te7, four of the five samples, comes from the paper on the influence of Mn doping on the properties of Ge4Sb2Te7 -- so the parent is the n=4 member of the (GeTe)n(Sb2Te3) homologous series, with manganese replacing one germanium. That series is the taxonomy entry gst_homologous: trigonal P-3m1 or R-3m stacks of GeTe blocks separated by Sb2Te3 quintuple-like units, with the block thickness set by n. Ge0.8Mn0.1Sb0.1Te, the fifth sample, is a different material: it is GeTe with about 10% manganese and 10% antimony on the cation site, and its paper is the JACS work on rhombohedral to cubic conversion of GeTe via MnTe alloying. The title states the structural outcome -- at that manganese level the rhombohedral distortion is suppressed and the material is cubic rocksalt at room temperature -- so it is neither a homologous GST phase nor rhombohedral GeTe, and rocksalt is the alternate. Marked mixed; the split is clean on the Ge:Te ratio, 3:7 against roughly 1:1. Medium because no reference block is returned for this host at all, so both calls rest on the composition and the paper titles with nothing to test them against, and no mp_id is recorded. Two consequences worth stating. The measured 299-823 K window would cross the GeTe rhombohedral to cubic transition if the fifth sample were undoped GeTe, but the whole point of that paper is that manganese has already converted it, so spans_transition is false rather than merely unset. And for the GST member the metastable cubic form that the taxonomy entry mentions is a thin-film and rapid-quench phase of phase-change memory work, not something these bulk samples reach on heating, so it is not recorded as a thermal phase either.

The host is a parse artefact and the only honest thing to do is say so. The single composition string is GeNW, which the parser split into germanium, nitrogen and tungsten; the paper is on the contribution of radial dopant concentration to the thermoelectric properties of germanium nanowires, so GeNW is Ge followed by the abbreviation NW for nanowire. There is no nitrogen and no tungsten in these samples. The material is elemental germanium, which is diamond cubic in Fd-3m, and the 39-300 K window is low-temperature transport on nanowires. Confidence is high for the structure and the reading of the string; what is not high is the value of the host key itself, and a review pass should consider remapping these five samples onto a Ge host. No reference block is returned, which is itself consistent with the host being chemically meaningless. The radial dopant profile the paper is about is not recoverable from the composition string, so no dopant is recorded beyond flagging the two spurious elements.

dopant_roles.basis: The N of the abbreviation NW for nanowire, read as nitrogen. Not present in the material.
The W of the abbreviation NW for nanowire, read as tungsten. Not present in the material.

basis: None of the three papers is about a ternary Si-Ge-O compound; all three are about silicon or silicon-germanium dispersed in something else. The boron-doped silicon dioxide work makes silicon-rich particles from a reduced silica precursor; the quantum-dot paper embeds 5-7 nm germanium dots, whose sizes the curator has transcribed into composition_details, in a silica matrix; and the third is an n-type SrTiO3/SiGe composite, which is where the strontium, titanium and the Sr2.24Ti2.24O6.72Si80Ge20P1 string come from. So every sample is a two-phase or three-phase body: diamond-cubic Si or SiGe crystallites, an amorphous silica matrix, and in one case perovskite SrTiO3. composite_multiphase is the label that does not assert a structure none of them has. Medium, and marked mixed, because the constituent phases are individually clear even though the host is not. [ref 2] returns SiGeO3 Pbca (61) mp-769171 at hull 0.106 with no ICSD backing, a computed pyroxene-like ternary silicate, and I disagree with it: nothing in these papers makes a crystalline SiGeO3, and that entry is what a database offers when asked for a formula that is really a mixture. No mp_id is recorded. The film and epitaxial marker on this host is worth noting but does not change the call -- three of the samples are films, and a metastable polymorph would be reachable in principle, but the reported materials are nanocrystalline inclusions in a glass rather than an epitaxially strained phase.

dopant_roles.basis: (SiO2)80(GeO2)20B2.8 comes from the paper on silicon-based thermoelectrics made from a boron-doped silicon dioxide precursor. Boron is the standard p-type acceptor on the silicon site of the reduced crystallites; it is genuine doping, not matrix chemistry.

The lone phosphorus in Sr2.24Ti2.24O6.72Si80Ge20P1 is the n-type donor on the silicon site of the SiGe component of the SrTiO3/SiGe composite, which the paper describes as n-type. One part in a hundred of the SiGe is a plausible degenerate doping level.

Strontium and titanium in that same string are not dissolved in the SiGe at all -- they are the SrTiO3 that makes up the second phase of the composite. Recording them as dopants would be the exact failure mode the project README describes for graphene and nanotube additives, where an unscoped phrase rule relabels the host.
The other half of the SrTiO3 second phase; see the strontium entry.

basis: The compositions are Ni0.98Ti0.02Hx and Ni0.95Cr0.05Hx with the hydrogen content deliberately varied from 0.14 to 0.96, and the papers are on the transport properties of hydrogenated nickel-based alloys and on the effect of dissolved hydrogen on electron transport in nickel-chromium alloys. Hydrogen is the variable being swept, not an impurity. Nickel is face-centred cubic and hydrogen enters its octahedral interstices, filling them continuously up to the NiH composition at Fm-3m without changing the metal sublattice -- the classic interstitial metal hydride, which is what the taxonomy entry is for and whose exemplar PdH0.66 is the same physics. [ref 2] backs it: NiH Fm-3m (225) mp-24719 at hull 0.000 with an ICSD reference, alongside Ni2H P-3m1 mp-753890 with 2 references, which is the ordered half-filled variant of the same fcc host. The two computed entries at high hull, Ni3H at 0.519 and NiH3 at 0.230, are not candidates. Note the practical consequence for stage 3: the hydrogen fraction here is a filling of the interstitial sublattice and should be reported as x in NiHx, not as a dopant level on a metal site.

dopant_roles.basis: Ni0.98Ti0.02H0.9 and Ni0.98Ti0.02H0.5: titanium substitutes for nickel on the fcc metal site. In a hydrogenation study its function is to trap hydrogen and change the solubility, since Ti has a strong hydride-forming affinity; electronically it is a dilute alloy addition.

Ni0.95Cr0.05H0.96 and Ni0.95Cr0.05H0.14, from the paper on nickel-chromium alloys. Chromium on the nickel site at 5% is a conventional substitutional alloy addition, and the paper compares two hydrogen loadings at the same chromium content.

basis: All five compositions are HgSxTe1-x with x from 0.10 to 0.90, and the paper is on the galvanomagnetic and thermoelectric properties of HgSxTe1-x solid solutions. HgTe is zincblende at F-43m, and the sulfur-substituted solid solution retains that structure over most of the range -- metacinnabar, the cubic form of HgS, is the zincblende end member, so the two ends are structurally the same and the series is continuous in principle. Medium rather than high because of the sulfur-rich end. The thermodynamically stable form of HgS at ambient conditions is cinnabar, the trigonal P3_121 structure with helical Hg-S chains, not metacinnabar, and the transition sits near 618 K on heating. At x = 0.90 the composition is close enough to HgS that whether the sample is cubic or trigonal depends on how it was grown and cannot be settled from the formula. The taxonomy has no cinnabar entry, so I have not recorded an alternate prototype; what I want on the record is that one of the five compositions may not be zincblende at all, and that a cinnabar entry is a gap worth filling if more of this chemistry appears further down the tail. I also disagree with the reference: [ref 2] returns only Hg2TeS R3m (160) mp-1223955 at hull 0.044 with no ICSD backing, a computed ordered 2:1:1 superstructure, which is the usual database substitute for a random solid solution and does not describe these samples. No mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: anion
solid_solution_axis.note: S/(S+Te) spans 0.10-0.90 over five compositions, median 0.30. Both are group 16 and both occupy the zincblende anion site, so the shared_site call is safe. Isovalent substitution: it adds no carriers but opens the gap from the semimetallic HgTe end and scatters phonons by mass contrast, which is what the galvanomagnetic measurements are following. The parent compound is a per-composition question, and near x = 0.90 the structural question above applies as well.

basis: The host key is a parse artefact and the chemistry is unambiguous once that is seen. The composition strings read Mg2SI0.8Ge0.2Ag0.01 and, in one case, plain Mg2SI -- but the papers are on the solid state reaction synthesis and thermoelectric properties of Ag-doped Mg2Si and on the synthesis of Mg2Si for thermoelectric applications. Mg2SI is Mg2Si with the lowercase i of the element symbol read as a separate iodine atom, so the S and the I are two halves of one silicon. The material is Mg2Si1-xGex with x = 0.2 and silver doping, which is antifluorite -- the CaF2 antitype at Fm-3m with magnesium on the tetrahedral sites and the group-14 element on the cubic one -- and Mg2Si is the exemplar of that taxonomy entry. Mg2Si and Mg2Ge are fully miscible in the same structure, so the germanium content does not split the host. No reference block is returned, which is what one would expect for a formula that is not a real compound, and no mp_id is recorded. The structural call is high confidence; the host key is not, and a review pass should consider remapping these samples onto a Ge-Mg-Si host. Note also that the two host elements S and I are the artefact, so the usual reading of a host key as a set of real species fails here entirely.

dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions carry Ge0.2 against a nominal Si of 1, so this is Mg2Si0.8Ge0.2 -- a fifth of the group-14 sublattice, well past dilute doping. Germanium is isovalent with silicon and the two antifluorites form a continuous solid solution, so it adds no carriers; its function is mass-contrast phonon scattering to cut the lattice thermal conductivity, which is the standard move in this system. Recorded against Si even though the parser has split the silicon into S and I.

Silver from 0.008 to 0.016 per formula unit, swept across three compositions at fixed germanium content, and the first paper is explicitly on Ag-doped Mg2Si. Silver on the magnesium site is an acceptor, the standard route to p-type Mg2Si, and the sweep is a carrier-concentration optimisation.

basis: All four compositions are LaIn3 or LaIn3 with a little cerium on the lanthanum site, and the second paper names the family: the thermoelectric power of REIn3 single crystals with RE = La, Ce, Pr and others. REIn3 compounds are the cubic AuCu3 (L1_2) structure at Pm-3m -- rare earth at the cube corners, indium at the face centres -- and [ref 2] confirms it ICSD-backed at LaIn3 Pm-3m (221) mp-20729, hull 0.000, 6 references. The purpose of the host is clear from the papers, all three of which are about dilute Kondo behaviour in cerium compounds: LaIn3 is the non-magnetic reference lattice into which cerium is diluted, so the thermopower of the cerium impurity can be separated from the band contribution. The other reference entries -- La3In Pm-3m with 6 references, La2In, LaIn, LaIn2 -- are the other line compounds of this binary and none matches a composition here; La3In in particular is also Pm-3m and also well attested, so the space group alone would not have separated it and the 1:3 stoichiometry is what does. The 10-291 K window is the low-temperature regime the Kondo scattering lives in.

dopant_roles.basis: (Ce0.01La0.99)In3, (Ce0.1La0.9)In3 and (Ce0.2La0.8)In3.12 put cerium on the lanthanum corner site of the L1_2 cell, at a concentration deliberately swept over more than an order of magnitude. Chemically this is nearly isovalent -- both are trivalent rare earths of similar size -- but it is not isoelectronic in the sense the schema means, because the point of the substitution is the 4f moment cerium brings and lanthanum lacks. Each cerium is a Kondo scattering centre, and the dilution series is how the single-impurity contribution to the thermopower is extracted, which is what the third paper on dilute Kondo cerium compounds is doing. Recorded as substitutional rather than isoelectronic for that reason.

basis: All four compositions are Sr5In2Sb6 with zinc from 0.025 to 0.1 on the indium site, and both papers name it: enhanced thermoelectric properties of Sr5In2Sb6 via Zn-doping, and the thermoelectric properties and electronic structure of the Zintl phase. A5M2Pn6 is the 5-2-6 Zintl stoichiometry the taxonomy carries at Ca5Al2Sb6 -- Pbam, with corner-sharing MPn4 tetrahedra forming double chains of composition [M2Pn6]10- and the alkaline earth cations between them donating electrons to satisfy them. [ref 1] TEDesignLab, which is the reference the project ranks highest, gives Sr5(InSb3)2 Pbam (55) mp-649033 at hull 0.000 with an ICSD reference, matching both the formula and the space group exactly. That is as clean an agreement as this chunk contains, which is why this is high despite resting on a single ICSD entry. The mp_id mp-649033 is noted here for stage 2 rather than entered in a phases array, since there is one phase and no transition -- the 298-776 K window crosses nothing.

dopant_roles.basis: Sr5In1.9Zn0.1Sb6, Sr5In1.95Zn0.05Sb6 and Sr5In1.975Zn0.025Sb6 put zinc on the indium site of the anionic chain, and the first paper is on exactly this. Zn2+ for In3+ removes one electron per substitution from the polyanion, which is hole doping -- in a Zintl phase that is the standard carrier-concentration knob, because the valence-precise parent is a semiconductor with almost no free carriers. Arguably this is framework substitution in the sense that the zinc sits in the covalent chain rather than on the cation sublattice; substitutional is recorded because the electron count change here is a straightforward acceptor doping rather than the framework-tuning of a clathrate, but stage 2 should place it on the tetrahedral chain site.

basis: The single composition is KNO3 and the measured window is 611-679 K. KNO3 melts at about 607 K, so every point in this host is taken on the liquid -- the paper is on thermal conductivity measurement of molten salts by the transient hot-wire method, which is a technique for melts. Assigning any crystalline prototype would attach a structure these samples do not have at the temperature they were measured, so I have proposed molten_salt rather than reach for the nearest solid entry. The existing liquid_metal entry was considered and rejected: it is written for liquid metals and molten alloys with a Ga-Zn melt as exemplar, and a molten nitrate conducts by ion migration rather than electronically, so filing it there would assert the wrong mechanism. The solid sequence is recorded in the proposal for reference and is not reached here: aragonite-type orthorhombic Pmcn below about 401 K, then calcite-like trigonal R-3m up to the melt. I disagree with the reference block in the specific sense that matters: [ref 2] gives KNO3 Pnma (62) mp-5158 at hull 0.000 with 5 ICSD references and marks it PRIMARY and AMBIGUOUS, and that is a correct description of the ambient solid -- Pnma and Pmcn are the same group in different settings -- but it is not the phase measured. Its other entries, KN3O4, the two hexanitrite double salts and K2PrN5O17, are unrelated potassium nitrogen oxides and none is this compound. No mp_id is recorded, because a melt has no periodic structure for one to point at.

Two compounds and I can fix neither structure with enough confidence to name a prototype. La5Ni2Si3, four of the five samples, comes from a paper on inhomogeneous superconducting behaviour in it and from a second on the crystal structure and Kondo lattice behaviour of the cerium analogue -- so like the Ge-La-Ni host above, the lanthanum member is the non-magnetic reference for a cerium study. R5T2X3 is a real stoichiometry with several competing structure types and I cannot tell from the formula which one this adopts; the taxonomy has no entry that clearly covers it, and the reference block does not contain the compound. LaNi9Si4, the fifth sample, is on firmer ground: it is the CeNi8Si4 type in I4/mcm, and [ref 2] does return LaSi4Ni9 I4/mcm (140) mp-11726 at hull 0.000 with an ICSD reference, which is the same compound. But the taxonomy has no entry for that type either, and I have not proposed one for a single sample whose structure I am taking on recall. So both compositions are parked in unresolved_crystalline, which is what that entry is for, and the host is marked mixed because it genuinely holds two different structures rather than one unknown. Low confidence, recorded honestly: this is not a case where the reference disagrees with me, it is one where I do not have an answer. The rest of the reference block -- La(SiNi)2 I4/mmm mp-5898, LaSi2Ni Cmcm, LaSiNi4 Cmmm, LaSiNi I4_1md, all ICSD-backed -- describes other line compounds of this ternary and confirms that the system is rich in them, which is part of why the identification is hard.

Four of the five compositions are Sr2MnMoO6 with lanthanum from 0.1 to 0.3 on the strontium site, and the first paper names it: La doped effects on structure and thermoelectric properties of Sr2MnMoO6. A2BB-prime-O6 with manganese and molybdenum alternating on the octahedral sites is the B-site ordered double perovskite, and [ref 2] confirms it ICSD-backed at Sr2MnMoO6 P4_2/n (86) mp-705116 at hull 0.007, with a second ICSD-backed setting at I4/m (87) mp-1095141 at hull 0.008. The chunk marks the first AMBIGUOUS, and it is right to: the two entries are the same compound in two closely related tetragonal descriptions of the rock-salt ordering plus octahedral tilt, differing in how the tilt is indexed. Both are within this prototype, so the ambiguity does not reach the assignment. Worth noting for stage 2 that the second paper is on intrinsically disordered double perovskites, so the degree of Mn/Mo ordering in these particular samples is a live question even though the structure type is not -- here the ordering driver is reasonably strong, since Mn2+ and Mo6+ differ in both charge and size. The fifth composition, Sr3MnMo2O9, is a different stoichiometry at a Mo:Mn ratio of 2 rather than 1 and is not a simple double perovskite; it is one sample and is flagged here rather than split out.

dopant_roles.basis: Three compositions are Sr2-xLaxMnMoO6 with x from 0.1 to 0.3, lanthanum on the twelve-coordinate A site, and the first paper is on exactly this series. La3+ for Sr2+ is a donor: it reduces the B-site cations, raising the carrier concentration of a material that is otherwise close to an insulator, which is the standard route to thermoelectric performance in a double perovskite measured to 1246 K.

basis: Ni2MnSn is the L2_1 full Heusler at Fm-3m and [ref 2] attests it strongly: MnNi2Sn Fm-3m (225) mp-20440 at hull 0.010 with 12 ICSD references, far ahead of anything else in this host. The third paper is on the transport properties of Heusler alloys as ideal local-moment ferromagnets, which is the stoichiometric case. The two manganese-rich compositions, Ni50Mn36Sn14 and Ni50Mn37Sn13, are the metamagnetic shape memory members of the same family: the excess manganese occupies the tin site, and the first two papers are on their magnetic and thermoelectric properties in high magnetic fields. I have deliberately left spans_transition false, and the reason belongs on the record rather than being silently assumed. Those two compositions do undergo a martensitic transformation, and for Ni50Mn36Sn14 it sits near room temperature, inside the measured 14-400 K window. Stoichiometric Ni2MnSn does not transform at all. So the thermal sequence here is not a property of the host: one composition has a transition and another has none, and a single phases array would assert a transformation for samples that do not have one. That belongs at composition level, and this host should be picked up by the review queue on that basis. The remaining reference entries -- Mn2NiSn F-43m at hull 0.197, Mn3Ni3Sn2, Mn3Ni4Sn, Mn5Ni8Sn3 -- are computed phases with no ICSD backing and none is a candidate.

The five compositions are the same material written two ways: three as Sr2VMoO6 or Sr2-xVMoO6, two as SrV0.5Mo0.5O3. The papers are on the electrical conductivity of Sr2-xVMoO6-y, on the crystal structure, thermal stability and conductivity of the compound, and on vanadium-doped strontium molybdate as a fuel-cell anode. [ref 2] gives Sr2VMoO6 P4/mmm (123) mp-1218447 at hull 0.034 with no ICSD backing, which is an ordered model. Medium, because the two ways of writing the formula encode a real structural question that this evidence does not settle. Rock-salt ordering of a double perovskite B site is driven by a difference in charge and size between the two cations, and here there is almost none: in Sr2VMoO6 charge balance puts both vanadium and molybdenum at 4+, with similar ionic radii. That is the weak-driver regime, where the B site is usually disordered and the material is better described as the simple cubic perovskite SrV0.5Mo0.5O3 -- which is exactly how two of the compositions are written, and is consistent with these being metallic conductors rather than the semiconductors that ordering would tend to produce. So double_perovskite is recorded as the label because the literature and the reference both name the compound that way, with perovskite as a genuine alternate, and the disorder question flagged for stage 2 rather than decided here. Note the oxygen deficiency in the Sr2-xVMoO6-y series is a separate variable that the first paper sweeps and that the formulas here only partly capture.

Every composition is Tl0.3MoO3 or a lightly substituted version of it, and the papers name it three times over: transverse thermoelectric power in the molybdenum blue bronze K0.3MoO3, the effect of impurities on thermoelectric power in thallium blue bronze Tl0.3MoO3, and charge-density wave instability and nonlinear transport in Tl0.3MoO3. The A0.3MoO3 blue bronzes with A = K, Rb or Tl are the taxonomy entry exactly, monoclinic C2/m, built from slabs of edge- and corner-sharing MoO6 octahedra with the alkali or thallium cation between them. [ref 2] supports it: Tl(MoO3)3 C2/m (12) mp-615697 at hull 0.042 with an ICSD reference is Tl0.33MoO3, the blue bronze itself, in the right space group. That entry is not the block primary -- Tl2MoO4 C2 with 2 references is -- but Tl2MoO4 is an ordinary molybdate at a completely different stoichiometry and is not what any composition here is. This is a case where the composition settles it and the reference ranking does not. The physics matters for the measurement: the 25-298 K window spans the Peierls transition of the charge-density wave, which sits near 175 K in the thallium bronze. That is an electronic transition accompanied by a lattice superstructure, not a change of structure type, so it is not recorded in phases -- but it is what the third paper is about and it is why the thermopower is strongly temperature dependent here.

dopant_roles.basis: Tl0.3Mo0.96W0.04O3, two samples, and the second paper is on the effect of impurities on the thermopower. Tungsten sits on the molybdenum octahedral site; it is isovalent and nearly the same size, so it adds no carriers and acts as a scattering centre that pins the charge-density wave, which is precisely the impurity effect being studied.

Tl0.24K0.06MoO3 replaces a fifth of the thallium with potassium on the interlayer cation site. K0.3MoO3 and Tl0.3MoO3 are the same structure with different A cations, so this is alloying between two members of the blue bronze family rather than doping, and it shifts the Peierls temperature. Recorded as substitutional because it is a straightforward site replacement, but stage 3 should treat the level as an alloy fraction of the A site, not a dopant concentration.

basis: Three papers, three different materials, and no single structure covers them. Ti34O34N33, Ti33O29N37 and Ti41O12N47 are titanium oxynitrides with roughly one metal per anion and are rocksalt: TiN is Fm-3m, TiO dissolves into it continuously, and the whole TiN-TiO join is one defect rocksalt solid solution, which is the taxonomy entry rocksalt_nitride_carbide.
