basis: Three compositions written as atomic percentages of a four-element mixture, CuxAs40-xTe54Se6 at x = 25, 27.5 and 30, and the paper is titled on the thermal stability and thermoelectric properties of CuxAs40-xTe60-ySey -- thermal stability being the language of glasses, not of line compounds. As-Te with a chalcogen and a metal modifier at these proportions is a classic chalcogenide glass former, and the compositions vary continuously in a way no crystalline stoichiometry does. Neither reference printed an entry for the host.
note: mp_id is null and must stay null; the README lists amorphous as a stage 2 skip. Measured 300-375 K, a strikingly narrow window, which is itself consistent with a glass: the measurement stops below the crystallisation onset because heating further would destroy the sample and change what is being measured. The selenium at 6 per cent is a host element by the 5 per cent rule and is a network former here rather than a dopant -- in these glasses selenium for tellurium raises the glass transition and the stability against crystallisation, which is what the title means by thermal stability. If any sample in this host turns out to be partly crystallised, it is a composite of glass and crystallites rather than a different glass.

basis: Three compositions of KxSr1-xFe2As2 at x = 0.12, 0.17 and 0.22, and the paper is on evidence of quantum criticality in the phase diagram of KxSr1-xFe2As2. SrFe2As2 is the strontium 122 iron arsenide, the ThCr2Si2 type, body-centred tetragonal I4/mmm, with FeAs layers separated by strontium. [ref 2] confirms it: Sr(FeAs)2 I4/mmm (139) mp-4488 at hull 0.000 with 6 ICSD references, top-ranked. Potassium for strontium is the canonical hole doping of that family.

dopant_roles.basis: K at 12 to 22 per cent of the strontium site, which the taxonomy already names as the doping variable of this family. Monovalent potassium replacing divalent strontium removes one electron per substitution from the FeAs layers, suppressing the magnetic and structural order of the parent and bringing on superconductivity -- the phase diagram the paper maps. It is the working variable, not an impurity, and stage 3 should report x rather than a doping level in the ordinary sense.

note: One transition worth stating even though spans_transition is false. Undoped SrFe2As2 undergoes a tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion at about 205 K, locked to its spin-density-wave ordering, and the measured window here is 12-319 K, so the parent compound would cross it squarely. Potassium doping pushes that temperature down fast, and at x = 0.12 to 0.22 it should have fallen to somewhere between roughly 100 and 175 K -- still inside the window. spans_transition is left false because the distortion is a symmetry lowering within the ThCr2Si2 framework, from I4/mmm to Fmmm, not a change of prototype, and the taxonomy has no separate entry for the orthorhombic form. But transport across it is not one regime, and the doping dependence means the crossing temperature differs for each of the three samples. The curator note records that the Seebeck coefficient was calculated from S/T, so the stored values are derived rather than directly digitised. The other [ref 2] entry, NaSr4(FeAs)10 I4/m mp-1221018, is a computed sodium-containing ordering and is not relevant.

basis: The three compositions are Sn17.8In4.0As21.7I8, Sn15.1In8.0As21.5I8 and Sn14.6In9As21.5I8, and the arithmetic settles it. Framework atoms Sn plus In plus As come to 43.5, 44.6 and 45.1 against the 46 framework sites of a type I clathrate, and the iodine is fixed at exactly 8, which is the number of cages. This is the cationic clathrate family Sn24-xInxAs22I8, the arsenic analogue of Sn24P19.3I8, where the framework carries the positive charge and iodine is the guest anion rather than the usual arrangement of a metal guest in an anionic framework. The shortfall from 46 is tin vacancies, which that family is known for. One paper is on anomalously low thermal conductivity, the other is titled on the synthesis, crystal structure and thermoelectric properties of a clathrate.
note: Neither reference printed anything for this host, so mp_id is null and stage 2 must resolve a Pm-3n type I cell from the literature. Indium is a host element here, not a dopant: it runs from 4.0 to 9 atoms per formula unit across the three compositions and substitutes for tin on the framework, which is the electron-count knob of a cationic clathrate -- replacing Sn4+ by In3+ is how the framework charge is balanced against the eight iodide anions. Because indium and tin are not in the same group this is not an isoelectronic axis in the sense the project records, so solid_solution_axis is left null, but the In:Sn ratio is a real compositional series and stage 2 should keep it. Measured 77-333 K, low and narrow, consistent with a cage compound studied for its glass-like thermal conductivity.

basis: InAs1-xPx at x = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4, and the paper is titled InAs1-xPx as a Thermoelectric Material. Both end members are ordinary III-V semiconductors in the zincblende structure, F-43m, and InAs-InP is a continuous solid solution across the whole range with phosphorus and arsenic sharing the anion site. There is nothing else this can be.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: anion
solid_solution_axis.note: As/(As+P) across the three compositions. A continuous zincblende solid solution; the lattice parameter and band gap interpolate and the prototype does not change anywhere along it.

note: I do not follow [ref 2] here and want to say so plainly. It offers In2AsP R3m mp-1223837, In4As3P Pmm2 mp-1223887, In4AsP3 Amm2 mp-1223884 and In2AsP P-4m2 mp-1223851, all at hulls of 0.013 to 0.018 and none carrying an ICSD reference. Those are computed ordered superstructures of the alloy -- the standard set of small-cell decorations a hull calculation generates for a pseudobinary -- not observed phases. InAsP grown for transport measurements is a disordered zincblende solid solution on a single F-43m lattice, and assigning one of these orderings would claim a long-range cation-anion ordering that no one has reported here. mp_id is left null; stage 2 should take the InAs and InP end members and interpolate, or use a disordered representation. Measured 291-1064 K, entirely within the stability range of the zincblende phase.

basis: The single composition is Na2Ti2As2O and the paper is on the physical properties of the layered pnictide oxides Na2Ti2Pn2O with Pn = As or Sb. This is the arsenic member of exactly the family proposed earlier in this project for the Na-O-Sb-Ti host: anti-CuO2 Ti2O sheets with oxygen at the centre of each Ti4 square, capped above and below by arsenic, with sodium between the slabs, body-centred tetragonal I4/mmm. [ref 2] confirms it directly -- Na2Ti2As2O I4/mmm (139) mp-1025360 at hull 0.000.
note: The prototype was proposed from the antimony member in an earlier chunk; this is the arsenic member, so the proposal now has two hosts behind it rather than one, which is worth noting when it is reviewed for a v4 seed file. The other two [ref 2] entries, NaTi2(AsO4)3 R-3c mp-1200852 and NaTiAsO5 P2_1/c mp-1201259, are arsenate salts with As5+ in AsO4 tetrahedra -- a completely different chemistry from the As3- square net here, and the sort of formula-similarity trap this reference throws up in oxide-pnictide systems. Measured 10-301 K. Na2Ti2As2O has a density-wave-like anomaly near 320 K, just above the top of the robust window (the full span reaches 348 K), so a curve or two may graze it; the anomaly is electronic and does not change the prototype.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [139], ICSD-backed references for this host report [14, 167]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: PtAs2 is sperrylite, the platinum arsenide mineral, and it is a textbook pyrite-type compound: cubic Pa-3, platinum in octahedral coordination with As-As dumbbells occupying the anion positions of a distorted rocksalt. [ref 2] puts it first without ambiguity -- As2Pt Pa-3 (205) mp-2513 at hull 0.000 with 8 ICSD references. The paper is on enhancing the high-temperature thermoelectric properties of PtAs2 by Rh doping.

dopant_roles.site: the 4a octahedral cation site
dopant_roles.basis: Rh at 0.5 and 1 per cent of the platinum site, and the paper names it as the doping mechanism in its title. Rhodium sits one column to the left of platinum, so each substitution removes an electron from a filled-band semiconductor and dopes it p-type -- this is straightforward acceptor doping to tune the carrier concentration, not alloying. The two levels are a dilute series, which is the signature of a deliberate carrier-concentration study.

note: The two AsPt3 entries in [ref 2], P6_3/mmc mp-1183320 and Pm-3m mp-1183186, sit at hulls of 0.232 and 0.234 with no ICSD references and are irrelevant to a 1:2 composition; they are flagged AMBIGUOUS in the reference for good reason. Measured 11-599 K over 15 curves, a wide window with no known structural transition in PtAs2 inside it.

basis: The paper title says it: Thermoelectric Properties of Diphasal Systems Combining As2Te3 and Tl2Te. Diphasal means two phases, and the compositions decompose exactly onto those two. Taking the first, As17.65Sb11.76Se8.82Te44.12Tl17.65: the pnictogens sum to 29.41 so x(As,Sb)2(Te,Se)3 has x = 14.7, the thallium gives y Tl2Te with y = 8.82, and 3x plus y comes to 52.94 against a measured chalcogen total of 52.94. The other two compositions close the same way. So each sample is a mechanical mixture of an (As,Sb)2(Te,Se)3 phase and Tl2Te, not a single ternary compound, and the antimony and selenium are substituting inside the first phase.
note: is_mixed is left false deliberately, and the distinction matters. is_mixed in this project means different compositions in the host resolve to different prototypes, which would be split per composition in stage 2. Here every composition is the same two-phase mixture, so splitting by composition would not separate anything -- the mixture is the material. The README lists composite_multiphase as a stage 2 skip and that is the right outcome. For the record the constituents are alpha-As2Te3, monoclinic C2/m layered, which the taxonomy has no entry for and which is not a tetradymite despite the Te3 stoichiometry, and Tl2Te, monoclinic C2/c. Neither reference printed anything for this host and mp_id is null. Measured 103-335 K; As2Te3 and Tl2Te both melt low, which is presumably why the window stops near room temperature.

basis: ThAsSe in P4/nmm is the PbFCl or matlockite type, which is the structure essentially every actinide and rare-earth pnictide-chalcogenide ThXY adopts: alternating square nets of thorium, arsenic and selenium stacked along c, with the two anions on crystallographically distinct sites rather than disordered together. [ref 2] gives ThAsSe P4/nmm (129) mp-1019357 at hull 0.000, which is the matlockite space group exactly. The samples are single crystals and the paper is on thermoelectric power in the off-stoichiometric ThAsSe system.
note: The second composition, ThAs0.67Se0.33, is the off-stoichiometry the paper title refers to: the anion ratio moves away from 1:1 while the structure stays matlockite, with the excess selenium or arsenic taken up as site mixing and vacancies in the arsenic square net. That disorder is the subject, because ThAsSe is one of the non-magnetic compounds that nevertheless shows Kondo-like resistivity attributed to structural disorder rather than to f moments. So the deviation is the working variable, not a synthesis imperfection, and I have not recorded it as a dopant role -- both elements are host constituents. The other [ref 2] entry, Th2AsSe2 P4/mmm mp-1207178, sits at hull 1.887 and can be disregarded. Measured 12-316 K.

basis: Three compositions, three different structures, one per sample, from a 1974 thermal diffusivity paper on Be4B, Be2B and BeB6. Be2B is the antifluorite: cubic Fm-3m with boron on the calcium positions of CaF2 and beryllium on the fluorine positions, and [ref 2] gives Be2B Fm-3m (225) mp-1432 with 3 ICSD references, the best-attested entry for the binary. I have made that the host prototype because it is the one member whose structure is unambiguous and well attested, but it covers only one of the three samples and the host is genuinely mixed.
note: This host needs a composition-level split and the split rule is simply the B:Be ratio. Be2B goes to antifluorite, mp-1432. Be4B is tetragonal P4/nmm, mp-27757 at hull 0.000 with one ICSD reference -- a metal-rich beryllide that is not antifluorite and has no taxonomy entry, so it is parked at unresolved_crystalline rather than forced into one. BeB6 is the boron-rich end; the beryllium borides above BeB2 are icosahedral boron frameworks with beryllium in the interstices, which is why alb12_icosahedral is listed as the nearest idea, but [ref 2] offers nothing at that stoichiometry -- its boron-rich entry is Be4B25 P2/c mp-1227634 at hull 0.213 with no ICSD reference -- and the beryllium-boron phase diagram above BeB2 is genuinely unsettled in the literature. Confidence is medium for the host as a whole because two of its three samples are not the prototype named. Measured 323-1297 K with the full span reaching 1785 K.
annotator_note: BeB6 is the one composition here I would not defend. If stage 2 reaches it, it should be treated as an open question rather than as alb12_icosahedral on my say-so.

basis: The compositions are written as two-phase mixtures and mean what they say: (B4C)50(HfB2)50, (B4C)65(HfB2)35 and (B4C)70(HfB2)30, mole per cent of boron carbide and hafnium diboride. The paper is on the effect of microstructure on the mechanical, electrical and thermal properties of such a ceramic, which is a composite study, not a compound study. There is no HfBC line compound involved.
note: The alt_prototype_ids are the two constituents rather than alternative readings of one structure: B4C is boron_carbide, R-3m, and HfB2 is alb2, P6/mmm. is_mixed is false for the same reason as the As-Sb-Se-Te-Tl host -- every composition is the same mixture, so a per-composition split would not separate anything, and the composite is the material being measured. [ref 2] offers only HfBC P6_3/mmc mp-1232375 at hull 0.550 with no ICSD reference, which is a computed ternary carbide that does not exist here and would be a bad thing to record; mp_id is null. Measured 296-972 K. At these fractions the diboride forms a percolating conductive network in an insulating carbide matrix, so the transport is a percolation property of the microstructure rather than of either phase alone, which is precisely what the paper is about.

basis: HoB17CN is a member of the rare-earth boron carbonitride homologous series, and all three papers on this host name it: thermoelectric properties of homologous p- and n-type boron-rich borides, homologous rare earth boron cluster compounds as a possible n-type counterpart, and the doping effect in n-type rare earth boron carbonitrides. The structure is a layered framework of B12 icosahedra separated by B6 octahedra and C-B-C chains, with holmium on a discrete site between the layers -- the rare earth is what makes these n-type, which is the whole reason they were made, since almost every other boron cluster compound including B4C is p-type.
note: Prototype proposed in this chunk; see taxonomy/prototypes_proposed.jsonl. Neither reference printed a single entry for this host, so nothing external corroborates the assignment and mp_id is null. The space group recorded on the proposal is monoclinic C2/m and I have flagged there that I am not confident of the setting -- that uncertainty belongs to the prototype entry, not to whether this composition is a member of the series, which the papers state outright. Carbon and nitrogen are framework constituents, not dopants: they are below the threshold only because there are seventeen borons per formula unit. Measured 301-1038 K, the high-temperature window these materials are aimed at.

basis: The host key is a parse artifact and the material is YBa2Cu3O7. The composition string in the database is the literal text YBCO, which the composition parser read as the four elements Y, B, C and O -- hence a host system containing boron and carbon that contains neither. The curator composition details field confirms the string was YBCO and nothing more, the samples are single crystals and a polycrystal, the measured window is 30-140 K which brackets the 92 K superconducting transition, and the paper is on the interaction of carriers with phonons in single- and poly-crystalline high-Tc material. Every one of those points at the 123 cuprate.
note: This host should not exist and I would recommend it be merged into the Ba-Cu-O-Y host upstream rather than carried as a separate structure assignment. I have assigned it rather than leaving it unresolved because the material is not in doubt, but is_authoritative on this record is questionable in a way no field here captures: the three samples belong under the real YBCO host. The [ref 2] entry is the same artifact propagating into Materials Project -- YBCO7 Pbca (61) mp-1197370 at hull 0.560 is a computed yttrium-boron-carbon-oxygen compound generated from the same misread formula, and following it would be a genuine error. mp_id is left null; stage 2 should resolve the ordinary orthorhombic Pmmm YBa2Cu3O7 cell. The oxygen content delta is the doping variable of this family, as the taxonomy already records, but no delta is recoverable from a composition string that is just four letters.
annotator_note: Flagging for the input pipeline rather than for stage 2: the composition parser should either reject bare acronyms or route them through composition_details. YBCO is unlikely to be the only one.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [47], ICSD-backed references for this host report [61]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All three compositions are explicit phase mixtures and the curator transcribed the paper as TiB2-doped graphites. Two of them, (TiB2)0.1(C)0.9 and (TiB2)0.2(C)0.8, are graphite matrices with a titanium diboride second phase; the third, (TiB2)73.61(SiC)11.27(C)15.12, inverts that and is a diboride matrix with silicon carbide and free carbon. So the majority phase is not even the same across the host. The papers are on thermal transport in TiB2-doped graphite and on silicon carbide and graphene nanoplatelet reinforced ceramics -- both composite studies.

dopant_roles.basis: Silicon appears only in the one diboride-matrix composition and only as silicon carbide, a deliberately added third phase at 11 mol per cent. It is not dissolved in anything and does not substitute for a host element; it is a reinforcing particulate. Calling it a dopant would be exactly the composite-additive error the project README warns about.

note: is_mixed is true here, unlike the other two composites in this chunk, because the majority phase genuinely differs between compositions -- graphite for two of them and TiB2 for the third -- so a per-composition split would separate something real. The alt list names the three constituents: graphite_layered for the carbon, alb2 for TiB2, sic_polytype for the SiC. [ref 2] offers TiBC P6_3/mmc mp-1232377 at hull 0.307 with no ICSD reference, a computed ternary that is not what any of these samples contain; mp_id is null. Measured 298-1016 K. Note the sample form field says SingleCrystal for two of three samples, which cannot be right for a particulate composite and is probably a curation default rather than a claim.

basis: The paper is titled on the electronic properties of calcium borate glasses containing iron oxide, and the compositions are written the way glass batches are written: (CaO)30(B2O3)56(Fe2O3)14 and two others with the calcium oxide fixed at 30 mol per cent while the borate and iron oxide trade off continuously. B2O3 with an alkaline earth modifier is one of the classic glass-forming systems, and the iron oxide content is being varied to study small-polaron hopping between Fe2+ and Fe3+ in the glass network, which is what the electronic properties in the title refers to.
note: mp_id is null and stays null; the README lists amorphous as a stage 2 skip. Neither reference printed anything for this host, which is itself consistent -- a glass has no entry to print. The measured range is 418-501 K, a window of 83 K, and that narrowness is evidence rather than an inconvenience: these borate glasses have glass transitions in the 700-800 K region and the conductivity measurement stops well below it, but the low end at 418 K is above room temperature, which suggests the samples were too resistive to measure lower. Iron is a host element at 14 mol per cent of Fe2O3 and is the conduction mechanism, not an impurity.

basis: CePd3Bx at x = 0.25, 0.3 and 0.4. CePd3 is an ordered L12 Cu3Au-type intermetallic, cubic Pm-3m with cerium at the corners and palladium on the face centres, and it is one of the best-known intermediate-valence compounds. Boron does not replace anything: it enters the empty octahedral hole at the body centre of the cube, giving a filled L12 or anti-perovskite arrangement CePd3B with partial boron occupancy, and that filling is the variable being studied. [ref 2] gives CeBPd3 Pm-3m (221) mp-19948 with 2 ICSD references, which is the fully filled x = 1 end of the same structure.

dopant_roles.site: the 1b octahedral hole at the cube body centre
dopant_roles.basis: Boron is not a substituent anywhere in this system. It occupies the octahedral interstice of the Cu3Au cell, which is empty in CePd3 and fully occupied in CePd3B, and at x = 0.25 to 0.4 it is partially filling that one site. Each boron donates electrons to the conduction band and expands the lattice, which drives cerium from intermediate valence towards trivalent local-moment behaviour -- that valence crossover is what the thermoelectric study is measuring. So x is the working variable of the experiment, like the oxygen content in a cuprate, and stage 3 should report the site occupancy rather than an impurity level.

note: Boron is above 5 atomic per cent here (0.25 boron in a formula unit of 4.25 atoms is about 6 per cent) so it is treated as a host element by the threshold and does not appear in the dopant candidates line, but I have recorded its role anyway because the interstitial filling is the entire point of the compound and a stage 2 structure lookup that returns bare CePd3 would lose it. mp-19948 is the x = 1 end member, not the measured composition, so I have not put it in phases -- a partially occupied interstitial site is not the same structure as a fully occupied one and stage 2 should resolve the occupancy rather than inherit it. The other [ref 2] entry, Ce2BPd6 P4/mmm mp-1226779 at hull 0.117, is a computed ordering of the half-filled case and may in fact be closer to these compositions, but it carries no ICSD reference. Measured 13-297 K, the low-temperature window appropriate to a heavy-fermion or intermediate-valence study.

basis: The paper is on the magnetic and thermoelectric properties of B-substituted NaCoO2 and the compositions are Na0.7Co1-xBxO2 at x = 0.25, 0.375 and 0.75. The parent is the layered sodium cobaltate: CoO2 sheets of edge-sharing octahedra with sodium partially occupying the interlayer, the archetypal large-thermopower oxide. Sodium is fixed at 0.7 across all three, which is the standard NaxCoO2 composition, and boron is being put onto the cobalt site.
note: I do not follow [ref 2] and the reason is worth stating. Every entry it offers is a genuine borate -- Na2Co2(B4O7)3 C2/m mp-704577, Na3Co(BO3)2 P2_1/c mp-773604, Na6Co2B4SO16 Fd-3 mp-851008, NaCoBO3 C2/m mp-1101692 -- in which boron sits in BO3 or BO4 groups and forms the anion framework. That is the thermodynamically sensible thing for this element set and is probably what a Na-Co-B-O sample would become at equilibrium, but it is not what the paper made. The paper substituted boron into the cobalt site of a layered cobaltate, which is a metastable arrangement reached by solid-state synthesis, and the reference cannot see it. mp_id is null; stage 2 should resolve gamma-Na0.7CoO2, P6_3/mmc. Boron is a host element by the threshold at 0.25 to 0.75 per formula unit and its role is framework substitution on the cobalt site rather than doping -- at x = 0.75 it is the majority occupant of that site, and whether a CoO2 layer survives 75 per cent boron substitution is a real question the paper would have to answer. Measured 15-300 K.
annotator_note: The x = 0.75 composition strains belief as a single-phase layered cobaltate. If stage 2 reaches it, check whether the paper reports a second phase.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [194], ICSD-backed references for this host report [15]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: YCrB4 is the type compound of its own structure: orthorhombic Pbam, with a planar boron net built from fused five- and seven-membered rings, the large yttrium sitting in the seven-membered ring and the smaller chromium in the five-membered one. [ref 2] gives YCrB4 Pbam (55) mp-20450 at hull 0.000, the correct space group. YCrB6 is the next member of the same idea, with six- and seven-membered rings. The paper is an electron-counting screen for prospective boride thermoelectrics, so the family was chosen deliberately.

dopant_roles.site: the large-cation site in the seven-membered boron ring
dopant_roles.basis: Ce at 5 per cent of the yttrium site in Y0.95Ce0.05CrB6. Cerium and yttrium are both trivalent rare earths of similar size and cerium goes onto the same seven-ring site, so this adds no carriers directly. What it adds is an f electron: the second paper on this host is a physical-review study of thermoelectricity and electronic structure, and a dilute cerium substitution in a rare-earth boride is the standard way to introduce Kondo scattering and look for an enhanced thermopower. The substitution is deliberate and the level is dilute, so this is doping in the ordinary sense.

note: Prototype proposed in this chunk; see taxonomy/prototypes_proposed.jsonl. The mp_id recorded in phases is for YCrB4, which is one of the three compositions; the two YCrB6 compositions have no reference entry at all and stage 2 will need to resolve that stoichiometry separately. I have not marked the host mixed, because the B4 and B6 members share the same planar ring-net motif, the same space group and the same prototype entry -- the difference is the ring size, not the structure type. The measured window is 10-1002 K with the full span reaching 1073 K, which is unusually wide and suggests the host pools a low-temperature magnetic or Kondo study with a high-temperature thermoelectric one.

basis: Two of the three samples are ErB12, cubic UB12 type, Fm-3m, with the erbium enclosed in a framework of B12 cuboctahedra -- and one of the three papers is titled on the thermal conductivity of metal dodecaborides with a UB12 structure, which names both the compound and the structure. [ref 2] confirms ErB12 Fm-3m (225) mp-1104598 at hull 0.000. The third sample, Er1.12B17.64CN, is not this at all: it is a rare-earth boron carbonitride from the homologous series proposed for the B-C-Ho-N host in this same chunk, and the third paper is on the doping effect in n-type rare earth boron carbonitrides.

dopant_roles.site: the C-B-C chain positions between icosahedral layers
dopant_roles.basis: Carbon appears only in the Er1.12B17.64CN composition, where it is a structural constituent of the carbonitride framework and sits in the C-B-C chains between the icosahedral layers. It is under 5 atomic per cent only because there are nearly eighteen borons per formula unit. It is absent from the two ErB12 samples entirely, so a host-level statement that carbon dopes ErB12 would be false.

dopant_roles.site: the discrete nitrogen site of the carbonitride framework
dopant_roles.basis: Nitrogen, like the carbon, belongs only to the carbonitride composition and is a framework constituent of it. Together with the rare earth it is what makes this series n-type, which is the reason these compounds were made; the third paper on this host is on exactly that doping effect.

note: Split this host by whether carbon and nitrogen are present. ErB12 goes to ub12_boride, mp-1104598. Er1.12B17.64CN goes to reb17cn_boron_carbonitride, proposed in this chunk. The third entry in alt_prototype_ids, cab6_hexaboride, is there because the curator recorded that 8 per cent ErB6 and 4 per cent ErB4 were added to the ErB17CN sample -- so that sample is a deliberate three-phase composite, with ErB6 being cubic hexaboride and ErB4 tetragonal P4/mbm, and stage 2 should expect it to be multiphase rather than a clean carbonitride. [ref 2] lists ErB4, ErB6, ErB2 and ErB12 with 5, 4, 3 and 1 ICSD references respectively, and the single reference on ErB12 makes it the weakest-attested of the four -- but the papers name dodecaborides explicitly, so reference count is not the right tiebreaker here. Measured 11-1037 K.

basis: Fe40Ni40P14B6 is Metglas 2826A, one of the original commercial amorphous ferromagnetic alloys, and both papers say so in their titles: thermoelectric power in some ferromagnetic Fe-based amorphous alloys, and transport properties of Fe-Ni glasses. The sample form is Ribbon for two of three samples, which is melt-spinning, the only way this composition is made. The metalloid content of 20 atomic per cent phosphorus plus boron is the classic metal-metalloid glass-forming ratio.
note: mp_id is null and stays null; the README lists metallic_glass as a stage 2 skip. Neither reference printed anything, as expected for a glass. Phosphorus and boron are host constituents and network stabilisers, not dopants -- they are what makes the alloy vitrify, and removing them would not give a doped crystal, it would give a different material. Measured 20-508 K. The top of that window is worth noting: Metglas 2826A crystallises somewhere around 650-700 K, so 508 K is below it and the samples should still be amorphous throughout, but a thermopower measurement taken on a ribbon heated towards 500 K may show structural relaxation effects that are not reversible. The Curie temperature of this composition is near 520 K, right at the top of the window, so the magnetic contribution to the thermopower will not be constant across it.

basis: Fe2OBO3 is the iron warwickite, and the second paper names it outright: electrical transport in charge-ordered Fe2OBO3. The first is on the role of t2g versus eg interactions in the physical properties of A2OBO3, which is the family. The diagnostic is the oxygen that is not part of the borate group -- Fe2(O)(BO3), with ribbons four octahedra wide of edge- and corner-sharing FeO6 running along the short axis, isolated from each other by triangular BO3 units. The iron is half Fe2+ and half Fe3+ and orders below about 317 K, which is what gives this compound its Verwey-like transition and the resistive switching in the second title.
note: Prototype proposed in this chunk; see taxonomy/prototypes_proposed.jsonl. I do not follow [ref 2]: its five entries -- Fe3B7IO13 R3c mp-1194881, Fe2B2O5 P-1 mp-19333, Fe3BO6 Pnma mp-25746, FeBO3 R-3c mp-19097 and Fe5(BO3)6 Pmmn mp-1198168 -- are all ordinary borates in which every oxygen belongs to a boron-oxygen group. None of them is an oxyborate with a free oxide ion, which is the whole structural point here. mp_id is left null. spans_transition is false because the 317 K charge-ordering transition is a symmetry lowering within the warwickite framework from orthorhombic to monoclinic, not a change of prototype, and the taxonomy has no separate entry for the ordered form. But it sits squarely inside the 163-649 K measured window and transport across that window is two regimes, not one, so anything read off a single fitted curve here will be misleading.

basis: The compositions read LuNi2B2 and its ytterbium substitutions, but the paper is titled on the physical properties of Lu1-xYbxNi2B2C -- the carbon is present in the material and missing from the parsed composition string. This is the rare-earth nickel borocarbide, tetragonal I4/mmm, with NiB4 tetrahedral layers alternating with rare-earth-carbon rocksalt sheets, the family that includes the superconductors LuNi2B2C at 16 K and YNi2B2C at 15 K. Single crystals, measured 10-296 K, which is the window that family is always studied in.

dopant_roles.site: the rare-earth site of the carbon-containing rocksalt sheet
dopant_roles.basis: Yb at 7.5 and 20 per cent of the lutetium site. Both are trivalent rare earths at the same site, so the size change is small, but ytterbium is the one that carries an f hole and YbNi2B2C is the heavy-fermion end of this series while LuNi2B2C is the closed-shell superconductor. Substituting one for the other is a continuous tuning between those two limits, which is exactly what the paper maps; the same series is measured from the other end in the B-Ni-Yb host. Below 5 atomic per cent only at the dilute end -- the 20 per cent composition is well into alloying.

note: The missing carbon is the thing to fix. Every composition in this host should read LuNi2B2C, and the host key should be B-C-Lu-Ni; as parsed, this host and B-Ni-Yb are two ends of one Lu1-xYbxNi2B2C series that the parser has also split apart on the Lu:Yb ratio. I do not follow [ref 2] at all: it lists Lu3Ni7B2 mp-865190, Lu2(Ni5B3)3 mp-1201139, Lu2(Ni7B2)3 mp-1193129, Lu2(NiB2)3 mp-8771 and Lu4NiB13 mp-1200891, every one of them a carbon-free binary or ternary boride, because the carbon it would need to find the right compound is absent from the formula it was given. This is a clear case of a parse artifact propagating into a reference lookup and it would have produced a wrong structure if followed. mp_id is null; stage 2 should resolve LuNi2B2C in I4/mmm.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [139], ICSD-backed references for this host report [191, 194, 55, 65]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: YMoB4 is the molybdenum analogue of YCrB4 and takes the same structure: orthorhombic Pbam with a planar boron net of fused five- and seven-membered rings, yttrium in the seven-ring and molybdenum in the five-ring. [ref 2] gives YB4Mo Pbam (55) mp-7691 at hull 0.000, the correct space group. The paper is the same electron-counting screen for prospective boride thermoelectrics that covers the B-Cr-Y host, so the two hosts are the same study sampling two members of one family.

dopant_roles.site: the planar boron ring net
dopant_roles.basis: YMoB3.8C0.2 puts carbon on the boron net at 5 per cent of that site. The paper applies an electron counting rule to screen these borides, and carbon for boron adds one electron per substitution to the covalent net -- that is the direct way to move the Fermi level in an electron-counting framework, so this is deliberate n-type-side tuning rather than contamination. Recorded as substitutional rather than framework_substitution because it is a dilute replacement on one crystallographic site, not a compositional variable of the structure type.

dopant_roles.site: the small-cation site in the five-membered boron ring
dopant_roles.basis: YMo0.8Fe0.2B4 substitutes iron for molybdenum at 20 per cent of the small-cation site. Iron and molybdenum sit in different rows and carry different electron counts, so this is the other lever of the same electron-counting screen, applied to the metal site instead of the boron net. At 20 per cent of the site it is alloying rather than dilute doping; it falls under the 5 atomic per cent threshold only because there are four borons per formula unit.

note: Prototype proposed in this chunk; see taxonomy/prototypes_proposed.jsonl. Both substitutions here are small and deliberate and neither changes the prototype, so the host is not mixed. The other [ref 2] entry, YB2Mo Amm2 mp-1215920 at hull 0.098 with no ICSD reference, is a computed lower boride and not relevant. Measured 315-1031 K, a clean high-temperature thermoelectric window with no known transition in this structure type inside it.

basis: One composition, BN, three samples, two papers, and the papers are the reason for the call: one is Slack on nonmetallic crystals with high thermal conductivity, the other the 2018 measurement of high thermal conductivity in boron arsenide. Both are about the small set of high-thermal-conductivity covalent solids, and the boron nitride that belongs in that set is the cubic zincblende form, c-BN, at roughly 750 W per metre kelvin. [ref 2] ranks BN F-43m (216) mp-1639 first on ICSD evidence with 20 references, the most of any entry for the formula. Confidence is medium rather than high because a bare BN composition string cannot distinguish the polymorphs and hexagonal BN is the far more common material in general.

other_polymorphs.note: Hexagonal BN, hull 0.000 with 11 ICSD references, and the thermodynamically stable form at ambient pressure. Listed as another polymorph rather than as a thermal phase because heating does not convert cubic BN into it at any accessible temperature -- the two are made by different routes, c-BN by high pressure. Slack also measured pyrolytic hexagonal BN, so one of the three samples here may well be this.

Wurtzitic w-BN, hull 0.093 with 7 ICSD references, and the polymorph [ref 1] TEDesignLab selects. It is a shock-compression product, metastable, and not what a thermal conductivity study of a bulk crystal would be made of.

note: This is a disagreement with [ref 1] and I want it recorded rather than smoothed over. TEDesignLab gives BN P6_3mc (186), the wurtzitic form, as its single entry, and project precedence says prefer TEDesignLab where it covers a formula. I am not following it here, because w-BN is a shock-synthesis metastable phase that no one measures thermal conductivity on, while both papers are squarely about the high-conductivity covalent solids where c-BN is a standard member. The reference is describing a phase that exists in this chemistry, not the phase these papers made -- the Al-O-Zn case in the README exactly. is_mixed is true because three samples across two papers on a formula with three real polymorphs almost certainly do not all share one structure, and a sample-level rather than composition-level split would be needed to separate them -- one composition string cannot carry three structures. mp_id is left null at host level for that reason. Measured 13-295 K with the full span to 600 K.
annotator_note: This host is a candidate for determined_at sample_required rather than host, in the same way Fe2O3 is. One composition string, three genuine polymorphs, and the papers are the only thing that can separate them.

basis: The compositions are written as phase mixtures -- (TiB2)8Si3N4, (TiB2)3Si3N4, (TiB2)4.7Si3N4 -- and the paper is on the fabrication and contact resistivity of W-Si3N4 / TiB2-Si3N4 / p-type junctions, which is an electrode and joining study on a ceramic composite. TiB2-Si3N4 is a standard electroconductive ceramic: conductive titanium diboride particles in an insulating silicon nitride matrix, made conductive by percolation. There is no quaternary Ti-B-Si-N compound here.
note: Only one of the two constituents has a taxonomy entry: TiB2 is alb2, P6/mmm. Silicon nitride does not appear in the taxonomy at all -- beta-Si3N4 is hexagonal P6_3/m with corner-sharing SiN4 tetrahedra, and alpha-Si3N4 is P31c -- and I have not proposed an entry for it, because it turns up here only as the inert matrix of a composite and never as the thermoelectric itself. If a later chunk has silicon nitride as a host material in its own right it would need one. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null. is_mixed is false because every composition is the same two-phase mixture at a different ratio. Measured 291-1163 K, the working range of a contact-resistivity study on a high-temperature module.

basis: The same series as the B-Lu-Ni host and the same paper, Lu1-xYbxNi2B2C, seen from the ytterbium-rich end: YbNi2B2, Lu0.1Yb0.9Ni2B2 and Lu0.2Yb0.8Ni2B2 as parsed, all of them YbNi2B2C in the material. Rare-earth nickel borocarbide, tetragonal I4/mmm, NiB4 tetrahedral layers alternating with rare-earth-carbon rocksalt sheets. YbNi2B2C is the well-known heavy-fermion member of that family, with a large low-temperature specific heat and no superconductivity, and the single crystals measured from 10 to 295 K here are what such a study looks like.

dopant_roles.site: the rare-earth site of the carbon-containing rocksalt sheet
dopant_roles.basis: Lu at 10 and 20 per cent of the ytterbium site, the mirror image of the ytterbium substitution recorded on the B-Lu-Ni host. Lutetium has a full f shell and no moment, so diluting the ytterbium with it suppresses the heavy-fermion coherence and moves the alloy towards the superconducting Lu end. The same physical series, entered from the other side; which element counts as the dopant here is an artifact of where the 5 atomic per cent line happens to fall, not a statement about the chemistry.

note: Carbon is missing from every composition string here exactly as in B-Lu-Ni, and the two hosts are one Lu1-xYbxNi2B2C series that the host-system key has split in two -- B-Lu-Ni holds x = 0 to 0.2 and this host holds x = 0.8 to 1. Both should be B-C-Lu-Ni-Yb. I do not follow [ref 2] for the same reason as in the other host: YbNiB4 mp-21181, Yb2(Ni2B)5 mp-1204889, Yb2(Ni7B2)3 mp-1193375, Yb3Ni13B2 mp-865970 and Yb2(NiB2)3 mp-14344 are all carbon-free borides found by matching a formula that is missing an element. mp_id is null; stage 2 should resolve YbNi2B2C in I4/mmm.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [139], ICSD-backed references for this host report [55, 191, 61, 65]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: One composition, (TiB2)19.46(ZnO)80.54, written as a two-phase mixture, and the paper is titled on the preparation and thermoelectric properties of ZnO-TiB2 composites. Zinc oxide is the matrix at 80 mol per cent and titanium diboride is a conductive dispersed phase; neither dissolves appreciably in the other, and the point of adding the diboride is to raise the electrical conductivity of a wurtzite ZnO matrix without the usual aluminium doping.
note: This is the borderline case the project README warns about in both directions. Read one way, the additive is relabelling its host and the record should say wurtzite ZnO -- 80 mol per cent is a clear majority. Read the other way, 19.46 mol per cent is far too much to be a dispersion in any meaningful sense, the title says composites, and the transport being measured is the composite response rather than the matrix response. I have gone with composite_multiphase because the diboride fraction is well above the percolation range and the measured conductivity is not a ZnO property at that loading, and I have put wurtzite first in alt_prototype_ids so the matrix is not lost. If stage 2 needs a single structure it should take wurtzite ZnO, P6_3mc. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null. Measured 175-852 K.

basis: Both papers are on vanadium-doped beta-rhombohedral boron: one on the vanadium concentration dependence of its thermoelectric properties, the other on the low critical concentration of its metal-insulator transition. Two of the three compositions, V11B89 and V32B68, are written as atomic percentages of a boron-rich mixture, which is how that work is reported -- metal atoms entering the partially occupied interstitial sites of the 105-atom beta-boron cell, moving transport from variable-range hopping towards metallic as they fill. The third composition is plain VB2 and is not this structure at all.
note: Prototype proposed in this chunk; see taxonomy/prototypes_proposed.jsonl, which also explains why beta-boron is being split out of boron_carbide. Confidence is medium and the arithmetic is the reason. V32B68 is V:B of 1:2.13, which is within rounding of VB2 itself, and the accepted solubility of vanadium in beta-rhombohedral boron is a few atomic per cent, not 32. Even V11B89 at 1:8 is far above it. So either these are nominal starting compositions rather than the composition of the doped boron phase, or the samples are two-phase with VB2 precipitated alongside vanadium-saturated boron -- the second is what the boron-rich end of the V-B phase diagram would predict. I have kept beta_rhombohedral_boron as the host prototype because that is what both papers are studying and what the thermoelectric behaviour belongs to, but stage 2 should expect a second phase and the split rule by V:B ratio would put V32B68 on the wrong side of any threshold set naively. VB2 goes to alb2, P6/mmm, mp-1491, which [ref 2] attests strongly at 17 ICSD references. Measured 52-299 K robust, with the full span reaching 1080 K.
annotator_note: The V32B68 composition is the one I would check first against the papers. If it is really VB2 by another name, this host is two thirds diboride and the primary prototype should flip.

basis: BaBiO3 with antimony substituting bismuth at 10 and 20 per cent, and the paper is on electrical conduction and thermoelectric properties of perovskite-type oxides. BaBiO3 is the textbook charge-disproportionated perovskite: nominally Bi4+, actually an ordered alternation of Bi3+ and Bi5+ on the B site, which produces a breathing distortion of the oxygen octahedra plus a tilt, lowering the symmetry from cubic to monoclinic. [ref 2] puts BaBiO3 C2/m (12) mp-22942 first with 10 ICSD references, which is that distorted cell.

dopant_roles.site: the perovskite B site
dopant_roles.basis: Sb at 10 and 20 per cent of the bismuth site. Antimony sits directly above bismuth in group 15 and is isovalent with it, so no carriers are added, but antimony does not disproportionate the way bismuth does -- it stays Sb5+ -- so substituting it dilutes and eventually destroys the Bi3+/Bi5+ charge ordering that the breathing distortion depends on. That is the lever the paper is pulling, and it continues into the Ba-Bi-O-Sb host where the substitution reaches 50 per cent. At 10 to 20 per cent of one site this is closer to alloying than to dilute doping.

note: BaBiO3 has a known sequence of tilt transitions on heating -- monoclinic to rhombohedral near 405 K and rhombohedral towards cubic above roughly 800 K -- and the measured window is 417-971 K, so the samples are never in the monoclinic ground state during measurement and probably cross the second transition near the top. spans_transition is left false because every one of those forms is a tilted perovskite and the prototype does not change; the taxonomy has no separate entries for the tilt variants. But it does mean the mp-22942 monoclinic cell recorded in phases is not the structure that was actually measured, and stage 2 should be aware that the measured phase is the rhombohedral or cubic one. The remaining [ref 2] entries are other barium bismuthates at different stoichiometries and are not relevant. The curator note on one composition records that logarithmic values in a figure were converted by exponentiation, so those data are derived rather than directly digitised.

basis: BaBi1-xSbxO3 at x = 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 -- the continuation of the Ba-Bi-O host from the same paper, past the point where bismuth and antimony order. At x = 0.5 the composition is Ba2BiSbO6 and the two B-site cations take up a rocksalt ordering, which is the defining feature of a double perovskite. [ref 2] supports it directly: Ba2BiSbO6 R-3 (148) mp-23091 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references, first on evidence, with a C2/m variant mp-23127 behind it at 2 references. R-3 is the rhombohedral tilted double perovskite, not a coincidence of formula.
note: The split between this host and Ba-Bi-O is an artifact of the 5 atomic per cent rule falling in the middle of one substitution series -- x = 0.1 and 0.2 land in Ba-Bi-O with antimony as a dopant candidate, x = 0.3 to 0.5 land here with it as a host element -- and the two should be read together. That said, the split happens to be physically reasonable: somewhere in this range the B-site cations go from disordered to rocksalt-ordered, and that is a real change of prototype from perovskite to double_perovskite. Whether the x = 0.3 composition is already ordered is not something composition can settle, which is why perovskite is listed as the alternative. Ba2BiSbO6 also replaces the Bi3+/Bi5+ charge disproportionation of the parent with an ordinary Bi3+/Sb5+ alternation, so the breathing distortion is gone and the material is a wide-gap insulator rather than a bad metal. Measured 474-973 K.

basis: Ba3Co2O6(CO3)0.7, and the paper title says it contains one-dimensional chains. The structure is a hexagonal perovskite derivative: columns of face-sharing CoO6 octahedra running along the hexagonal axis, separated by barium, with carbonate groups occupying the channels between the columns and setting the cobalt oxidation state through their partial occupancy. That face-sharing octahedral column is the 2H hexagonal perovskite motif, which is why I have filed it here rather than under the chain cobaltite entry.
note: Confidence is medium because the choice between the two candidates is a real one and I am not certain of it. Ca3Co2O6 has the same A3B2O6 stoichiometry and also has one-dimensional cobalt chains, but its chains alternate face-sharing octahedra with trigonal prisms in the K4CdCl6 arrangement, R-3c, and it has no anion group in the channels. Ba3Co2O6(CO3)0.7 is built on columns of octahedra alone with carbonate between them, which is the hexagonal perovskite side of the family. If the published refinement turns out to show alternating octahedra and prisms, ca3co2o6_chain is the right entry and this record should flip. Neither reference printed anything for this host and mp_id is null. The carbonate is a structural constituent and a charge-setting variable, not an impurity -- its 0.7 occupancy is what fixes the cobalt valence -- and the carbon is a host element by the threshold, so no dopant role is recorded. Measured 298-1109 K. Carbonate-containing oxides decompose on heating in air, and 1109 K is high enough that carbonate loss during measurement is a real possibility worth checking against the paper.

basis: PrBa1-xCaxCoCuO5 at x = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. The LnBaM2O5+delta stoichiometry with a trivalent rare earth and barium in a one-to-one ratio is the A-site ordered double perovskite: praseodymium and barium alternate in layers along one axis rather than mixing, which is what makes it layered rather than a plain perovskite, and the oxygen vacancies order into the rare-earth layer. The paper is on these as cathode materials for solid oxide fuel cells, where the ordered form is prized for its fast oxygen transport. [ref 2] offers Ba2PrCoCu2O7 Pmmm mp-1214590, a related A-site ordered cell in the same family.

dopant_roles.site: the alkaline-earth layer of the ordered A site
dopant_roles.basis: Ca at 10 to 30 per cent of the barium site, and the paper names the series in its title. Calcium is isovalent with barium and much smaller, so this is chemical pressure rather than charge doping: it contracts the lattice, tilts the octahedra and shifts the oxygen non-stoichiometry delta, which in turn changes the cobalt and copper valence. The carrier concentration moves, but indirectly through delta rather than by the substitution itself. At 30 per cent this is alloying, not dilute doping.

note: The oxygen content delta is the real doping variable in this family, exactly as the taxonomy records for the cuprates, and it is not recoverable from these composition strings -- all three are written as O5 with no delta. Stage 3 should not read a carrier concentration out of the calcium fraction alone. mp_id is left null: mp-1214590 is Ba2PrCoCu2O7, a different cation ratio with two coppers per cobalt rather than one, so it is evidence that the family is real but not the structure of these samples. Measured 374-1123 K, the operating range of a fuel cell cathode.

basis: BayFe4-xCoxSb12 -- the second paper gives that formula in its title and the compositions match it exactly: Ba0.9Fe2Co2Sb12, BaFe3Co1Sb12, Ba0.86Fe3CoSb12, all with twelve antimonies and four transition metals. This is the filled skutterudite, cubic Im-3, with the Sb4 rings and the transition metal on the octahedral site, and barium sitting in the icosahedral void of the framework. The barium occupancy below unity in two of the three compositions is the signature of a filled skutterudite rather than a line compound -- the cage is never quite full.
note: Barium is a host element here at about 5 per cent of the atom count and does not appear on the dopant candidates line, but its role is cage_filler and that is what the prototype is named for: it rattles in the oversized void and scatters the heat-carrying phonons, which is the entire design principle. The iron-cobalt ratio is the other variable -- FeSb3 is not stable unfilled, so filling and iron content are coupled, and the cobalt substitution is what sets the electron count. Both are host elements so neither gets a dopant role, but stage 3 should record the barium filling fraction y and the cobalt fraction x as the two working variables. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null. Measured 15-493 K.

basis: The paper is on the synthesis, transport and magnetic properties of Ba-Co-Ge clathrates, so the family is stated; the question is which type, and the three compositions do not agree. Ba6Co2Ge23 and Ba6Co5Ge20 both have six barium and twenty-five framework atoms, which is the Ba6Ge25 arrangement, the chiral cubic type IX clathrate in P4132. Ba8Co3Ge43 has eight barium and forty-six framework atoms, which is type I. Two compositions to one for the Ba6 form, so that is the host prototype, but the host is genuinely mixed.
note: The split rule is the guest-to-framework ratio: 6:25 goes to clathrate_iii_ix, 8:46 to clathrate_i. Confidence is medium because Ba6Co5Ge20 is a long way from the Ba6Ge25 parent in cobalt content -- five of twenty-five framework sites -- and I am taking it on the ratio alone. [ref 2] is no help: its only entry is Ba(CoGe)2 I4/mmm mp-1070253, a ThCr2Si2-type line compound with no cage at all, found by formula proximity. mp_id is null for both forms. Measured 12-302 K, which is a magnetic and low-temperature transport study rather than a thermoelectric performance one, consistent with the paper title.

basis: PrBa0.5Sr0.5Co2O5+delta and two barium-deficient variants of it, and one paper names the series in its title as A-site Ba-deficient PrBa0.5-xSr0.5Co2O5+delta. Same family as the Ba-Co-Cu-O-Pr host: the LnBaCo2O5+delta A-site ordered double perovskite, with praseodymium and the alkaline-earth layer alternating along the c axis and the oxygen vacancies ordering in the rare-earth layer. Both papers are solid oxide fuel cell cathode studies, where that layered ordering is the reason the material is used.
note: Strontium is fixed at 0.5 in all three compositions and is a host element, not a dopant -- the half-and-half barium-strontium occupancy of the alkaline-earth layer is the standard composition of this cathode material, chosen for its thermal expansion match rather than as a doping step. The variable being studied is the A-site deficiency: praseodymium at 0.94 and barium at 0.46 in two of the compositions, against full occupancy in the third. Vacancies on the A site raise the cobalt valence and the oxygen content, so the deficiency is the carrier-concentration knob here, and stage 3 should read it from the site occupancies rather than treating the missing fraction as a parse error. Neither reference printed anything; mp_id is null. Measured 321-1072 K.

basis: PrBaCuFeO5 and La0.25Pr0.75BaCuFeO5, with the curator transcribing the series from the paper as La1-xPrxBaCuFeO5+delta. One paper is titled on the thermoelectric properties of layered ferrocuprates LnBaCuFeO5+delta, which names both the layering and the family. This is the A-site ordered double perovskite again -- rare earth and barium alternating along c, with the oxygen vacancies ordered into the rare-earth layer -- but with an ordered or partly ordered copper and iron B site rather than cobalt. [ref 2] gives BaPrFeCuO5 P4mm mp-1206136 at hull 0.000, the same formula and a tetragonal layered cell.

dopant_roles.site: the rare-earth layer of the ordered A site
dopant_roles.basis: La at 25 per cent of the praseodymium site, and the second paper is on the structure and properties of exactly that La1-xPrxBaCuFeO5+delta solid solution. Lanthanum and praseodymium are both trivalent and go to the same layer, so no carriers are added directly; lanthanum is larger, so the substitution expands the rare-earth layer and shifts the oxygen non-stoichiometry delta, which is where any change in carrier concentration comes from. At a quarter of the site this is alloying rather than dilute doping, and it is under the threshold only because there are eight other atoms in the formula.

note: mp-1206136 is the right formula in a plausible space group but carries no ICSD reference, and P4mm is polar, which is a strong claim for a computed structure -- the reported symmetry for this family is usually P4/mmm. I have not put it in phases; stage 2 should resolve it properly rather than inherit a hull-generated cell. The other [ref 2] entry, Ba4Pr4Fe4Cu4O21 I4/mmm mp-1228619, is the same chemistry at a different oxygen content, which is a reminder that delta is a real variable here and not a decoration on the formula. As in the other members of this family in this chunk, delta is the doping variable and cannot be recovered from a composition string written as O5. Measured 294-1085 K.

basis: Ba8Cu5Si6Ge32Sn3. The framework atoms Cu plus Si plus Ge plus Sn sum to exactly 46 and the barium count is exactly 8, which is the type I clathrate to the atom: two dodecahedral and six tetrakaidecahedral cages per unit cell, each holding one guest. The paper is on nanostructured clathrates and clathrate-based nanocomposites. A four-element framework with copper on it is the standard way of tuning a type I clathrate, and the silicon-germanium-tin mixture is mass disorder deliberately introduced to scatter phonons.
note: Copper is a host element at 5 of 46 framework sites and its role is framework_substitution, the case the taxonomy already names for Ga, Al and Cu in Ba8Ga16Ge30: it sets the electron count of the anionic framework against the eight Ba2+ guests rather than doping in the ordinary sense. Silicon, germanium and tin share the remaining framework sites; they are all group 14 and mutually substitutional, so that part is an isoelectronic alloy on one sublattice, but with a single composition in the host there is no range to record and solid_solution_axis is left null. Neither reference printed anything; mp_id is null and stage 2 should resolve a Pm-3n cell. The paper title mentions nanocomposites, so some samples in this host may carry a second phase deliberately; nothing in the composition string shows one. Measured 422-824 K.

basis: LuBa2Cu3O7 and two strontium-substituted versions of it, and the paper is on structure and superconductivity studies of LnBa2-xSrxCu3O7 with Ln including Yb and Lu. This is the 123 cuprate with lutetium in place of yttrium: orthorhombic Pmmm, two CuO2 planes sandwiching the rare earth, with CuO chains between the barium layers, and the oxygen content setting the doping. Nearly every trivalent rare earth except cerium, praseodymium and terbium forms it. [ref 2] gives Ba2LuCu3O7 Pmmm (47) mp-20324, the 123 cell at the right stoichiometry.

dopant_roles.site: the barium site between the CuO2 plane and the CuO chain
dopant_roles.basis: Sr at 20 and 25 per cent of the barium site, which is what the paper varies. Strontium is isovalent with barium and smaller, so it applies chemical pressure: the barium layer contracts, the apical copper-oxygen distance shortens, and the chain oxygen ordering and Tc shift as a result. No carriers are added by the substitution itself. At a quarter of the site this is alloying; it falls below 5 atomic per cent only because a 123 formula unit has thirteen atoms.

note: mp-20324 carries a single ICSD reference and sits at hull 0.037, and the better-attested [ref 2] entry is Ba2Lu(CuO2)3 P4/mmm mp-21868 with 2 references -- that is the tetragonal oxygen-deficient form, the non-superconducting O6 end of the same compound. Which of the two describes a given sample depends entirely on the oxygen content, and the composition strings here all say O7, the orthorhombic superconducting end. I have taken the orthorhombic reading and left mp_id null rather than pick between them on reference count. The oxygen content delta is the doping variable of this family, as the taxonomy records, and O7 written flat gives no delta to work with. Measured 60-289 K, consistent with a superconductivity study; Tc for the lutetium 123 is near 90 K, inside that window.

basis: Tl2Ba2CuO6 is Tl-2201, the single-CuO2-layer member of the Tl2Ba2Can-1CunO2n+4 series, and the paper is on systematic thermopower measurements of the thallium cuprates. It is the same structure family as Tl-2212 that the taxonomy entry is named for, just with n = 1 instead of 2 and therefore no calcium: a double thallium-oxide rocksalt block between single copper-oxide planes. [ref 2] gives Ba2Tl2CuO6 Cmce (64) mp-6027 at hull 0.006 with 3 ICSD references, which is the orthorhombic form of exactly this compound.
note: Worth flagging for review: the taxonomy entry is called tl_2212_cuprate and this compound is 2201. They are consecutive members of one homologous series and share the thallium-oxide double block, the rocksalt-perovskite intergrowth and the space group family, so filing it here is right, but the entry name will read as wrong to anyone scanning the ledger and a v4 taxonomy might reasonably rename it to cover the whole Tl-22(n-1)n series. Tl2Ba2CuO6 exists in both tetragonal I4/mmm and orthorhombic Cmce forms depending on the excess oxygen in the thallium layer, and that oxygen is the doping variable -- the compound runs from overdoped non-superconducting to Tc near 90 K with it. The composition string gives O6 flat, so the doping level is not recoverable here. I have recorded mp-6027 at medium confidence for that reason; the tetragonal form may be what was measured. Measured 27-286 K.

basis: Two of the three compositions are PrBaFe2O5+delta -- PrBa0.97Fe2O and PrBaFe2O5 as parsed -- and one paper is titled on evaluating Ba-deficient PrBa1-xFe2O5+delta. That is the A-site ordered double perovskite, praseodymium and barium alternating along c with ordered oxygen vacancies in the rare-earth layer, the iron analogue of the cobalt and copper members elsewhere in this chunk. The third composition, BaCe0.2Fe0.5Pr0.3O3, is not that at all: it is a plain ABO3 perovskite with a mixed B site, from a second paper on BaCe0.2Fe0.8O3-delta cathodes.

dopant_roles.site: the perovskite B site
dopant_roles.basis: Cerium appears only in BaCe0.2Fe0.5Pr0.3O3, where it is a B-site constituent of a barium cerate-ferrite perovskite at 20 per cent of that site -- the parent of that paper is BaCe0.2Fe0.8O3-delta, so cerium is not a dopant there either but a named component. It is absent from the two layered double perovskite compositions entirely, so a host-level claim that cerium dopes PrBaFe2O5 would be false. Recorded at 20 per cent of a site, which is alloying.

note: Split this host by whether praseodymium and barium are in a one-to-one ratio. PrBa0.97Fe2O and PrBaFe2O5 go to layered_double_perovskite; BaCe0.2Fe0.5Pr0.3O3 goes to perovskite, where praseodymium is a B-site or A-site substituent in a barium cerate-ferrite rather than the ordered rare-earth layer. Confidence is medium for the host because of that split and because the first composition, PrBa0.97Fe2O, has lost its oxygen subscript in parsing -- read literally it is O1, which is chemically impossible for this family; it should be O5+delta. [ref 2] offers only Ba6Pr2Fe4O15 Cc mp-1228608, a computed cell at a different cation ratio with no ICSD reference, and I do not follow it; mp_id is null. Measured 573-1073 K, a fuel-cell cathode window.
annotator_note: The PrBa0.97Fe2O composition string is malformed -- the oxygen stoichiometry is missing. Worth flagging upstream; it will also distort any at.% threshold computed from it.

basis: Ba8Ga16-xInxGe30 at x = 3, 6 and 9, and the paper is on the effect of indium additions on the thermoelectric properties of the type-I clathrate. The arithmetic is exact in all three: eight barium guests and forty-six framework atoms, Ga plus In plus Ge summing to 46 every time. Ba8Ga16Ge30 is the best-studied type I clathrate there is, and indium for gallium is a straightforward framework substitution on it.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: framework
solid_solution_axis.note: Ga/(Ga+In) across the three compositions. Gallium and indium are both group 13 and share the anionic framework sites, so the substitution is isoelectronic and the electron count against the eight Ba2+ guests is unchanged -- what changes is the mass contrast and the cage size, which is the phonon-scattering lever the paper is pulling. Recorded as a solid solution rather than as doping.

note: Gallium and indium are both host elements at these levels so neither carries a dopant role; their combined count of 16 against 30 germaniums is the electron-balance condition of the framework, not a doping choice. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null and stage 2 should resolve a Pm-3n cell. Measured 323-949 K.

basis: Three compositions and three different clathrate types, which is unusual enough to be the main finding here. Ba24In12Ge88 has 24 guests and 100 framework atoms, the Ba24Ge100 arrangement, which is type III -- and the first paper is titled on the crystal structure and thermoelectric properties of a type-III clathrate, so that is stated rather than inferred. Ba6Ge21.93In3.07 has 6 guests and 25 framework atoms, the chiral cubic Ba6Ge25 arrangement, type IX; the second paper is on the structure and thermoelectric properties of Ba6Ge25-x and Ba6Ge23Sn2. Ba8In16Ge30 has 8 guests and 46 framework atoms, type I. The taxonomy entry covers types III and IX together and two of the three compositions fall under it.
note: Split by the guest-to-framework ratio, which separates all three cleanly: 24:100 and 6:25 to clathrate_iii_ix, 8:46 to clathrate_i. Note that 24:100 reduces to 6:25, so a rule written on the reduced ratio alone would merge type III with type IX -- which is what the taxonomy entry does anyway, so no harm here, but a rule that also has to catch type I needs the unreduced counts. Confidence is medium only because the taxonomy lumps III and IX and I cannot tell from composition which of the two Ba24In12Ge88 is; the paper says type III. Ba6Ge25 in P4132 is chiral, which matters for stage 2: a centrosymmetric approximation would be the wrong structure. [ref 2] offers only BaInGe P3m1 mp-1227944 at hull 0.041 with no ICSD reference, a computed line compound with no cage, and I do not follow it; mp_id is null. Measured 83-925 K.

basis: BaMn2Sb2 is a 122 Zintl phase in the ThCr2Si2 structure, body-centred tetragonal I4/mmm, with MnSb4 tetrahedral layers separated by barium -- the second paper calls it a Zintl compound in its title and the first is on the synthesis and thermoelectric properties of BaMn2Sb2 single crystals. The 1:2:2 stoichiometry with a divalent alkaline earth and a transition metal pnictide layer is the defining formula of that entry, and the same structure holds across BaMn2As2, BaMn2Sb2 and BaMn2Bi2.
note: I do not follow [ref 2]. Its only entry is BaMnSb2 I4/mmm (139) mp-29206 at hull 0.089 with one ICSD reference, and although the space group is right the stoichiometry is not: BaMnSb2 is the 112 HfCuSi2-type structure, with a square antimony net and half the manganese, and it is a different compound with different physics -- a Dirac semimetal rather than a Zintl semiconductor. Matching on space group alone would have hidden that. mp_id is left null; stage 2 should resolve BaMn2Sb2 itself. Measured 297-778 K. BaMn2Sb2 orders antiferromagnetically well above room temperature, in the region of 400 K, so the Neel transition falls inside the measured window; spans_transition is left false because that is a magnetic ordering rather than a structural change and the prototype is unaffected, but the transport is not one regime across it.

basis: BaMn2-xZnxSb2 at x = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, and the paper is on the preparation and thermoelectric properties of BaMn2-xZnxSb2 Zintl compounds -- the continuation of the Ba-Mn-Sb host from the same group. Same ThCr2Si2 structure, I4/mmm, with zinc replacing manganese in the tetrahedral layer.
note: Zinc is a host element at 15 to 35 per cent of the atom count and takes no dopant role, but what it does is worth recording for stage 3: Mn2+ and Zn2+ are both divalent so the Zintl electron count is preserved and the compound stays a semiconductor, but zinc has a filled d shell and no magnetic moment, so the substitution dilutes the manganese antiferromagnetic lattice and removes the local-moment scattering. That is a magnetic substitution at fixed carrier count, not doping. This host and Ba-Mn-Sb are one series split by the 5 atomic per cent rule, and they share a paper. Neither reference printed anything here; mp_id is null. Measured 298-725 K, which will cross the manganese ordering temperature at the low-zinc end and probably not at the high-zinc end, since diluting the lattice pushes the Neel temperature down.

basis: The paper is on the electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity of NdBa2(Cu1-zZnz)3O7-delta, which is the neodymium 123 cuprate with zinc substituted onto the copper site. All three compositions are that compound at z = 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8. It is the same Pmmm 123 structure as YBa2Cu3O7 -- two CuO2 planes around the rare earth, CuO chains between the barium layers -- with neodymium in place of yttrium. Measured 11-118 K, which is the window a 123 study uses.

dopant_roles.site: the CuO2 plane and CuO chain sites
dopant_roles.basis: Copper is listed as a dopant candidate here, and it is nothing of the kind -- it is the structural backbone of the compound. The composition strings read NdBa2(Cu0.06Zn0.04)3O7 and similar, in which the bracketed site occupancies sum to 0.1 instead of 1, so the parser sees 0.18 copper atoms per formula unit instead of about 1.8 and puts copper below the 5 atomic per cent threshold. The intended formula is NdBa2(Cu1-zZnz)3O7 with z = 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8. Recorded as a parse artifact so that stage 3 does not compute a copper doping level for a cuprate.

dopant_roles.site: the CuO2 plane copper site, in-plane rather than chain
dopant_roles.basis: Zinc for copper is the classic non-magnetic impurity substitution in the cuprates and the actual subject of the paper. Zn2+ has a filled d shell, replaces Cu2+ in the CuO2 plane without changing the carrier count, and suppresses superconductivity extremely efficiently -- a few per cent kills Tc -- which is why it is used as a probe of the pairing state. The levels here, z = 0.2 to 0.8 of the copper site, are far past that and well into the non-superconducting regime. Like copper, this element is under the threshold only because of the malformed bracket, so the parsed fraction is not the real site occupancy.

note: I do not follow [ref 2] and the reason is the same parse problem. Because copper was read as a trace element, the host system key came out as Ba-Nd-O with no copper in it, and the reference lookup returned barium neodymium oxides -- BaNd2O4 Pnma mp-2892 with 5 ICSD references, BaNdO3 R-3c mp-754307 and BaNdO3 Pm-3m mp-755877. Those are real compounds but they are not this material, and following the best-attested one would have assigned a rare-earth barium oxide to a cuprate superconductor. mp_id is null; stage 2 should resolve NdBa2Cu3O7 in Pmmm. The host key itself should be Ba-Cu-Nd-O and this is a second instance in one chunk of a cuprate losing its identity in parsing, after the YBCO acronym in B-C-O-Y.
annotator_note: Two cuprate hosts in this chunk are wrong at the composition-parsing stage, in two different ways -- a bare acronym and a bracket whose occupancies do not sum to one. Both produce host keys that omit copper. Worth a targeted check upstream for other formulas with parenthesised site occupancies.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [47], ICSD-backed references for this host report [62]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: Bi0.85Sb0.15 with carbon added, and the paper is on unravelling the thermoelectric performance of bismuth antimony with graphene. Bi-Sb alloys across the whole range keep the A7 rhombohedral structure of elemental bismuth and antimony, R-3m, a Peierls-distorted simple cubic lattice with puckered bilayers. Bi0.85Sb0.15 specifically is the classic low-temperature n-type thermoelectric, sitting at the composition where the alloy is a narrow-gap semiconductor rather than a semimetal, and the 149-361 K measured window is exactly where that material is used.

dopant_roles.basis: The carbon is graphene, added deliberately as a second phase at 8 and 12 per cent of the formula, and the paper title names it. It does not dissolve in the bismuth-antimony lattice and does not substitute for anything -- it sits at grain boundaries, scattering phonons and modifying the interfacial carrier transport. Recorded as a secondary phase rather than as a dopant, which is what the composition string would otherwise suggest; there is no such thing as carbon-doped BiSb.

note: Antimony at 15 per cent is a host element and part of the alloy definition, not a dopant -- Bi and Sb are both group 15 and form a continuous solid solution, and Bi0.85Sb0.15 is named as a composition in its own right rather than as doped bismuth. With a single Bi:Sb ratio across the host there is no range to record, so solid_solution_axis is left null. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null and stage 2 should resolve the R-3m alloy. Strictly these samples are composites of an A7 matrix and graphene, but unlike the ceramic composites elsewhere in this chunk the additive is a few per cent by volume and the transport is still a bismuth-antimony property, so the matrix prototype is the right label here rather than composite_multiphase.

basis: Both compositions are p-type bismuth antimony telluride with silicon carbide dispersed in it -- (Bi0.26Sb0.74)2Te3(SiC)0.9 and (Bi0.5Sb1.5Te3)70.9(SiC)29.1 -- and the papers say so: effects of SiC nanodispersion on the thermoelectric properties of p-type material, and a review of Bi2Te3 from bulk to nanomaterials. (Bi,Sb)2Te3 is the tetradymite structure, R-3m, with Te-Bi-Te-Bi-Te quintuple layers stacked by van der Waals gaps, and Bi0.5Sb1.5Te3 is the single most common composition in this dataset.

dopant_roles.basis: Silicon is present only as silicon carbide, added as a nanodispersion, and the first paper names that in its title. SiC is chemically inert against the telluride, does not dissolve in it and does not substitute on either sublattice; it is a phonon-scattering particulate at grain boundaries. Recorded as a secondary phase for the same reason as the carbon.
The other half of the silicon carbide. Carbon and silicon here are one additive counted as two elements by the composition parser, and neither is a dopant.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: cation
solid_solution_axis.note: Bi/(Bi+Sb) is 0.26 in the first composition and 0.25 in the second, so both sit at the standard p-type alloy composition with no spread. Recorded for completeness; the prototype is tetradymite at either value and the README notes that Bi0.5Sb1.5Te3 is an alloy by universal convention rather than Bi-doped Sb2Te3.

note: The second composition is written in mole per cent with SiC at 29.1, which is a very high loading for a nanodispersion -- high enough that the material is arguably a composite rather than a dispersion-strengthened telluride. I have kept tetradymite as the prototype because the transport is still the telluride matrix response and SiC is an insulator that contributes nothing electrically, unlike the conductive diboride composites elsewhere in this chunk where the additive carries the current. Neither reference printed anything for this host; mp_id is null. Measured 304-524 K.

basis: Both papers are on lead-substituted bismuth cuprates -- a thermoelectric study of PbxBi2-xSr2Ca2Cu3Oy superconductors, and a contribution of electronic structure to thermoelectric power in (Bi,Pb) material. The compositions are the n = 3 and n = 1 members of that family: PbBiSr2Cu3O8, and (Bi1.35Pb0.85)(Sr,La)2CuO6 which is Pb-substituted Bi-2201. The structure is the bismuth cuprate intergrowth, double Bi-O rocksalt blocks with their characteristic incommensurate supermodulation alternating with perovskite copper-oxide blocks, and lead substituting for bismuth in the rocksalt layer is the standard way of suppressing that modulation.

dopant_roles.site: the strontium site of the perovskite block
dopant_roles.basis: La at 0.38 and 0.45 against strontium at 1.47 and 1.40, so roughly a fifth to a quarter of that site, and the second paper is about the electronic structure of exactly this substitution. Trivalent lanthanum for divalent strontium removes holes from the CuO2 plane, which is the direct carrier-concentration control for Bi-2201 -- La-doped Bi-2201 is the standard system for sweeping a cuprate from overdoped to underdoped. So this is the working doping variable, not an incidental impurity, and it is under the threshold only because the formula has a dozen atoms.

note: The two compositions are different members of the homologous series -- one CuO2 layer in the 2201 pair and three in PbBiSr2Cu3O8 -- and calcium is absent from the parsed formula of the latter even though the paper title has Ca2 in it, so that string is incomplete. I have not marked the host mixed, because all members of the Bi-Sr-Ca-Cu-O series share the one prototype entry and the layer count is a variable within it rather than a different structure type. [ref 2] offers only Sr4CaYCu4Bi2(PbO8)2 P2/c mp-1218870 at hull 0.016 with no ICSD reference, a computed yttrium-containing cell that is not any of these compositions; I do not follow it and mp_id is null. Measured 73-390 K.

basis: Bi8Cu4.8Si41.2, and its two silicon carbide composites, from the same paper on nanostructured clathrates and clathrate-based nanocomposites that supplies the Ba-Cu-Ge-Si-Sn host in this chunk. The framework atoms Cu plus Si sum to 46.0 exactly and the guest count is exactly 8, which is the type I clathrate to the atom, and Ba8Cu4.8Si41.2 is a compound that group actually works on. I read this as a type I silicon clathrate.
