[ref 2] gives Sr2NdSmMn4O12 in Cm, which is a fully ordered cell at this stoichiometry; the real material has the A-site cations distributed at random, so that entry represents rather than describes it and no mp_id is recorded.

basis: Ni76Mn24 is the Ni3Mn composition, which orders into the cubic L1_2 superstructure of face-centred cubic below about 790 K: manganese at the cell corners, nickel on the face centres. [ref 2] gives MnNi3 in Pm-3m (221) at hull 0.000 with an ICSD reference, which is that structure. The second sample is the same alloy with two percent palladium.

dopant_roles.site: the face-centred nickel site of the L1_2 cell
dopant_roles.basis: Palladium at 2 at.% sits directly below nickel in group 10 and is fully miscible with it, so it takes the nickel site. The paper is on how it changes the exchange bias, which works through the local magnetic coupling rather than the carrier count, so this is not doping in the semiconductor sense even though it is an ordinary substitution.

note: Confidence is medium on the order-disorder question rather than on the chemistry. Ni3Mn can be either the ordered L1_2 phase or a disordered face-centred cubic solid solution depending entirely on heat treatment, the two have the same lattice apart from the superstructure, and the composition string cannot tell them apart. The paper points slightly the other way: exchange bias in Ni-Mn alloys is usually attributed to antiferromagnetic manganese-rich clusters embedded in a ferromagnetic matrix, which is a partially disordered state rather than a fully ordered one. I have recorded the ordered prototype because it is the compound the composition names and the one the reference backs, and flagged the alternative, solid_solution_alloy, here rather than in alt_prototype_ids, because it is a competing reading of the same sample rather than a second phase known to be present.

basis: Both compositions are PbZr0.52Ti0.48O3 with La0.65Sr0.35MnO3 in stated proportion, written as a layered stack, and the paper is on the effect of a PZT thin layer on the structure and magnetism of the manganite. Both constituents are ABO3 perovskites, PZT at the morphotropic phase boundary and LSMO as a hole-doped manganite, so the assignment is the same for both halves.

dopant_roles.site: the twelve-coordinate A site of the manganite layer
dopant_roles.basis: Lanthanum is not a dopant here: it is the majority A-site cation of the La0.65Sr0.35MnO3 constituent, and it reads as a minor element only because the PZT outweighs the manganite by two to one in the formula string. Calling it a dopant would invert the relationship.

dopant_roles.site: the twelve-coordinate A site of the manganite layer
dopant_roles.basis: Strontium at 0.35 of the manganite A site is the hole doping that puts La0.65Sr0.35MnO3 at its ferromagnetic metallic optimum, which is what makes it useful in a magnetoelectric stack. It too is diluted below the candidate threshold by the PZT rather than by being dilute in its own phase.

note: The space group is deliberately null. PZT at the 52 to 48 ratio sits on the morphotropic phase boundary, where rhombohedral R3m and tetragonal P4mm coexist along with a narrow monoclinic bridging phase, and which of them dominates depends on strain from the substrate; the manganite layer is rhombohedral. Two perovskites with three candidate settings between them cannot be reduced to one number. is_mixed is left false because both constituents carry the same prototype, so nothing would be gained by splitting, and neither reference covers the host. The window is 16 to 346 K and crosses the manganite Curie temperature, which is magnetic rather than structural.

basis: MnPr2W2O10 matches the R2MW2O10 archetype exactly, with praseodymium as the rare earth and manganese as the divalent metal, both of which the prototype already names. The structure is built from edge-sharing W2O10 octahedral dimers with the rare earth and the divalent cation between them, and the paper reports three new ceramic tungstates, which is the family this belongs to.
note: The space group is left null because the prototype itself does not fix it: the family is reported in both P2_1/c and C2/c and the composition does not decide between them, which the entry says in as many words. Neither reference covers this host, so there is no evidence to settle it here and no mp_id is recorded. This host is the manganese analogue of Cd-O-Pr-W, the host the prototype was originally proposed from, so the two should be reviewed together. The measured window is narrow, 297 to 495 K, and the paper is a dielectric and magnetic study rather than a thermoelectric one.

basis: TmMnO3 is an RMnO3 manganite with a small heavy rare earth, and the taxonomy entry names exactly that range, R = Sc, Y, Ho-Lu. Thulium sits inside it, so the compound takes the hexagonal P6_3cm structure with five-coordinate manganese in trigonal bipyramids rather than the orthorhombic perovskite the larger rare earths give. The two samples are a single crystal measured in the ab plane and along the c axis, which is a measurement that only makes sense for the strongly anisotropic layered form.
note: I disagree with [ref 2] here. It offers Tm2Mn2O7 pyrochlore and TmMn2O5, and neither is the measured compound: the composition is TmMnO3 at 1:1:3, the paper is a low-temperature heat transport and magnetism study of TmMnO3 single crystals, and the Materials Project snapshot simply has no TmMnO3 entry. Both reference phases carry one ICSD reference each, so this is a gap in the snapshot rather than evidence against the assignment, and no mp_id is recorded. The 13 to 184 K window crosses the antiferromagnetic ordering of the manganese sublattice near 80 K and the thulium moments order lower still, but those are magnetic transitions inside one structure, so spans_transition stays false.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [185], ICSD-backed references for this host report [227]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: Elemental molybdenum, which is body-centred cubic Im-3m from room temperature to the melt, with no allotropic transformation. [ref 2] gives Mo Im-3m mp-129 at hull 0.000 with sixteen ICSD references against one each for four computed alternatives, which is as clean as the evidence gets. The taxonomy files unalloyed metals under solid_solution_alloy with the lattice recorded, as it already does for W, Nb, Ta and Cr.
note: The two samples are not the same material in spirit. One is commercial molybdenum from a 1964 survey of low-temperature transport in commercial metals, and the curator has transcribed its impurity certificate: 1 to 2 volume percent thoria, 0.01 to 0.1 percent Fe and Si, 0.001 to 0.01 percent Al, Cb, Cu. Cb is the old symbol for niobium. The other is a Mo-TiC cermet from a nuclear materials paper, so its titanium carbide is a deliberate second phase. Neither appears in the parsed composition, which is bare Mo, so dopant_roles is empty; the thoria and the carbide are dispersoids rather than solutes in any case. The robust window is 12 to 277 K but the full span reaches 1080 K, which is the cermet measurement.

basis: Y2Mo2O7 is an A2B2O7 molybdate and both papers name the family in their titles, RE2Mo2O7 pyrochlores and R2Mo2O7 pyrochlore compounds. [ref 2] carries Y2Mo2O7 in Fd-3m at mp-19679, which is the pyrochlore setting, so composition, paper and reference agree.
note: [ref 2] ranks Y5(MoO6)2 above the pyrochlore on ICSD count, two references against one, and lists three further yttrium molybdates. That ranking is about which yttrium molybdates exist, not about which compound was measured, and the composition Y2Mo2O7 picks the pyrochlore unambiguously. Y2Mo2O7 is the textbook geometrically frustrated spin glass, which is why its thermopower and magnetism were measured in the 1980s; the frustration is magnetic and does not change the structure across the 12 to 274 K window.

basis: Both compositions are Mo2.5Ru0.5Sb7-xTex, which is the Mo3Sb7 phase with ruthenium on part of the molybdenum site and tellurium on part of the antimony site, and the paper title states that series directly. The taxonomy entry is explicitly Mo3Sb7 / Ir3Ge7-type and already names Mo-Sb and Mo-Sb-Te among its host systems, so this is the same family with the transition metal alloyed.
note: dopant_roles is empty because neither substituent falls below the five atomic percent cut: ruthenium is 0.5 of ten atoms and tellurium 0.5 to 1 of ten. Their roles are still worth stating. Ruthenium substitutes molybdenum in the Mo8 cube framework and adds electrons, and tellurium substitutes antimony, so the two act together as the electron-count knob on a compound whose parent Mo3Sb7 is a metal; that is what the transport and magnetism paper is about. Neither reference covers this host, so no mp_id is recorded.

basis: Mo4Ru2Se8 is a Mo6Se8 Chevrel cluster with two of the six cluster sites taken by ruthenium, and Ti0.3Mo5RuSe8 is the same cluster with titanium in the channel. The paper title says so outright, thermoelectric and structural properties of a new Chevrel phase. The taxonomy entry has the AxMo6X8 archetype and Mo6Se8 as its exemplar.

dopant_roles.site: the channel site between Mo6Se8 clusters, the A site of AxMo6X8
dopant_roles.basis: In a Chevrel phase the guest cation sits in the cavity between the octahedral clusters rather than on a framework site, and it donates its electrons into the cluster band. Titanium at x = 0.3 in Ti0.3Mo5RuSe8 is that guest, and it is the whole point of the paper: the cluster framework is fixed and the filler sets the carrier count and scatters phonons.

note: I record the rhombohedral R-3 Chevrel setting rather than following [ref 2], which offers Mo2RuSe4 in P-1 at mp-1221499 and P1 at mp-1221491 with no ICSD references at all. Those are computed orderings of molybdenum and ruthenium over the cluster sites, which lowers the symmetry on paper; the physical phase is the rhombohedral cluster framework with the two metals mixed, so no mp_id is carried. The measured window runs to 1273 K, well above the range where these selenides are usually cycled, so the high-temperature end may involve selenium loss rather than a structural change.

basis: Mo5Si3 is the W5Si3 (D8_m) type, body-centred tetragonal I4/mcm, and the paper is on single crystals of Mo5X3 with X = Si, so the 5:3 silicide is what was grown and measured. [ref 2] gives Si3Mo5 in I4/mcm at mp-1332, hull 0.000 with five ICSD references, which is that structure. The taxonomy had no D8_m entry, so the prototype is proposed.
note: Confidence is medium because of the second composition, MoSi3, which is not a phase that exists in the Mo-Si binary. The plausible readings are a digitisation slip for Mo5Si3, which is what the paper is about, or for MoSi2, the C11b disilicide, which is the other well-known Mo-Si compound and has an entry at mosi2_c11b. I have not put mosi2_c11b in alt_prototype_ids because that would assert a second phase is present when what is actually wrong is the string; the host should be rechecked against the paper. Note also that this is the one place the D8_m and Cr5B3 types must be kept apart: both are I4/mcm with 32 atoms per cell, and the Mo5SiB2 T2 phase of chunk 039 is the Cr5B3 branch of the same chemistry.

basis: The compositions are molecular N2 measured from 11 to 24 K, which is solid nitrogen in its alpha form: a face-centred cubic packing of linear molecules in Pa-3, the same arrangement the taxonomy entry carries for dry ice, CO and N2O. [ref 2] puts N2 Pa-3 at mp-25 as the primary with four ICSD references, ahead of four other computed settings.
note: Two things to flag. First, one of the two papers is titled high thermal conductivity of solid nitrous oxide, so its material is N2O rather than N2 and the composition string has probably lost the oxygen; the assignment survives either way, because alpha-N2 and N2O are the same Pa-3 molecular arrangement and the taxonomy entry has N2O as its exemplar. The second paper is a cryocrystal study of linear molecules, which is the same family. Second, solid nitrogen does have a second thermal phase, hexagonal beta-N2 above about 35.6 K, but the measured window stops at 24 K so it is never reached; I have left it out of phases and out of other_polymorphs rather than give it an id, since the taxonomy has no entry for the hexagonal molecular packing and inventing one for a phase nobody measured here would be worse than the note.

basis: (NpN)(PuN) in both proportions is a mononitride solid solution, and the paper is explicitly on the thermal conductivity of actinide mononitride solid solutions. NpN and PuN are both rocksalt Fm-3m, they are completely miscible on the cation site, and the solution keeps that structure at every ratio, which is the whole basis for using mixed nitride nuclear fuel.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the octahedral cation site of the rocksalt cell
solid_solution_axis.note: Pu/(Np+Pu) across the two compositions, 33 and 67 percent. Neptunium and plutonium are adjacent actinides of the same valence and nearly the same ionic radius, so this is a random substitutional series rather than an ordered ternary, and the measurement is of how that disorder suppresses the lattice thermal conductivity. There is no transition temperature to shift along the axis.

note: Neither reference covers this host and no mp_id is recorded. The 756 to 1627 K window is a fuel-relevant range rather than a thermoelectric one; mononitrides stay rocksalt throughout it, and the risk at the top end is nitrogen loss, not a phase change.

basis: PuN is the plutonium mononitride, rocksalt Fm-3m, and [ref 2] carries exactly one entry for the chemistry, PuN Fm-3m at mp-1719, hull 0.000 with seven ICSD references. Both papers treat it as a nuclear fuel nitride, one alongside ZrN and one as the mixed uranium-plutonium nitride.
note: One of the two papers is a molecular dynamics study of uranium-plutonium mixed nitride, so its numbers are computed rather than measured and the composition recorded here, bare PuN, is the end member of that calculation. The window reaches 1874 K and the full span 1981 K, above which PuN dissociates rather than transforming, so there is no second phase to record.

basis: Both compositions are Si3N4 at 98 to 99 percent with a few percent of Y2O3 and Nd2O3, which is the standard oxide sintering aid package for silicon nitride ceramics, and both papers are on the thermal conductivity of sintered or Y2O3-doped Si3N4. Sintering converts the alpha starting powder to beta, so the measured body is beta-Si3N4, P6_3/m; [ref 1] makes that the primary with 41 ICSD references at mp-988.

other_polymorphs.note: alpha-Si3N4, P31c, the same tetrahedral network with a different stacking. It is the form the starting powder is in and it converts irreversibly to beta during sintering, so it is not a thermal phase of the measured ceramic. Seventeen ICSD references.
cubic spinel c-Si3N4, Fd-3m, made only above about 15 GPa. Listed at hull 0.147 with four ICSD references and irrelevant to a pressureless-sintered body.

dopant_roles.site: the intergranular glass, not the Si3N4 lattice
dopant_roles.basis: Yttria is added as a sintering aid. It reacts with the silica on the powder surfaces to form a Y-Si-O-N liquid that densifies the body and then freezes as an intergranular glass or a crystalline yttrium silicate at the grain boundaries. Yttrium does not enter the Si3N4 structure, and the point of the second paper is precisely that this boundary phase controls the thermal conductivity.

dopant_roles.site: the intergranular glass
dopant_roles.basis: Nd2O3 is the second oxide of the aid package in the 99 percent sample and behaves the same way as the yttria, staying in the boundary phase. Using two rare earths together lowers the eutectic of the sintering liquid.

dopant_roles.site: the intergranular oxynitride glass
dopant_roles.basis: The oxygen arrives with the Y2O3 and Nd2O3 and with the native silica on the powder, so it is part of the boundary glass rather than milling residue or a substituent on the nitrogen site. A small amount can dissolve in the lattice as a SiAlON-like substitution, but with no aluminium present that route is not open here.

note: The prototype entry beta_si3n4 was proposed from chunk 041 for a graphene composite where Si3N4 was only the matrix; this host is the ceramic itself, so the entry is now doing the work it was written for. The measured window is wide, 11 to 1217 K, and spans two quite different experiments: a 4 to 1000 K conductivity study and a grain-growth study at high temperature. Neither reports a structural change, and beta-Si3N4 has none below dissociation.

basis: This host holds two unrelated materials and neither is a single-phase compound. W3.8Si3N4 is the tungsten-Si3N4 electrode of a paper on the contact resistivity of W-Si3N4 against TiB2-Si3N4, which is metallic tungsten dispersed in a silicon nitride matrix. The other composition is the literal string SiNW from a paper on the thermoelectric properties of nanowires with a graphitic shell, where SiNW is the usual abbreviation for silicon nanowire, so its material is silicon with a carbon shell and contains no nitrogen or tungsten at all.
note: The host exists because of a parse artifact: SiNW was read as the elements Si, N and W. Without that string the host would be W-Si3N4 alone. Stage 2 must split it per composition rather than label it: W3.8Si3N4 is tungsten metal plus beta-Si3N4, and SiNW is diamond-cubic silicon in a graphitic sheath. I have put both constituent prototypes in alt_prototype_ids and left phases empty, because no single thermal sequence covers a two-phase electrode and a mislabelled nanowire at once. The 50 to 1167 K window is likewise two different experiments stitched together.

basis: Ti0.6U0.4N is a mononitride solid solution: TiN and UN are both rocksalt Fm-3m, and the paper measures the thermophysical properties of several nitrides made by spark plasma sintering, which is how these mixed nitrides are consolidated. The nitrogen sublattice is unchanged and the two metals share the octahedral cation site.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the octahedral cation site of the rocksalt cell
solid_solution_axis.note: U/(Ti+U) at the single measured composition, 0.4. Titanium and uranium are far apart in size, so unlike the Np-Pu case this solution has real lattice strain and a miscibility limit; spark plasma sintering is used partly because it is fast enough to avoid demixing. The axis is recorded so stage 3 treats uranium as an alloying partner rather than a dopant.

note: Neither reference covers this host, so no mp_id is recorded. This is the same paper as the N-U-Zr host at rank 2313, which is the zirconium analogue at the same 0.6 to 0.4 ratio; the two should be read together.

basis: Zr0.6U0.4N is a (Zr,U)N mononitride solid solution. ZrN and UN are both rocksalt Fm-3m and are mutually soluble across the whole range, and the paper is the same spark-plasma-sintering nitride study as the titanium analogue, so the product is a disordered rocksalt with both metals on the cation site.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the octahedral cation site of the rocksalt cell
solid_solution_axis.note: U/(U+Zr) at the single measured composition, 0.4. Both nitrides are rocksalt and fully miscible, so the series is continuous and the assignment holds at any ratio.

note: I disagree with [ref 2] on this one. It offers ZrUN2 in I4_1/amd at mp-35739, marked primary and ambiguous, and a rhombohedral R-3m alternative, both at hull 0.000 and neither with an ICSD reference. Those are computed cation-ordered superstructures of the rocksalt lattice at exactly 1:1:2. The measured material is a sintered solid solution at Zr:U of 6:4, which cannot be that ordered compound, and a spark-plasma-sintered nitride has neither the stoichiometry nor the time at temperature to order. So the prototype is the disordered rocksalt and no mp_id is recorded; if a structure is wanted, it is the end members rather than the ordered ternary.

basis: Na1-xSrxNbO3 at x = 0.15 and 0.20 is an ABO3 perovskite with sodium and strontium sharing the A site and niobium on the octahedral B site. The paper calls these niobium bronzes, but that is a name for their conduction rather than their structure: the framework is corner-sharing NbO6 with a filled A site, which is a perovskite, not a tunnel bronze.

dopant_roles.site: the twelve-coordinate A site
dopant_roles.basis: Divalent strontium on a monovalent sodium site is the electron doping of the series: each substitution either adds a carrier to the niobium 4d band or creates a compensating A-site vacancy, which is exactly the conduction mechanism the paper sets out to explain. It is not an isoelectronic alloying partner.

note: The space group is left null deliberately. [ref 2] gives NaNbO3 in Pm-3m at mp-3136 with 34 ICSD references, but that is the cubic aristotype, which pure NaNbO3 reaches only above about 900 K; at and below room temperature it runs through a sequence of antiferroelectric and ferroelectric orthorhombic settings, Pbcm being the ambient one, and strontium substitution shifts those boundaries. The measured window is 14 to 276 K, inside that low-temperature regime, so recording 221 would assert the wrong setting and recording one orthorhombic number would overstate what the composition can tell us. The prototype is unaffected: every one of those settings is a tilted perovskite.

basis: Na0.83RhO2 is a layered AMO2 with RhO6 octahedral sheets and sodium between them, and the paper title names the 3R phases, which is the O3 stacking of the alpha-NaFeO2 type in rhombohedral R-3m. [ref 2] has NaRhO2 in R-3m at mp-8830, hull 0.000, which is that structure. The O3 entry rather than the P2 one is therefore the right choice, and the sodium is octahedrally coordinated.
note: The sodium content, x = 0.83 rather than 1, is the carrier-concentration knob exactly as it is in NaxCoO2: it sets the rhodium valence between 3+ and 4+. Sodium is a host element here, not a minor one, so there is nothing to put in dopant_roles, but stage 3 should treat the deficiency as the doping variable rather than as non-stoichiometric error. The paper is on hydrated phases and the water is not in the composition string; if the measured samples were the hydrate, the interlayer spacing differs while the RhO2 sheet and its stacking do not, so the prototype still holds. The discrimination that matters is against naxcoo2_layered, which is the P2 type with prismatic alkali coordination.

basis: Na0.25WO3 and Na0.46WO3 are sodium tungsten bronzes: a WO3 framework of corner-sharing octahedra with sodium partly filling the A sites, the classic AxWO3 bronze the taxonomy entry covers alongside the tetragonal form. The paper is on cubic NaxWO3 thin films across the composition range, and the partially filled A site is what makes these metallic rather than the insulating WO3 parent.
note: The two compositions straddle a symmetry boundary within one prototype. Above roughly x = 0.4 the sodium bronze is the cubic perovskite-like bronze, which is the mp-19328 Pm-3m entry [ref 2] lists with three ICSD references, and Na0.46WO3 is on that side. Below it the structure is the tetragonal bronze, so Na0.25WO3 is nominally on the other; the paper reports these as cubic films, which thin-film growth can stabilise outside the bulk range. Both settings are the same partially filled AxWO3 framework and share this entry, so the phase is recorded once at the cubic setting with medium confidence rather than split. Note that [ref 2] ranks Na2WO4 first on ICSD count; that is the scheelite-type tungstate, a different compound entirely, and the composition rules it out.

basis: The two compositions are the two silicon clathrates, and they are different structures. Na8Si46 is type I, the Pm-3n framework of Si20 and Si24 cages with sodium in every cage, and Na22Si136 is type II, the Fd-3m framework of Si20 and Si28 cages. [ref 2] backs the type I framework with Na4Si23 in Pm-3n at mp-186, 18 ICSD references, and the papers name the two compounds separately in their titles.
note: This host is mixed on stoichiometry alone and splits cleanly: Si/Na of 5.75 is type I, 6.18 is type II, so no paper is needed to separate them. The type I record is put first only because it is the better attested of the two in the snapshot. The type II compound is the more interesting sample: Na22Si136 has sodium in the large cages only and is the one whose synthesis and structure the first paper reports. Neither is a doped material; the sodium is the cage guest and the framework is pure silicon, which is why the taxonomy keeps the two clathrate types as separate prototypes rather than one entry with a variable guest.

basis: 80 mol percent ZrO2 with 10 each of Y2O3 and Nb2O5 is co-doped stabilised zirconia: enough trivalent and pentavalent cation to hold zirconia in its cubic fluorite form at all temperatures. The paper is on the thermal properties of zirconia co-doped with trivalent and pentavalent oxides, which is that experiment, and the point of pairing Y3+ with Nb5+ is that the two compensate each other so the oxygen vacancy count stays low while the cation disorder stays high.
note: dopant_roles is empty because at 10 mol percent each neither yttrium nor niobium is below the atomic-fraction cut, so neither is a dopant candidate in this host; both are substitutional on the zirconium site and together they are the stabiliser. Neither reference covers the host and no mp_id is recorded. This is a thermal-barrier-coating study rather than a thermoelectric one, which is why only thermal conductivity is measured over 377 to 1261 K. The sister host O-Ta-Y-Zr at rank 2344 is the tantalum version of the same experiment.

basis: Rh3Nb is an A3B intermetallic that orders into the cubic L1_2 superstructure of face-centred cubic, with niobium at the cell corners and rhodium on the face centres. The second paper says so in its title, thermal conductivity and thermal expansion of L1_2 intermetallic compounds, and [ref 2] gives NbRh3 in Pm-3m at mp-2449, hull 0.000, which is that structure.
note: Unlike the Ni3Mn case in chunk 046, there is no order-disorder ambiguity here: Rh3Nb is a congruently melting ordered compound, not an alloy that can be quenched disordered, and the papers study it as an ultra-high-temperature structural material. [ref 2] also lists NbRh, Nb3Rh and two computed phases in the same binary; the 3:1 composition selects the L1_2 one.

basis: (Yb1.90S2)0.62NbS2 and (Yb2S2)2NbS2 are written in the two-subsystem form the misfit family uses, and both papers say misfit-layered sulfide in their titles. The curator has transcribed the assignment from the paper: the NbS2 slab is subsystem 1 and the Yb2S2 block is subsystem 2, which is the defining feature of the prototype, two mutually incommensurate layer stacks with no common periodicity in the plane.
note: Flagged for stage 2 as the prototype's own notes require: an incommensurate composite has no single Materials Project entry, so it must be resolved as two subsystems, a rocksalt-like YbS block and a trigonal-prismatic NbS2 slab, with their own lattices and a misfit ratio. The space group is null for the same reason; each subsystem has one, the composite does not. The two compositions differ in the stated Yb:Nb ratio, 1.18 against 4, which is unusual for a misfit sulfide and suggests the second string is a different member of the series or a transcription of the composite formula rather than a second phase, so is_mixed stays false.

basis: Ta1-xNbxTe2 at x = 0.2 and 0.5 are distorted-octahedral ditellurides, and the paper title says distorted 1T outright. TaTe2 and NbTe2 are both the monoclinic C2/m distortion of the 1T layer, in which the metal atoms displace into ribbons of metal-metal bonds, and the taxonomy entry names both compounds and that C2/m setting explicitly.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the octahedral metal site within the distorted 1T layer
solid_solution_axis.note: Nb/(Nb+Ta) across the two single crystals. Niobium and tantalum are the same group and nearly the same size, so this is a genuine isoelectronic series on one site; both end members carry the same C2/m ribbon distortion, so the prototype does not change along it. What does change is the periodicity of the distortion, which is why the crystals were grown across the range.

note: [ref 2] offers only TaNbTe4 in P1 at mp-1217942, hull 0.004, with no ICSD reference. That is a computed 1:1 ordering of the two metals in the lowest possible symmetry, not a measured phase, so I do not take it as the structure; a solid solution grown from the melt has the metals mixed on one site and keeps the C2/m cell. No mp_id is recorded. The entry mote2_1t_prime was proposed in chunk 019 and this host is a second, independent use of it, which strengthens the case for folding it into v4.

basis: Elemental neodymium, which is double hexagonal close packed at ambient conditions, the fourfold ABAC stacking that the light rare earths share. [ref 2] gives Nd in P6_3/mmc at mp-123, hull 0.000 with ten ICSD references, well ahead of the face-centred and body-centred alternatives at two each, and those are the high-pressure and high-temperature forms respectively.

other_polymorphs.note: face-centred cubic neodymium, hull 0.011 with two ICSD references. Reached under pressure, not on heating from the dhcp form at ambient pressure.

note: Same paper as the La-Nd host of chunk 046, on the thermoelectric power of Nd1-xLax and Ce1-xLax alloys; this record is its pure neodymium end member and takes the same prototype, which was proposed from that host. The single crystals were measured from 10 to 291 K, a window that crosses the antiferromagnetic ordering of neodymium near 20 K; that is magnetic and does not change the stacking. Body-centred cubic neodymium exists only above about 1130 K, far outside the window, so it is not recorded.

basis: The composition is NdO at 1:1, and the rare-earth monoxides are rocksalt Fm-3m; [ref 2] carries NdO in Fm-3m at mp-754545. The paper is on the transport properties of SmO, so this is the neodymium member of that same family of metallic monoxides, measured in the same study, rather than a sesquioxide.
note: Recorded as a disagreement with the evidence rather than a clean call, which is why confidence is medium. [ref 2] ranks Nd2O3 in P-3m1 first with eleven ICSD references; that is the A-type sesquioxide and it is the only neodymium oxide that is straightforwardly stable in air, whereas the rocksalt monoxide is an oxygen-deficient metallic phase usually made under reducing conditions or pressure and carries no ICSD reference at hull 0.080. So the best-attested phase in this chemistry is not the one I have assigned. I assign the monoxide anyway because the composition says NdO and the companion paper is a monoxide transport study, and the reference describes which neodymium oxides exist rather than which one was measured. If the samples turn out to be sesquioxide, the right entry is a_type_re2o3; I have left it out of alt_prototype_ids because that would claim a second phase is present rather than that the first might be wrong.

basis: Nd2Ru2O7 is an A2B2O7 ruthenate pyrochlore, and [ref 2] gives it in Fd-3m at mp-19930 with eleven ICSD references, the best-attested entry in the chemistry. The papers are on the structural disorder, magnetism and transport of the compound and on nano-sized rare-earth ruthenates, both of which are the pyrochlore family.
note: [ref 2] also lists three settings of Nd3RuO7, one of them marked ambiguous, at lower hull energies. Those are the 3-1-7 weberite-related ruthenate, a different compound, and the 2:2:7 composition excludes them. Nd2Ru2O7 is a Mott insulator whose antiferromagnetic order sets in near 150 K, below the 294 K measurement start, so nothing magnetic or structural is crossed in this window.

basis: Nd2Sn2O7 is a stannate pyrochlore, Fd-3m, and [ref 2] carries exactly that at mp-17114, hull 0.000. The second composition dilutes it with 20 percent Yb2Zr2O7, and the paper is on the low thermal conductivity of rare-earth zirconate-stannate solid solutions, so both samples are the same pyrochlore framework with mixed occupancy on the two cation sites.

dopant_roles.site: the eight-coordinate A site of the pyrochlore
dopant_roles.basis: Ytterbium arrives as the A cation of the Yb2Zr2O7 end member, not as a dilute impurity: the sample is a 20 to 80 solid solution of two pyrochlore-family oxides and ytterbium falls under the five percent cut only because it is one of four elements. Its job is mass and radius contrast on the A site, which is what suppresses the thermal conductivity.

dopant_roles.site: the six-coordinate B site of the pyrochlore
dopant_roles.basis: Zirconium is the B cation of the same end member and substitutes for tin on the octahedral site. Zirconate pyrochlores sit close to the fluorite boundary, so adding zirconium also increases the cation antisite disorder, which the paper uses deliberately.

note: Yb2Zr2O7 is itself at the pyrochlore-to-defect-fluorite borderline, since the Yb:Zr radius ratio is near the stability limit, so a zirconium-rich member of this series would be better described as a disordered fluorite. At 20 percent it is not, and both samples stay pyrochlore. The sister host O-Sm-Sn at rank 2341 is the samarium version of the same experiment and takes the same reading.

basis: NiP2 has two polymorphs and the paper measured both: its title is NiP2, a story of two divergent polymorphic multifunctional materials. The ambient-pressure form is the monoclinic C2/c structure, which [ref 2] gives at mp-486 with three ICSD references, the best-attested NiP2 in the snapshot; the other is the cubic pyrite-type phase made under pressure. The taxonomy had pyrite but no entry for the monoclinic form, so it is proposed.
note: This is a host where composition cannot decide, and the split is between polymorphs of one formula rather than between two compounds. Two samples and six curves for a single composition string is consistent with the paper measuring both forms, so is_mixed is true and pyrite is in alt_prototype_ids. I have deliberately not put the cubic form in other_polymorphs: that field is for structures the measurement does not pass through, and here it probably is one of the two measured samples. Stage 2 will need the paper, not the formula. Note that the cubic form is not reached by heating the monoclinic one, so this is not a thermal sequence either way, and spans_transition stays false.

basis: U3Ni1.9Co0.1PtSb4 is a U3T3Sb4 compound: the transition-metal content sums to 2.9 against three uranium and four antimony, which is the A3M3X4 archetype of the Y3Au3Sb4 type, cubic I-43d. U3Ni3Sb4 and U3Cu3Sb4 are the known uranium members of that family, and the paper is a survey of uranium-based thermoelectric materials, where this family is the semiconducting one.

dopant_roles.site: the tetrahedral transition-metal site of the I-43d framework
dopant_roles.basis: Cobalt at 0.1 of the 1.9 nickel sits on the same transition-metal site, one electron short of nickel, so it acts as a hole dopant on a compound that is a narrow-gap semiconductor or Kondo insulator. It is a genuine dilute substitutional dopant, unlike the platinum, which is a full unit of the framework.

note: Neither reference covers this host, so no mp_id is recorded. Platinum is not in dopant_roles because at one atom per formula it is above the cut and is a framework constituent: the compound is better read as U3(Ni,Pt)3Sb4 with nickel and platinum sharing the transition-metal site. The Y3Au3Sb4 type is a Th3P4 derivative, so the discrimination against th3p4 matters in stage 2; the ordered 3-3-4 cation arrangement is what makes it a separate entry.

basis: The host holds two different compounds. NiSb is the NiAs-type B8 phase, hexagonal P6_3/mmc, which [ref 2] makes the primary at mp-810 with twelve ICSD references, and the first paper studies it as a secondary phase in skutterudite CoSb3. Ni4Sb12 is four formula units of NiSb3, the binary skutterudite framework, from the second paper on nickel-substituted skutterudites.
note: Mixed, and it splits on stoichiometry alone: Sb:Ni of 1 is the NiAs-type phase and 3 is the skutterudite. [ref 2] supports both sides, NiSb at mp-810 and NiSb3 in Im-3 at mp-1106023 with two ICSD references, the latter being the skutterudite setting. Neither sample is really a target material; both papers are about what nickel and antimony do to CoSb3, so this host is a by-product of studying that one. Confidence is medium on the host label rather than on either compound, because one label cannot stand over both.

basis: The single composition is written as a two-component heterostructure, 26 percent Sn12Sb2Te15 and 74 percent NiTe2, and the paper is on Hall-effect measurements and transport in heterostructures. NiTe2 is the majority phase and is the CdI2-type 1T layered ditelluride, so that is the prototype recorded; the minority component is a tin antimony telluride.
note: Sn12Sb2Te15 is (SnTe)12(Sb2Te3), a member of the pseudobinary series between rocksalt SnTe and Sb2Te3. At twelve SnTe units per Sb2Te3 block it is far from the layered homologues and is best read as rocksalt SnTe with antimony and extra tellurium dissolved in it, which is why alt_prototype_ids carries rocksalt rather than gst_homologous; the layered homologous description only applies at low SnTe counts. Neither reference covers the host and no mp_id is recorded. Stage 2 must treat this as a two-phase composite, not as a compound: a CdI2-type ditelluride and a rocksalt telluride have nothing structurally in common.

basis: Both compositions are stated mixtures of TmNiSb and TmNiSn, and the paper is on power factor enhancement in a composite based on a half-Heusler antimonide. TmNiSb is the half-Heusler, cubic F-43m, and it is the majority component of the first sample at 75 percent. The two constituents are different structures, not a solid solution.
note: The reason this is mixed rather than a substitution series is that the two RNiX compounds do not share a structure. RNiSb with a heavy rare earth is the cubic half-Heusler, as YNiSb at rank 2332 is; RNiSn with a heavy rare earth is the orthorhombic TiNiSi type, as YbNiSn at rank 2336 is, where [ref 2] confirms Pnma with five ICSD references. So the composite is genuinely two phases and the second sample, at 70 percent TmNiSn, is majority TiNiSi-type rather than half-Heusler. The record keeps half_heusler as the label because it is what the paper builds on, and stage 2 must split per composition; confidence is medium for that reason and no mp_id is recorded, since neither reference covers this host.

basis: ZrNiSn with antimony on part of the tin site is the workhorse n-type half-Heusler, cubic F-43m, and both papers name it: high-temperature thermoelectric properties of NiZrSn half-Heusler compounds, and thermoelectric properties of half-Heusler alloys Zr1-xYxNiSn1-ySby. The 18-electron ZrNiSn composition with antimony donors is the standard recipe.
note: dopant_roles is empty because the antimony is at 20 and 28 percent of the tin site, well above the five percent cut, so it is not a dopant candidate in this host. Its role is still the interesting one: Sb5+ for Sn4+ adds one electron per substitution and is the n-type doping of ZrNiSn, and 28 percent is a very heavy level for that, which is what the papers are exploring. The two compositions are the same material written two ways, NiZrSn0.72Sb0.28 and ZrNiSn0.8Sb0.2. [ref 2] offers only Zr10NiSnSb4 in I422 at mp-1215855 with no ICSD reference, a computed phase at an unrelated stoichiometry, so no mp_id is recorded.

basis: YNiSb is a half-Heusler, and [ref 2] gives it in F-43m at mp-11520, hull 0.000, which is that structure. Both papers treat it as a member of the RNiSb series, one on the thermoelectric properties of ScMSb and YMSb compounds and one on the properties and electronic structure of RNiSb compounds, which is the half-Heusler family with a rare earth on the tetrahedral cation site.
note: YNiSb is an 18-electron half-Heusler and a narrow-gap semiconductor, which is why it appears in these early RNiSb surveys; the yttrium analogue is the non-magnetic reference point for the magnetic rare-earth members. The only ICSD reference behind mp-11520 is a single entry, so the primary is weak by the chunk file's own standard, but the composition and both paper titles agree with it. The other [ref 2] entry, Y5Ni2Sb in I4/mcm, is a rare-earth-rich phase at a different stoichiometry.

basis: UNi2Si2 is an RT2X2 compound and [ref 2] gives U(SiNi)2 in I4/mmm at mp-20596, hull 0.000 with six ICSD references, which is the ThCr2Si2 body-centred tetragonal stack: alternating uranium layers and Ni2Si2 slabs. The paper measures susceptibility, thermopower and specific heat of the single crystal, the standard set for a 122 heavy-fermion compound.
note: UNi2Si2 orders antiferromagnetically in a sequence of commensurate and incommensurate structures below about 124 K, and the 14 to 294 K window crosses all of them. Those are magnetic transitions on a fixed lattice, so spans_transition stays false and phases holds one entry. The four other [ref 2] entries for this chemistry are different stoichiometries, 3-4, 2-2-3, 1-5-2 and 2-3-1, none of which matches 1:2:2.

basis: YbNi2Si2 is an RT2X2 compound in the ThCr2Si2 type, and [ref 2] confirms it as Yb(SiNi)2 in I4/mmm at mp-5916, hull 0.000 with two ICSD references. The second composition, YbNi4Si, is a different structure: an AB5 phase in which silicon substitutes for part of the nickel in the hexagonal CaCu5 framework. Both papers are ytterbium heavy-fermion studies, one specifically on YbNi4Si.
note: Mixed on stoichiometry and it splits cleanly: Ni:Yb of 2 with two silicon is the 122, and Ni:Yb of 4 with one silicon is the CaCu5-derived 1-4-1. Confidence is medium because of the second composition rather than the first. The RNi4Si compounds are reported as CaCu5 derivatives with silicon ordered onto one of the nickel sites, which in some members lowers the symmetry to an ordered superstructure of P6/mmm rather than leaving the parent cell; I have recorded the parent cacu5 entry in alt_prototype_ids rather than picking between the ordered variants the taxonomy carries, ceco4b_ordered_cacu5 and prni2al3_ordered_cacu5, because the composition alone does not establish which ordering applies. [ref 2] has no YbNi4Si entry at all, so there is nothing to check it against.

basis: Zr1-xYxNiSn at x = 0.2 and 0.25 is ZrNiSn with yttrium on part of the zirconium site, and the paper title is the synthesis, electronic transport and magnetic properties of Zr1-xYxNiSn. The half-Heusler F-43m framework is unchanged; yttrium simply takes the four-coordinate cation site.
note: Yttrium is at 20 to 25 percent of the zirconium site, above the five percent cut, so there is no dopant candidate in this host and dopant_roles is empty. Its role is acceptor doping rather than isoelectronic alloying: Y3+ for Zr4+ removes one electron per substitution from an 18-electron semiconductor, which is what makes this series interesting against the antimony-doped ZrNiSn of rank 2331, where the doping runs the other way. Neither reference covers the host, so no mp_id is recorded. Yttrium substitution beyond a few percent is close to the solubility limit in ZrNiSn, so a second phase is plausible at 25 percent; the paper would settle it.

basis: YbNiSn is an equiatomic RTX compound and [ref 2] gives it in Pnma at mp-22162, hull 0.000 with five ICSD references, which is the TiNiSi ordered-Co2Si structure the taxonomy entry carries. The first paper studies it as a ferromagnetic Kondo lattice with crystal field excitations, which is the orthorhombic RTX family, not a cubic one.
note: This record is the evidence behind the mixed reading of Ni-Sb-Sn-Tm at rank 2330: a heavy-rare-earth RNiSn is orthorhombic TiNiSi type, not a half-Heusler, so a TmNiSb and TmNiSn composite is two structures. YbNiSn orders ferromagnetically near 5.5 K, below the 10 K measurement start, and the window crosses nothing structural. The three other [ref 2] entries are Yb-Ni-Sn phases at 5-4-10, 7-4-13 and 1-4-1 stoichiometries, none of which matches 1:1:1.

basis: Both compositions are 95 percent or more Y0.08Zr0.94O2, which is yttria-stabilised zirconia in the cubic fluorite structure, with 4 to 5 percent Ca0.5Sr0.5Zr4P6O24 added. The paper is on the role of NZP additions in plasma-sprayed YSZ, so the material is a YSZ coating and the phosphate is a minority second phase, not a constituent of the matrix.

dopant_roles.site: the eight-coordinate cation site of the fluorite cell
dopant_roles.basis: Yttrium at 8 percent of the zirconium site is the stabiliser that holds zirconia cubic instead of letting it transform to the monoclinic form on cooling, and each Y3+ pair brings one oxygen vacancy. That vacancy population is what gives YSZ its low thermal conductivity and its oxygen conduction, so this is the defining substitution of the material rather than incidental doping.

dopant_roles.site: the A-site channel of the NZP phase
dopant_roles.basis: Calcium is not in the zirconia at all: it is half of the A-site occupancy of the Ca0.5Sr0.5Zr4P6O24 additive, where the divalent cation half fills the channel of the phosphate framework. It reads as a dilute element only because the additive is a few percent of the whole.

dopant_roles.site: the A-site channel of the NZP phase
dopant_roles.basis: Strontium is the other half of the same A site. Mixing calcium and strontium is how the additive is tuned: it shifts the thermal expansion of the NZP phase to match the YSZ so the sprayed coating does not crack.

note: Mixed, and the two phases are the reason phosphorus appears in this host at all. The matrix is cubic fluorite YSZ and the additive is the NZP framework phosphate, which the taxonomy did not carry; nasicon_nzp is proposed for it and put in alt_prototype_ids. Confidence is medium on the host label rather than on the matrix, which is unambiguous. Neither reference covers the host and no mp_id is recorded; [ref 2] lists zirconium pyrophosphates and a caesium aluminophosphate, none of which is either phase here. Stage 2 should resolve the two separately, and the README's warning about composite additives applies in reverse here: the additive must not relabel the coating, but it does have to be named or the phosphorus goes unexplained.

basis: Pb2Re2O7 is an A2B2O7 rhenate pyrochlore and the first paper says so in its title, the structural and electronic properties of pyrochlore-type lead rhenate. That settles the majority of the host. The second composition, written PbRe2O5, is the subject of the second paper on the spin-orbit-coupled metal candidate PbRe2O6, which is a different compound at AB2O6.
note: I have not invented a prototype for the second phase. PbRe2O6 is an AB2O6 rhenate and the plausible readings are a defect pyrochlore with the A-prime oxygen site vacant, for which the taxonomy has defect_pyrochlore_a2b2o6 and beta_pyrochlore_ab2o6, or a rosiaite-type PbSb2O6 layered arrangement; I cannot settle that from the formula and the paper title alone, so it is parked at unresolved_crystalline in alt_prototype_ids and flagged for review. Note also the stoichiometry mismatch: the composition string reads PbRe2O5 while the paper it comes from is about PbRe2O6, so one oxygen has probably been lost in transcription. [ref 2] is no help here, offering five computed lead rhenates at other stoichiometries with one ICSD reference between them, so no mp_id is recorded.

basis: SrRu1-xSnxO3 at x = 0.44 and 0.67 is an ABO3 perovskite with strontium on the A site and ruthenium and tin sharing the octahedral B site, and the paper is on the effects of tin substitution in SrRuO3 epitaxial films. Both end members are perovskites, SrRuO3 as the orthorhombic ferromagnetic metal and SrSnO3 as a wide-gap insulator, so the whole series is one prototype.
note: The space group is left null because these are epitaxial films: SrRuO3 is orthorhombic Pbnm in bulk, tin substitution pushes the tilt system toward the tetragonal and cubic settings, and the substrate strain can select among them independently of composition. The prototype is the same in every case. Tin is above the five percent cut so dopant_roles is empty, but its role is worth stating: Sn4+ is isovalent with Ru4+ and has an empty d shell, so substitution dilutes the ruthenium 4d network and drives the film from a ferromagnetic metal toward an insulator, which is what the measurement is about. Neither reference covers the host and no mp_id is recorded.

basis: Y2Ru2O7 and Bi0.5Y1.5Ru2O7 are A2B2O7 ruthenates, and [ref 2] gives Y2Ru2O7 in Fd-3m at mp-20643 with two ICSD references, the pyrochlore setting. Bismuth substitution on the yttrium A site is a standard way of closing the gap in these ruthenate pyrochlores, and it does not change the framework.

dopant_roles.site: the eight-coordinate A site of the pyrochlore
dopant_roles.basis: Bismuth takes the yttrium A site at a quarter of it in Bi0.5Y1.5Ru2O7. It is isovalent as Bi3+, so it adds no carriers directly, but its 6s lone pair hybridises with the oxygen states and narrows the gap, turning an insulating ruthenate pyrochlore metallic as the bismuth content rises. It falls below the atomic-fraction cut only because there are eleven atoms in the formula.

note: The paper attached to this host is titled thermoelectric properties of CuO-added AgSbO3 ceramics, which contains neither yttrium nor ruthenium. AgSbO3 is itself a defect-pyrochlore-family oxide, so the yttrium ruthenate is most likely a comparison material measured in the same study rather than a mismatched record, but the link between composition and paper is indirect here and the paper cannot be used as evidence for the assignment; the composition and [ref 2] carry it instead.

basis: Sm2Sn2O7 is a stannate pyrochlore and [ref 2] gives it in Fd-3m at mp-2883, hull 0.000 with two ICSD references. The second composition dilutes it with 20 percent Yb2Zr2O7, and the paper is the same rare-earth zirconate-stannate solid solution study as the neodymium host, so both samples are one pyrochlore framework with mixed cation occupancy.

dopant_roles.site: the eight-coordinate A site of the pyrochlore
dopant_roles.basis: Ytterbium is the A cation of the Yb2Zr2O7 end member rather than a dilute impurity; the sample is a 20 to 80 solid solution of two pyrochlore-family oxides. The size and mass contrast it puts on the A site against samarium is the mechanism the paper uses to lower the thermal conductivity.

dopant_roles.site: the six-coordinate B site of the pyrochlore
dopant_roles.basis: Zirconium is the B cation of the same end member and takes the octahedral tin site. It also pushes the structure toward the pyrochlore-fluorite boundary, increasing cation antisite disorder.

note: Sister host to Nd-O-Sn at rank 2325, same paper and same reading. A thermal-barrier-coating study rather than a thermoelectric one, which is why only thermal conductivity is reported over 298 to 1272 K.

basis: SrTi0.7Ta0.3O3 and its strontium-deficient variant Sr0.85Ti0.7Ta0.3O3 are ABO3 perovskites: strontium on the A site, titanium and tantalum sharing the octahedral B site. The curator records both with an oxygen deficit as SrTi0.70Ta0.30O3-d, and the paper is on boosting thermoelectric performance by controlled defect chemistry engineering, which is the SrTiO3 perovskite family.
note: Three separate defects are at work and none of them is a dopant candidate in this host, so dopant_roles is empty. Tantalum at 30 percent of the B site is above the cut and is the donor: Ta5+ for Ti4+ adds one electron each, which is what makes the material n-type. The strontium deficiency in the 0.85 sample is an A-site vacancy population, and the curator's minus-delta is an oxygen deficiency; together they are the controlled defect chemistry of the title. Cubic Pm-3m is recorded because heavily substituted strontium titanate stays cubic over this window, well above the 105 K antiferrodistortive transition of pure SrTiO3, but no mp_id is given: [ref 2] offers only three computed Sr-Ta-Ti oxides at 3-2-6-21, 3-4-4-21 and 3-4-1-15, which are hexagonal and monoclinic phases at unrelated stoichiometries, not this solid solution.

basis: SrWO4 is a scheelite: isolated WO4 tetrahedra with eight-coordinate strontium between them, tetragonal I4_1/a. [ref 2] gives exactly that at mp-19163, hull 0.000 with ten ICSD references, the strongest primary in the chemistry, and the paper is on the growth and thermal properties of the SrWO4 single crystal, which is grown precisely because the scheelite structure makes a good Raman laser host.
note: The prototype was proposed from the Ba-O-W host and this is a second, independent use of it at the strontium member, which is worth noting for the v4 review: the AWO4 scheelites are a family in this dataset rather than a one-off. The measured window is narrow, 303 to 544 K, and scheelite SrWO4 has no transition in it; the four other [ref 2] entries are strontium-rich tungstates at 3-1-6, 2-1-5, 5-3-14 and 3-2-9, none of which matches 1:1:4.

basis: 80 mol percent ZrO2 with 10 each of Y2O3 and Ta2O5 is co-doped stabilised zirconia held in the cubic fluorite structure, and the paper is the same study of zirconia co-doped with trivalent and pentavalent oxides as the niobium host. Pairing Y3+ with Ta5+ compensates the charge so the cation disorder is high while the oxygen vacancy count stays low.
note: Sister host to Nb-O-Y-Zr at rank 2318, same paper and same reading; yttrium and tantalum are both above the five percent cut, so there is no dopant candidate and both are substitutional stabilisers on the zirconium site. Neither reference covers the host and no mp_id is recorded. At this total dopant level a tetragonal or an ordered zirconate phase can appear instead of the cubic solid solution, which is part of what the study measures, so the fluorite assignment is the intended structure rather than a confirmed single phase.

basis: TeO2 in its stable form is paratellurite, alpha-TeO2, the chiral tetragonal P4_12_12 framework of corner-sharing TeO4 trigonal bipyramids. [ref 2] gives it at mp-557 with ten ICSD references, the primary for the chemistry, and the second paper is on the temperature dependence of the thermal conductivity of tellurium dioxide, which is measured on paratellurite single crystals. The taxonomy had no tellurium oxide entry, so the prototype is proposed.

other_polymorphs.note: beta-TeO2, tellurite, orthorhombic Pbca. The mineral form, built from the same TeO4 units with a layered linkage. It is metastable with respect to paratellurite and is not produced by heating it, so it is not a thermal phase of these samples. No Materials Project entry is recorded for it from this chunk.

note: The two samples come from different worlds: one is a paratellurite single crystal measured for its phonon transport, the other is from a paper on the thermoelectric properties of a NaNbO3 composite, where TeO2 is the matrix. Both are the same oxide. The chief thing to get right is not filing this under rutile: paratellurite is derived from the rutile cell but the tellurium lone pair drops the coordination to four and makes the cell enantiomorphic, which the proposal states as its main discrimination.

basis: YTiO3 is an orthorhombic ABO3 perovskite, the ferromagnetic Mott insulator at the end of the RTiO3 series, and [ref 2] gives it in Pnma at mp-4355 with five ICSD references. The paper is on evidence for two electronic phases in Y1-xLaxTiO3 from thermoelectric measurements, which is that perovskite titanate series with lanthanum on the A site.
note: I disagree with [ref 1] here, and it is the textbook case the README warns about. TEDesignLab returns Y2Ti2O7 pyrochlore at mp-5373 with fifteen ICSD references, which is genuinely the best-attested yttrium titanate; but it is not this compound. The measured composition is YTiO3 at 1:1:3, the paper is about the Y1-xLaxTiO3 perovskite series, and [ref 2] carries that perovskite separately. The reference is describing which yttrium titanates exist, not which one was synthesised. YTiO3 is trivalent titanium and the pyrochlore is tetravalent, so they are not even the same oxidation state, and making YTiO3 requires reducing conditions the pyrochlore does not.

basis: Ca0.1Y0.9VO3 is an ABO3 perovskite with calcium substituting yttrium on the A site, and the second paper is on local moment formation and the metal-nonmetal transition in Ca1-xYxVO3, which is that series. [ref 2] gives YVO3 in Pnma at mp-18883, hull 0.000 with fourteen ICSD references, the strongest entry in the chemistry, and it is the orthorhombic perovskite.

dopant_roles.site: the twelve-coordinate A site
dopant_roles.basis: Divalent calcium on a trivalent yttrium site is hole doping: each substitution takes the vanadium from 3+ toward 4+, and at 10 percent it is the doping that drives YVO3 from a Mott insulator toward a metal. That transition is what the paper measures, so this is the compositional variable of the study rather than an impurity.

note: The first composition is recorded as VYO, which is not a formula; read alongside the second composition and the papers it is YVO3 with the stoichiometry lost, and the first paper is a Y-doped vanadate ceramics study. I have assigned the perovskite on that reading. Note that YVO3 does change symmetry inside this window, from the orthorhombic Pnma setting through a monoclinic P2_1/b phase between roughly 77 and 200 K driven by orbital ordering; both settings are tilted perovskites of the same prototype, so phases holds one entry and spans_transition stays false, but the space group recorded is the room-temperature one and would be wrong at the bottom of the window. [ref 2] also lists YVO4 with nine ICSD references, which is the zircon-type orthovanadate, a different compound the 1:1:3 composition excludes.

basis: SrOs4Sb12 is an RT4X12 filled skutterudite: an Os4Sb12 framework of corner-linked octahedra with strontium in the icosahedral void. The paper is on the roles of spin fluctuations and rattling in the magnetic and thermoelectric properties of the compound, and rattling is the signature of the filler atom in an oversized cage, which is the defining feature of this prototype rather than the unfilled one.
note: Strontium is a host element at one atom per seventeen, so there is no dopant candidate and dopant_roles is empty, but the strontium is the cage filler and stage 3 should treat it as such rather than as a substituent. Neither reference covers this host and no mp_id is recorded. The window is 11 to 286 K with the full span reaching 499 K; the compound is a superconductor below about 5 K, outside the measured range.

basis: La0.3Ce0.7Ru4P12 and La0.2Ce0.8Ru4P12 are RRu4P12 filled skutterudites with lanthanum and cerium sharing the cage site, and the paper title is the lanthanum doping effect in the thermoelectric properties of skutterudite compounds. The Ru4P12 framework with a full complement of one filler per formula unit is the filled prototype, not the binary one.

dopant_roles.site: the icosahedral 2a void of the Im-3 framework
dopant_roles.basis: Cerium is the majority filler, 0.7 to 0.8 of one atom per formula unit. CeRu4P12 is the parent compound and a narrow-gap semiconductor, and the cerium sits in the cage rather than on a framework site; it is below the five percent atomic cut only because there are seventeen atoms in the formula.

dopant_roles.site: the same icosahedral void
dopant_roles.basis: Lanthanum replaces part of the cerium in the cage. Both are trivalent so the substitution is nominally isoelectronic, but lanthanum has no f electron, so diluting the cerium is how the paper separates the f-electron contribution from the ordinary band transport. Together the two fillers total one atom per formula unit, so the cage is full.

note: The host name is misleading and worth flagging: it reads P-Ru because both fillers fall just under the five percent atomic cut, 4.1 percent for cerium and 1.8 for lanthanum, so the element that defines the compound has been routed out of the host key. The material is not a binary ruthenium phosphide. [ref 2] accordingly offers only binary Ru-P phases, P2Ru, PRu, PRu2, P4Ru and P3Ru, none of which is a skutterudite, and no mp_id is recorded. RuP3 itself, the unfilled binary skutterudite, does not appear in the reference list at all.
reference_disagreement: assigned sg [204], ICSD-backed references for this host report [58, 62, 2, 14]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: ThPS is a tetragonal MXY compound and [ref 2] gives it in P4/nmm at mp-12876 with two ICSD references, which is the PbFCl arrangement: a cation layer between two chemically distinct anion sheets, the phosphorus taking the position the halide holds in PbFCl. The taxonomy entry already names the actinide members UAsS, UAsSe and UPSe, and ThPS is the thorium phosphosulfide of that family; the paper reports its crystal growth, structure and electrical properties.
note: The discrimination that matters is against zrcusias_1111, which is the filled PbFCl type with a fourth site; ThPS has only three sites, so it is the unfilled parent. Of the other [ref 2] entries, Th(PS3)2 is a thiophosphate with molecular anions and the two P4/mmm phases sit at hull 1.7 and 3.5, which is far enough above the hull to be computational artefacts. Single crystals measured from 10 to 315 K, with no transition in that range.

basis: Both samples are U3P4, the eponymous 3:4 actinide pnictide of the Th3P4 type, cubic I-43d, and the paper is on giant anisotropic magnetoresistance and magnetothermopower in cubic 3:4 uranium pnictides. [ref 2] gives U3P4 I-43d at mp-787, hull 0.000.
note: [ref 2] ranks rocksalt UP (mp-2011, 16 ICSD) first for this chemistry. That describes the monophosphide, not the 3:4 composition measured here, so it is not a disagreement about U3P4. The U3P4 entry rests on 3 ICSD references, which the chunk convention flags as weak, but it matches the paper title. U3P4 orders ferromagnetically near 138 K, inside the 11-148 K window; that is a magnetic transition, not a structural one, so no phase split is recorded.

basis: The compositions are written as two-phase mixtures, (PbTe)0.5(PtTe2)0.5 and (PbTe)0.67(PtTe2)0.33, and the paper is titled for binary-phased nanoparticles. At these fractions both phases are substantial: rocksalt PbTe plus PtTe2, which is the CdI2-type layered ditelluride. Neither phase is a minor additive, so no single crystalline prototype is assigned.
note: Disagrees with [ref 2]. Its only entry is a ternary TePtPb in P2_13 at mp-1217437 with no ICSD reference. That is a computed single-phase ordering, not the two-phase nanocomposite the paper describes, so no mp_id is recorded. Both compositions share the same two-phase situation, so is_mixed is false; alt_prototype_ids name the two constituents for stage 2. Whether the second phase is PtTe2 or Pt metal plus Te should be checked in the paper.

basis: (PbTe)75(PbSnS2)25 with a small PbI2 addition, from a paper titled PbTe-PbSnS2 thermoelectric composites. The matrix is rocksalt PbTe and the second phase is PbSnS2, teallite, a layered orthorhombic GeS-type sulfide; at 25 per cent it is a genuine second phase, not a dopant.

dopant_roles.basis: Iodine is added as PbI2, the standard n-type donor for PbTe: I on the Te site gives one electron each. It enters the PbTe matrix rather than the sulfide.

note: Disagrees with [ref 2]. Its only line is SnTe(PbS)4 in R3m at mp-1218922, hull 0.038, with no ICSD reference: a computed single-phase ordering of a different stoichiometry. It does not describe a PbTe matrix with a teallite precipitate, so no mp_id is recorded. Stage 2 should resolve the PbTe matrix as rocksalt.

basis: (PbS)1.18(TiS2)2 is the stage-2 misfit layer compound: one rocksalt PbS bilayer alternating with two CdI2-type TiS2 layers, incommensurate along one in-plane axis. The second paper is titled for low-thermal-conductivity (MS)1+x(TiS2)2 misfit layer compounds with M = Pb, Bi, Sn.
note: Neither reference covers this host. The composite has two incommensurate subsystems and no single MP entry, so phases is left empty, as the README directs for this prototype. The first paper describes PbS nanoparticles embedded in TiS2; its sample may be a nanocomposite rather than the ordered misfit, and it should be checked if the two samples disagree.

basis: SrPd4Sn5Sb7 and SrPd4Sn6Sb6 are RT4X12 filled skutterudites: a Pd4(Sn,Sb)12 framework with strontium in the icosahedral cage. The paper is titled for the crystal structure and physical properties of the skutterudites SrPd4SnxSb12-x. Tin replaces part of the antimony so that the electron count balances with Pd in place of the usual Co/Fe group.
note: All four elements are host species, so there are no dopant candidates. Sn and Sb share the pnictogen framework site, but they are not isoelectronic: Sn has one electron fewer, and the Sn:Sb ratio is the charge-balancing variable. For that reason it is not recorded as a solid_solution_axis. Strontium is the cage filler. Neither reference covers the host, so no mp_id is recorded.

basis: The host holds two unrelated structures, one sample each. YbPd2Si2 is the ThCr2Si2-type 122 phase, and [ref 2] gives it in I4/mmm at mp-4633. Yb3Pd20Si6 is a cubic cage compound of the Cr23C6-derived type, and the paper is titled for the cage compounds RE3Pd20Si6. The 122 is taken as primary because it is ICSD-backed; the cage compound is recorded as the alternative under a newly proposed prototype.
note: The host splits on the Pd:Si ratio: 1:1 is the 122 and 10:3 is the cage compound. For stage 2, Yb3Pd20Si6 is in [ref 2] as Yb3(Si3Pd10)2 Fm-3m at mp-1207621, but with no ICSD reference. YbPd2Si2 is backed by 3 ICSD references, which is weak by the chunk convention. The other [ref 2] lines, YbSiPd2, YbSi3Pd5 and YbSiPd, are orthorhombic phases at other stoichiometries and not polymorphs of either composition. Both samples are measured only at low temperature.

basis: U3Pt3Sb4 is the Y3Au3Sb4-type 3-3-4 compound, a filled Th3P4 derivative in I-43d, and the uranium member of the Ce3Pt3Sb4 Kondo-insulator family. [ref 2] gives U3Sb4Pt3 in I-43d at mp-1188604, hull 0.000.
note: The reference rests on a single ICSD entry, which is weak by the chunk convention, but it agrees with the family assignment. The measurements are on polycrystals from 12 to 346 K.

basis: TiPtSn is an 18-electron XYZ half-Heusler, and the second paper is titled for p-type half-Heusler compounds HfPtSn and its relatives. [ref 2] gives TiSnPt in F-43m at mp-30847, hull 0.000.
note: One ICSD reference, which is weak by the chunk convention, but it agrees with the chemistry. The first paper is on ordered structures in MNiSn, and Pt compounds are included for comparison. No transition in the 219-1073 K window.

basis: ZrPtSn is an 18-electron half-Heusler of the same series as TiPtSn and HfPtSn, from the same two papers. [ref 2] gives ZrSnPt in F-43m at mp-961713, hull 0.000.
note: The MP entry has no ICSD reference, so the space group rests on the family assignment and the paper title rather than on a measured structure. No transition in the window.

basis: Rh3Ta is one of the Rh3X ultra-high-temperature L12 intermetallics, and the second paper is titled for the thermal conductivity and thermal expansion of L12 intermetallic compounds. [ref 2] gives TaRh3 in Pm-3m at mp-1020, hull 0.000.
note: TaRh2 in Pnma, also listed by [ref 2], is a different stoichiometry and not a polymorph. The L12 order is retained to well above the measured window.

basis: Rh3Ti comes from the same pair of papers on Rh3X L12 intermetallics for ultra-high-temperature use. [ref 2] gives TiRh3 in Pm-3m at mp-1152, hull 0.000, with 5 ICSD references.
note: [ref 2] lists equiatomic TiRh in P4/mmm first, with the same ICSD count as TiRh3. That is the tetragonal shape-memory-type 1:1 phase, not this composition. Ti3Rh5 and Ti2Rh are likewise other stoichiometries. Nothing in the Ti-Rh list contradicts L12 for Rh3Ti.

basis: Rh3V comes from the same two Rh3X L12 papers. [ref 2] gives VRh3 in Pm-3m at mp-1185, hull 0.008, with 3 ICSD references.
note: [ref 2] ranks V3Rh first, the A15 Pm-3n phase at the vanadium-rich end of the diagram. That is the inverse stoichiometry and not a statement about Rh3V. The VRh3 entry has 3 ICSD references and sits slightly above the hull at 0.008, which is weak by the chunk convention but consistent with the papers.

basis: YbRh2Zn20 is a cubic RT2X20 cage compound: ytterbium in a Frank-Kasper Zn16 polyhedron within the Zn-Rh framework, space group Fd-3m. Both papers are on the YbT2Zn20 heavy-fermion series, the second on its enhanced thermoelectric performance.

dopant_roles.site: the 8a Frank-Kasper cage of the Fd-3m framework
dopant_roles.basis: Ytterbium is one atom in 23, so it falls under the five per cent cut, but it is the stoichiometric guest that defines the compound and carries the heavy-fermion physics. It is not dilute doping, and stage 3 should not compute a doping level for it.

note: The host key is misleading: the defining element was routed out as a dopant candidate. [ref 2] offers only binary Zn-Rh phases plus U(Zn10Rh)2 in Fd-3m at mp-1198503. That is the uranium isotype of this compound, not YbRh2Zn20 itself, so it confirms the structure type but its mp_id is not borrowed.

basis: Rh3Zr comes from the same Rh3X L12 papers, and [ref 2] agrees without qualification: ZrRh3 in Pm-3m at mp-229, hull 0.000, 8 ICSD references and the top-ranked entry.
note: The best-attested of the four Rh3X hosts in this chunk. Zr3Rh5, ZrRh and Zr3Rh are other stoichiometries.

basis: SrRu4Sb12 is an RT4X12 filled skutterudite with strontium in the icosahedral void of the Ru4Sb12 framework. The paper is on the roles of spin fluctuations and rattling, the companion of SrOs4Sb12 in chunk 047. [ref 2] gives Sr(Sb3Ru)4 in Im-3 at mp-22775, hull 0.000.
note: One ICSD reference, which is weak by the chunk convention. Sr(SbRu)2 in I4/mmm is a different stoichiometry. Strontium is the cage filler, although it is a host element here.

basis: SmRuSn3 belongs to the RERuSn3 series named in the second paper, cubic Pm-3n phases of the Yb3Rh4Sn13 or Remeika type. The nominal 1-1-3 formula is the usual label for the 3-4-13 framework. The first paper is on this compound as a new valence-fluctuating system. Assigned as La-Ru-Sn was in chunk 036.
note: [ref 2] ranks Sm(Sn3Ru2)2 in I-42m first. That is SmRu4Sn6, the ceru4sn6_tetragonal phase at a different stoichiometry, so it is not a disagreement about this sample. The mp_id recorded, SmSn3Ru Pm-3n mp-1201411, matches the sample formula and has 1 ICSD reference. The 3-4-13 entry, Sm3Sn13Ru4 Pm-3n mp-1209813, has none. The La-Ru-Sn precedent preferred the 3-4-13 entry for stage 2; here only the 1-1-3 one is ICSD-backed, so it is kept, and stage 2 should choose deliberately between them.

basis: Ru2Sn3 and the tin-deficient Ru2Sn2.85 are the tin member of the Ru2X3 Nowotny chimney-ladder family (Ru2Si3, Ru2Ge3, Ru2Sn3): a Ru tetragonal sublattice with helical Sn chains threading it. Ru-Si was filed under this prototype in an earlier chunk. [ref 2] gives Sn3Ru2 in P-4c2 at mp-680677, hull 0.000, the tetragonal chimney-ladder cell.
note: Unlike MnSi1.75, this is a commensurate chimney ladder, so the prototype applies without the incommensurate caveat. The phase split is from memory and should be checked against the paper: I recall a tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion of Ru2Sn3 on cooling near 160 K, the analogue of the orthorhombic ground state of Ru2Si3. The low-temperature space group is left null rather than guessed. The chunk printed no crossing line because the taxonomy entry carries no transition. [ref 2] ranks Sn7Ru3 in Im-3m first; that is the Ir3Ge7-type phase at a different Sn:Ru ratio. The P-4c2 entry has 2 ICSD references, which is weak. The delta in Ru2Sn3-delta is tin non-stoichiometry on a host site, so there is no dopant candidate.

basis: Sb2S3 is stibnite itself, the exemplar of this prototype: orthorhombic Pnma with (Sb4S6)n ribbons. TEDesignLab gives Sb2S3 Pnma at mp-2809, hull 0.000, with 31 ICSD references, the strongest reference line in the chunk.

other_polymorphs.note: Sb2S3 in Pmn2_1, hull 0.001, 1 ICSD reference: a polar subgroup description of the same ribbon structure, not a distinct thermal phase.

note: The papers are on (Bi1-xSbx)2S3 and on bournonite PbCuSbS3; Sb2S3 appears in both as an end member or reference compound. The other [ref 2] lines, SbS, Sb17S27 and Sb11S18, are computed off-stoichiometric P1 or P-1 cells and are not polymorphs.

basis: US is uranium monosulfide, confirmed by the curator detail. It is rocksalt, and [ref 2] gives US in Fm-3m at mp-2423, hull 0.000, with 22 ICSD references as the top-ranked entry.
note: US is ferromagnetic below about 178 K, under the 273 K start of the window, so the whole measurement is paramagnetic. US2, U3S5, U2S3 and US3 are other stoichiometries.

basis: Yb3.6Sm0.4Sb3 is Yb4Sb3 with a tenth of the ytterbium replaced by samarium. Yb4Sb3 has the anti-Th3P4 structure, I-43d, and the first paper is on complex antimonides with that structure. Assigned as Bi-Sb-Yb was in chunk 041.
note: Samarium is 5.7 atomic per cent, so it counts as a host element and not as a dopant candidate. Its role is still worth carrying to stage 3. Yb in Yb4Sb3 is mixed-valent, mostly Yb2+, while Sm enters as Sm3+ on the same site. The substitution therefore adds electrons and is aliovalent, not isoelectronic, which is the point of the second paper. No reference covers the host, so no mp_id is recorded.

basis: Sn0.95Sb0.05 and Sn0.9Sb0.1 are tin with 5 and 10 per cent antimony, inside or at the edge of the terminal solid solution of Sb in body-centred tetragonal beta-Sn. Elemental tin was filed under beta_sn_a5 in an earlier chunk. The paper is on the role of chemical doping in thermoelectric performance.
note: Low confidence, for two reasons. First, antimony solubility in beta-Sn falls well below 10 per cent at room temperature, so Sn0.9Sb0.1 probably contains SnSb precipitates, the rocksalt-derived beta phase. That is why rocksalt is in alt_prototype_ids. Second, the 10-330 K window lies mostly below the 286 K alpha-beta tin equilibrium. Alloyed tin normally stays beta metastably, and Sb inhibits the transformation, so no phase split is recorded. Still, the paper may be about gray alpha-Sn, and that should be checked. Disagrees with [ref 2], which ranks SnSb in Fm-3m first: the 1:1 compound, not these Sn-rich compositions. No mp_id is recorded because MP has no dilute Sn(Sb) entry. Sb is a host element here, at 5 to 10 per cent, so it has no dopant role entry, but it substitutes for Sn and donates electrons.

basis: USb is the rocksalt uranium monopnictide, and the paper is on single-ion Kondo resistivity and thermoelectric power in USb antiferromagnets. [ref 2] gives USb in Fm-3m at mp-519 with 9 ICSD references as the top-ranked entry.
note: The MP entry sits at hull 0.076 while U3Sb4 and USb2 are on the hull. That is a DFT artefact for a 5f compound; the ICSD count shows USb is well established. The whole 10-21 K window lies deep in the antiferromagnetic state, with TN about 241 K. The magnetic order causes at most a slight lattice distortion and is not recorded as a phase change.

basis: The host holds two compounds of different structure, one sample each. Tl9SmTe6 is a Tl9BiTe6-type member of the Tl5Te3 family, in which Sm3+ replaces the Bi on the mixed site; the first paper is on hot-pressed Tl9LnTe6 for the whole lanthanide series. TlSmTe2 is an ordered ABX2 layered rocksalt derivative in R-3m, the TlLnTe2 series of the second paper.
note: The host splits on the Tl:Sm ratio, 9:1 against 1:1. For Tl9SmTe6, [ref 2] gives Sm(Tl3Te2)3 in I4/m at mp-1188848. That is an ordered subgroup of the I4/mcm Tl5Te3 cell, and it is recorded as the reference for that composition. For TlSmTe2, [ref 2] gives SmTlTe2 in R-3m at mp-999132, which stage 2 should use. TlSmTe2 is filed under alpha_nafeo2_layered rather than rocksalt, although the seed tl5te3 entry calls TlBiTe2 rocksalt-derived. The R-3m cell with cations ordered in alternating layers is exactly the alpha-NaFeO2 arrangement. That inconsistency with the seed should be settled at v4 review.

basis: Sm2ZnTe does not correspond to any compound I know of, and neither reference covers it. The two papers are a 1954 study of electron scattering in metal alloys and a study of thermoelectric properties of rare-earth alloys. They are the same pair behind the Sm-Zn host, whose SmZn sample is a well-defined CsCl-type compound. Most likely this string is a mis-parse of an alloy designation or a merged table row, not a real ternary phase.
note: The composition should be checked against the source tables before any structure is attached. If it proves to be a Sm-based dilute alloy, the host would move to the samarium metal entry. Measured on a rod, 220-374 K.

basis: SmZn is the equiatomic rare-earth zinc compound of the CsCl type, like the other RZn phases. [ref 2] gives SmZn in Pm-3m at mp-2165, hull 0.000.
note: [ref 2] lists five Sm-Zn phases with 1 to 2 ICSD references each, ordered by count rather than by relevance. Sm2Zn17 is listed first, but SmZn in Pm-3m is the one that matches the sample. All are weak by the chunk convention.

basis: Two different ternary tellurides, one sample each: Tl4ZrTe4, from a paper on the syntheses and crystal structures of two new thallium tellurides, and Tl2ZrTe3, from a paper on its structural, thermal and physical properties. Both are crystalline and were structurally characterised by the authors. Neither reference covers the host, and I cannot place either compound in an existing prototype with confidence.
note: tl4tis4_type was considered for Tl4ZrTe4 on the 4-1-4 stoichiometry and rejected. That entry is defined by isolated tetrahedral MX4 anions, while Zr4+ in a telluride is normally octahedral and the paper title calls both compounds new. Recording the stoichiometric analogue would assert a structure the paper does not report. No prototype was proposed, because I cannot state the structures from memory. Stage 2 should read both refinements from the papers and may then add one or two entries. is_mixed is true because the two compositions are distinct compounds.

basis: YbTe, with and without 5 per cent YbSb, from a paper on the YbTe-YbSb system. YbTe is a rocksalt divalent-ytterbium monochalcogenide, and [ref 2] gives YbTe in Fm-3m at mp-1779, hull 0.000, with 7 ICSD references as the top entry. YbSb is also rocksalt, so the pseudobinary is a single-structure series.

dopant_roles.basis: Sb on the Te site of the rocksalt anion sublattice, one per cent of all atoms and five per cent of the anion site. Sb3- has one more negative charge than Te2-, so with ytterbium held divalent each substitution adds a hole, or pushes Yb toward 3+. This is aliovalent doping, not isoelectronic alloying.

note: The Yb2Te3 and YbTe2 entries in [ref 2] are other stoichiometries at high hull energies and are not relevant.

basis: Elemental vanadium measured as a reference metal; the first paper is on the intrinsic thermoelectric power of the group VB metals.
